all.name: US state well-file archives (Texas RRC, NDIC, OCC, etc.) used to automate legacy-well review for CO2 storage and lithium brine permits
all.jurisdiction: USA: Texas, North Dakota, Oklahoma, Louisiana, Kansas, Colorado, Wyoming and others
all.legal_basis: State conservation rules require operators to file completion, plugging and log records, and these become public records. In Texas, W-2/G-1 completion reports and W-3 plugging reports are public under the Public Information Act. Under 16 TAC §3.16, logs can be held confidential only briefly on request. Other states have similar 6-month to 1-year 'tight hole' periods. The second driver is EPA's Class VI rule (40 CFR 146.84), which requires a CO2 storage applicant to find and evaluate every artificial penetration in the Area of Review. That turns these old public records into a mandatory input for every CCS permit.
all.dataset: Several million US wells going back about 100 years. The records are mostly scanned TIFF/PDF files: handwritten plugging reports, raster logs, cement tickets and inconsistent forms. A minority are digitized (RRC bulk downloads, NDIC subscription). Coordinates are often missing or wrong. DOE estimates there are 300k to 800k undocumented orphaned wells.
all.current_users: Enverus and S&P Global (IHS) resell digitized headers and logs. DOE NETL/CATALOG (a national lab consortium) uses ML and old maps to locate undocumented orphan wells. Academic groups work on this, as do large consultancies (SLB legacy-well screening methods, Katalyst data management for CCUS). I found no funded startup selling 'automated Class VI AoR legacy-well risk scoring' as a product.
all.ml_unlock: A multimodal model that reads every scanned well file inside a candidate storage footprint and outputs a per-penetration leakage-risk score. It would combine document understanding, raster-log digitization, cement and plug reconstruction and a probabilistic location fix, plus detection of undocumented wells from historical imagery. The output is a permit-ready AoR corrective-action plan with a priced remediation cost. The same engine prices plugging liabilities for acquirers and finds leak paths for hydrogen and brine projects.
all.buyer_and_market: Buyers are CCS developers. At the end of Q1 2026, 106 Class VI applications covering 387 wells were pending (Enverus), and Enverus forecasts capacity above 300 Mtpa by 2030. AoR work plus legacy-well remediation runs $ millions per project. Federal IIJA orphan-well funds ($4.7B) and state agencies are a second buyer, as are lithium-brine (Smackover) and hydrogen-storage developers. The direct software and services market is maybe $200-500M/yr. Path to larger: become the risk and underwriting layer, i.e. MRV, insurance, and the long-term liability transfer that states take on after closure.
all.why_now: Class VI primacy is moving to the states (Louisiana, Texas, West Virginia, Arizona). There is a permit backlog. 45Q credits survived the 2025 budget law, and multimodal LLMs can now read handwritten 1950s well reports cheaply. One risk: new CCS filings are slowing (only 3 in Q1 2026).
all.novelty_risk: Medium. Enverus and S&P own the digitized layer and could add this. DOE labs work on orphan-well location but do not sell it. The CCS market is policy-dependent and growth has slowed. There is no clear venture-backed incumbent for the scanned-file-to-risk-score workflow.

all.name: Alberta AER well and facility records plus Petrinex production data, used to price closure liability
all.jurisdiction: Canada: Alberta, extendable to Saskatchewan and BC, and to US state commissions
all.legal_basis: AER rules require licensees to report well, facility, abandonment and reclamation status, and these records are public. Production volumes reported through Petrinex are public. Directive 088 (Licensee Life-Cycle Management, effective Dec 2021) imposes mandatory annual closure-spend quotas: $750M industry-wide for 2026, with about $900M actually spent in 2024 against a $700M quota. Directive 011 sets standard closure-cost tables, which critics say are badly out of date.
all.dataset: About 450k+ wells with license, status, spud, abandonment and reclamation-certificate history. Monthly production from Petrinex. Licensee transfers and insolvencies (Orphan Well Association inventory). Reclamation-certificate records and site-assessment PDFs. Mostly structured, but site-level environmental and reclamation documents are messy.
all.current_users: AER's own LMR/LCA models. Academics and law clinics (ABlawg, Parkland Institute). Consultancies such as Validere and Integrated Environmental use parts of it. Banks and acquirers buy closure estimates from engineers. I found no ML startup selling independent per-site closure-cost and timing predictions.
all.ml_unlock: An independent per-well and per-licensee closure-liability model. It would predict true decommissioning and reclamation cost and the probability that the operator goes insolvent, trained on realized closure costs, reclamation outcomes and the history of licensee failures. The output is a credit and insurance product: surety pricing, M&A due diligence, lender covenants, and a 'Moody's for asset retirement obligations'.
all.buyer_and_market: Buyers are oil and gas acquirers and their lenders, surety and insurance companies, the AER and other regulators, and orphan-well funds. Alberta's official liability is C$36.6B. A leaked 2018 AER estimate put it at about C$260B including oil sands and pipelines. US unfunded P&A liability is estimated in the tens of billions or more. Selling analytics into this is a niche of maybe $100-300M/yr. The path to a large company is to take on risk, as an ARO insurer or bonding provider underwritten by the model.
all.why_now: Directive 088 quotas started in 2023 and are rising. The Redwater Supreme Court decision put closure obligations ahead of creditors. US states are tightening bonding and the federal BLM bonding rule came in 2024. The orphan inventory is at a record high (OWA remaining cost C$1.12B).
all.novelty_risk: Low to medium. Few tech players are in this. The risk is that the market is mostly an analytics niche unless the company becomes an insurer, which is a much heavier lift. It is also politically sensitive.

all.name: Released offshore national data repositories (UK NSTA NDR, Norway Diskos, Australia NOPIMS, Netherlands NLOG) used for CO2 and hydrogen storage and decommissioning
all.legal_basis: Each regime makes licensees deposit data, which is released after a fixed period. UK: the Energy Act 2016 and the NSTA Information and Samples Plan require deposit in the National Data Repository, with release after set periods (about 3 years for most well data, longer for interpreted data). Norway: Diskos keeps raw and composite well data confidential for 2 years and interpreted data for 5 (Sodir). Australia: the OPGGS Act and its regulations release basic data after about 2 years and interpretive data after about 5 via NOPIMS. Netherlands: the Mining Act releases data after 5 years on NLOG.
all.dataset: Tens of thousands of offshore wells (logs, core reports, completion and end-of-well reports, often scanned PDFs) and petabytes of 2D/3D seismic, mostly downloadable for free. Format quality is mixed: Australian and UK legacy reports are scanned, while recent data is digital LAS/DLIS/SEG-Y.
all.current_users: Heavily used. TGS/PGS and CGG resell processed versions. SLB, Halliburton (runs Diskos), Katalyst, Cognite and Earth Science Analytics (an ML company built on Diskos and NDR data). Shell, Equinor and Northern Lights run their own CCS screening, and PGS has published CO2-site ranking papers. Academic ML on Volve/FORCE datasets is common.
all.ml_unlock: A foundation model across the North Sea and NW Shelf that ranks saline aquifers and depleted fields for CO2 and hydrogen storage. It would predict injectivity, caprock integrity and legacy-well leak risk, and could also predict decommissioning scope and cost per well for operators facing obligations under the Petroleum Act 1998.
all.buyer_and_market: Buyers are CCS licence holders (UK carbon storage licensing rounds, Norway's Northern Lights and Smeaheia, Australian GHG acreage) and decommissioning operators. North Sea decommissioning is roughly £2B/yr. A CCS screening software market is likely below $200M/yr.
all.why_now: The UK Track-1/Track-2 clusters have reached FID. Norway awarded more CO2 licences and the EU NZIA mandates 50 Mt of storage by 2030. Australia has offshore GHG acreage releases.
all.novelty_risk: High. These are the best-curated and most-mined subsurface datasets in the world, with well-capitalized incumbents. A startup's ML edge is thin here.

all.name: Public injection volumes and earthquake catalogs (Texas RRC H-10, Oklahoma OCC, TexNet), used to forecast disposal capacity and induced seismicity
all.jurisdiction: USA: Texas and New Mexico (Permian Basin), Oklahoma
all.legal_basis: Under 16 TAC §3.9/§3.46, operators of disposal and injection wells must file annual and monthly injection volumes and pressures (Form H-10), which are public. RRC permitting rules (seismicity review, Seismic Response Areas) and the 2023-2025 rule changes on deep disposal pressure and area of review add public operator-response filings. TexNet publishes an open seismic catalog.
all.dataset: About 10k+ Permian disposal wells with monthly volumes and pressures over decades. Permit files (W-14, H-1) are often scanned PDFs. Earthquake catalogs and well-status records are also public. Operator pressure data quality is poor.
all.current_users: B3 Insight (produced-water data), Enverus, academics at UT BEG/TexNet and Stanford, and water-midstream companies (Aris, WaterBridge, NGL) internally. I found ML work only in academic posters, not as a product.
all.ml_unlock: A spatiotemporal model of reservoir pressure and seismic hazard across the Permian. It would predict which disposal zones will hit pressure limits, trigger regulatory curtailment or cause surface-flow events, and forecast remaining injection capacity per acre. That is effectively a valuation engine for the produced-water disposal system.
all.buyer_and_market: Buyers are water-midstream companies and E&Ps, which handle 20+ million barrels/day of produced water at roughly $0.5-1/bbl, a $5B+/yr disposal market. Also lenders and acquirers of water assets, and insurers. Software for this is a niche of maybe $50-150M/yr. Owning disposal and pore-space strategy based on the model is a bigger, capital-heavy play.
all.why_now: Disposal is constrained: the RRC tightened deep-disposal rules in 2025 and shallow-zone overpressure is causing blowouts and surface breakouts. Seismic Response Areas are expanding. Water M&A is very active.
all.novelty_risk: Medium. B3 Insight and Enverus are close to this. The buyer pool is concentrated, and the market may be too small on its own.

all.name: Oil and gas bottom-hole temperatures and logs reused for geothermal prospecting
all.jurisdiction: USA (Basin and Range, Texas, North Dakota), Canada (WCSB), Australia
all.legal_basis: The same state and provincial well-reporting rules make log headers (including bottom-hole temperature) and drilling records public after short tight-hole periods. USGS, SMU's Geothermal Lab and NREL compile them.
all.dataset: Millions of bottom-hole temperature readings from log headers (noisy, needing drilling-disturbance correction), raster logs and drilling records. Combined with public gravity, magnetotelluric and heat-flow data.
all.current_users: Crowded. Zanskar raised a $115M Series C in 2025 for AI-driven geothermal discovery and confirmed its Pumpernickel (Nevada) discovery by drilling. Fervo, Sage, Eavor, Quaise and Project InnerSpace (open heat maps) are also active, along with NREL/DOE play-fairway ML projects.
all.ml_unlock: Subsurface temperature and permeability prediction for hidden hydrothermal systems and enhanced/closed-loop geothermal siting.
all.buyer_and_market: The buyer is geothermal developers selling power to data centres and utilities. The market is large ($ billions of capex) but the winning model is to become the developer, which is what Zanskar did.
all.why_now: Data-centre demand for firm clean power, geothermal tax credits kept in the 2025 budget law, and bipartisan permitting support.
all.novelty_risk: Very high. Zanskar is the clear funded leader with this exact thesis, and it is a Terranox-like play in a different resource.

all.name: Produced-water and brine chemistry filings for lithium brine targeting (Smackover and others)
all.jurisdiction: USA (Arkansas, East Texas, North Dakota), Canada (Alberta)
all.legal_basis: State and provincial rules require operators to file water analyses with permits and production reports, and the USGS National Produced Waters Geochemical Database compiles them. Arkansas has a 2023-2025 brine-royalty process for lithium extraction, set by the Oil and Gas Commission.
all.dataset: Tens of thousands of brine analyses (often scanned lab sheets attached to well files), plus well logs and production data.
all.current_users: USGS has already published a machine-learning lithium map of the Smackover (2024). Developers include Standard Lithium/Equinor, Exxon (Saltwerx), Chevron, Albemarle, TerraVolta and Lanxess. Smaller ML-exploration startups exist.
all.ml_unlock: Basin-scale lithium (and bromine, iodine) grade-and-flow models to guide brine-unit leasing and DLE well placement.
all.buyer_and_market: Buyers are lithium-brine developers and royalty landowners. The opportunity is real but cyclical with lithium prices. Leasing is already dominated by majors.
all.why_now: The Arkansas royalty rate was set in 2025, the first commercial DLE plants are reaching FID, and Exxon and Chevron have entered.
all.novelty_risk: High. USGS already did the flagship ML map, the majors own the acreage, and it is too close to a Terranox clone.

all.name: Mandatory mining technical reports (NI 43-101 / JORC / SEC S-K 1300 TRS) linked to later actual results: a 'feasibility reality-check' model
all.jurisdiction: Canada (CSA NI 43-101, filed on SEDAR+), US (SEC Regulation S-K subpart 1300, Exhibit 96 TRS on EDGAR, mandatory since FY2021), Australia (ASX Listing Rules Ch.5 + JORC Code 2012), plus PERC/SAMREC equivalents
all.legal_basis: Securities law: any listed issuer disclosing mineral resources, reserves, PEA/PFS/FS economics must file a Qualified-Person-signed technical report. Filed at the same time as the disclosure, so there is no confidentiality lag. Later actual capex, production and costs then become public through mandatory MD&A, 10-K and 40-F filings.
all.dataset: Tens of thousands of long PDFs (often 200-600 pages) on SEDAR+, EDGAR and ASX announcements going back to 2001, many of them scanned or table-heavy. They hold resource tables, grade-tonnage, recoveries, capex/opex, mine plans and NPV/IRR assumptions. SEDAR+ has no bulk API (scraping only), EDGAR has full-text search and bulk access, and ASX is scrapable. The unexploited part is the panel that links each study's forecasts to the same project's actual results reported years later.
all.current_users: Text extraction and search is crowded. MineGPT (Francisca Lombard, launched Nov 2025) turns NI 43-101, S-K 1300 and JORC reports into comparable metrics. Kscope offers a SEDAR NI 43-101 MCP server. TMX Datalinx 'Prospector' and S&P Capital IQ Pro Metals & Mining carry project-level data. OreFox (Australia) works on reports. McKinsey, Hatch and AMC have done one-off statistical studies of overruns. No one appears to sell a calibrated, project-level predictive model of how far a study will miss.
all.ml_unlock: A 'haircut engine'. Given a new PFS/FS (or a 43-101 in a deal data room), it predicts the distribution of the realized capex overrun, the ramp-up shortfall, the recovery and grade-reconciliation miss, and the probability the project is ever built. It is trained on 20+ years of study-versus-actual outcomes, with features extracted by an LLM (QP firm, deposit type, altitude, study stage, contingency %, metallurgical test-work depth). McKinsey's figures give the scale of the problem: only about 1 in 5 projects meets feasibility-stage returns, and overruns average 40-55%.
all.buyer_and_market: Royalty and streaming companies (Franco-Nevada, Wheaton, Royal Gold, OR Royalties), project-finance banks and ECAs, mining PE (Appian, Orion), major-miner corporate development, and sell-side analysts. Mining capex is roughly $100B+/yr. McKinsey sizes better feasibility studies at about $100B of value over 2020-25. Realistic software/data revenue is a few hundred $M/yr: S&P/Capital IQ metals and Wood Mackenzie metals are each in the low hundreds of millions. A path to a large company would need to move into underwriting or principal investing, for example an AI-driven royalty/stream fund, which is where the real money is.
all.why_now: Since FY2021, S-K 1300 has put US filings into a standardized format comparable to NI 43-101. LLMs can now reliably parse 500-page scanned reports and their tables. The critical-minerals capex wave (lithium, copper, uranium) and a string of high-profile overrun/impairment write-downs make study risk a live question for financiers.
all.novelty_risk: Medium-high. The extraction layer is commoditizing fast (MineGPT, Kscope, S&P, and the miners' own LLM pilots), so the moat would have to be the outcome-linked label set plus the predictive calibration. Incumbents (S&P, WoodMac) already own structured project data and could build this. The market is niche unless it becomes a fund.

all.name: Tailings facility disclosures (GISTM Principle 15, Global Tailings Portal, Brazil ANM SIGBM stability declarations, Chile SERNAGEOMIN tailings registry)
all.jurisdiction: Global (ICMM members via GISTM; Investor Mining & Tailings Safety Initiative); Brazil (Law 12,334/2010 as amended by Law 14,066/2020 after Brumadinho, ANM resolutions); Chile (DS 248 tailings regulation, SERNAGEOMIN catastro)
all.legal_basis: After Brumadinho (2019), investors forced disclosure through the Church of England/PRI investor letter to about 700 companies, which produced the Global Tailings Portal of around 1,800+ facilities. GISTM (2020) requires facility-level public disclosure (Principle 15): by Aug 2023 for 'extreme/very high' consequence facilities and Aug 2025 for all others at ICMM members. Brazil's law requires semiannual dam stability condition declarations (DCE), risk and damage-potential classification, and emergency plans, published in ANM's SIGBM. Chile publishes a national registry of tailings deposits.
all.dataset: Structured fields cover facility location, height, volume, construction method (upstream/downstream/centerline), consequence class, and the date of the last independent review. The unstructured part is hundreds of GISTM conformance PDFs per company. Brazil's SIGBM holds about 900 mining dams with a time series of stability declarations and emergency levels. Together these give labels for a risk model that could be fused with InSAR/optical satellite deformation time series. Access: the Portal is downloadable, SIGBM is a public web portal, and company PDFs must be scraped.
all.current_users: GRID-Arendal and the University of Sydney (Portal hosts) and ESG raters (MSCI, Sustainalytics) for scoring. Satellite InSAR monitoring vendors (TRE Altamira/CLS, SkyGeo, Planet, 3vGeomatics, Detektia) sell to mine operators. Insurers (WTW, Marsh, Aon) underwrite with engineering surveys. Academic ML work exists (UJ digital twin + ML framework). I found no company that combines the disclosure corpus with remote sensing into a portfolio-scale, priced failure-probability product.
all.ml_unlock: A 'tailings catastrophe model', the RMS/Verisk equivalent for tailings dams. It scores the annual failure probability and downstream loss for every facility on earth (about 8,000+, including undisclosed ones found by satellite). Inputs are disclosed design and consequence fields, a regulator stability-declaration history, InSAR deformation, rainfall/seismic hazard, and LLM-read independent-review findings. It would price the insurance, investor and lender exposure that disclosure regimes surfaced but nobody quantifies.
all.buyer_and_market: Mining property and liability insurers and reinsurers, investors (Church of England-style stewardship coalitions, which hold trillions of dollars AUM), lenders, and regulators (ANM, SERNAGEOMIN). The global mining insurance premium pool is in the low single-digit $B. Catastrophe-modelling as a category is $1B+ (Verisk Extreme Event Solutions, Moody's RMS), but tailings is a sub-slice. Single events are huge: Vale's Brumadinho settlement was about $7B, Samarco/Mariana about $30B+. Data-product revenue is likely $50-300M, which is borderline for this brief.
all.why_now: GISTM full-disclosure deadlines passed in Aug 2025, so the corpus just became complete for ICMM members. Brazil's post-2020 regime produces a clean time-series label set. Cheap SAR constellations (ICEYE, Capella, NISAR launched 2025) make global deformation monitoring feasible. The mining insurance market is softening and competing on underwriting edge.
all.novelty_risk: Medium. InSAR monitoring is crowded at the single-site level, but a cross-portfolio model that prices risk from disclosures is not obviously built. The risk is that actual failure labels are rare (about 2-5 major failures/yr), so a calibrated probability model is hard. The total addressable market is likely too small unless it extends into general cat-modelling of industrial infrastructure.

all.name: Mine closure / reclamation financial assurance and closure plans (bond amounts vs. true liability)
all.jurisdiction: US (SMCRA 1977 for coal: state/OSMRE bonds; BLM 43 CFR 3809 hardrock bonds; state programs), Canada (provincial Mining Acts: Ontario closure plans, BC Mines Act reclamation security, Quebec Mining Act 100% closure guarantee), Australia (WA Mining Rehabilitation Fund, Qld Financial Provisioning Scheme), Chile (Ley 20.551 closure plans, SERNAGEOMIN), plus IFRS IAS 37 / ASC 410 asset-retirement-obligation disclosures in listed miners' financials
all.legal_basis: Mining laws require an approved closure/reclamation plan with a cost estimate and posted financial assurance. Many regulators publish the plans, bond amounts and release decisions; Chile publishes closure plans and Quebec publishes guarantees. Securities and accounting rules force listed miners to disclose ARO provisions.
all.dataset: Heterogeneous: thousands of closure plan PDFs with engineering cost estimates, bond registries (state permit databases, OSMRE e-AMLIS for abandoned mine lands, WA MRF levy data), and ARO notes in 10-Ks and annual reports. EPA ECHO NPDES discharge-monitoring reports add the water-treatment liability signal. Mostly scattered, scanned and inconsistent, which makes it a real ML extraction problem.
all.current_users: NGOs and journalists (DeSmog, Earthworks, Center for American Progress, McGraw Center) do manual tallies showing chronic under-bonding (e.g., US coal self-bonding). GAO-12-189R audited BLM hardrock bonds. Consultants (SRK, Kuipers & Associates) estimate closure costs per site. Surety companies underwrite manually. I found no AI startup aggregating this.
all.ml_unlock: An independent 'shadow closure liability' estimate for every permitted mine. The model predicts true closure and perpetual water-treatment cost from site attributes (disturbance area from satellite, acid-generation geology, pit lakes, discharge exceedances in DMRs), then flags the gap against posted bonds and booked AROs. Uses: surety pricing, regulators sizing bonds, and acquirers and short-sellers finding hidden liabilities.
all.buyer_and_market: Surety underwriters (Travelers, Liberty Mutual, Lexon, Argonaut and other reclamation-bond writers), state regulators, M&A acquirers, distressed and short investors, and banks. The surety premium pool for mine reclamation is likely a few hundred $M/yr in the US, and the global closure liability stock is $100B+. A data product alone is probably a <$200M niche. It is more interesting as an 'AI surety/MGA' that writes reclamation bonds with a better model, which could become large if extended to oil & gas well-plugging bonds and solar/wind decommissioning bonds, an adjacent and much bigger forced-assurance regime.
all.why_now: Coal bankruptcies and orphaned-site cleanups (the IIJA put $11B+ into AML/orphan wells) put under-bonding under political scrutiny. Many states are tightening bonding (ending self-bonding). LLMs make closure-plan PDFs parseable. Satellite disturbance mapping is cheap.
all.novelty_risk: Low crowding but also weak commercial pull. Regulators are slow buyers and sureties are conservative. Mining alone is too small, so the opportunity only becomes venture-scale as an MGA across all decommissioning bonds (mines, wells, renewables).

all.name: Payments-to-governments / extractive transparency reports (ESTMA, EU Accounting Directive Ch.10, UK Reports on Payments, SEC Rule 13q-1, EITI)
all.jurisdiction: Canada (Extractive Sector Transparency Measures Act 2015), EU/UK (Directive 2013/34/EU Ch.10; UK Reports on Payments to Governments Regs 2014), US (Dodd-Frank §1504 / SEC Rule 13q-1, first filings for fiscal years ending after Sept 30, 2023), global (EITI Standard, ~50+ countries)
all.legal_basis: Statute forces extractive companies (mining, oil & gas) to publish annual project-level payments to every government: royalties, taxes, fees, production entitlements and bonuses. There is no confidentiality period; filing is annual.
all.dataset: ESTMA reports from about 600+ entities per year (standardized Excel/PDF on NRCan), UK Companies House filings, EDGAR Form SD (XBRL-tagged under 13q-1), and EITI country reports plus the EITI summary-data API. Together they cover tens of thousands of project-country-year rows since 2015. The data is semi-structured but fragmented across registries, and project naming is inconsistent.
all.current_users: NGOs (Publish What You Pay, NRGI's resourceprojects.org aggregator, Oxfam), tax-justice researchers and the EITI secretariat. I found no evidence of commercial ML use.
all.ml_unlock: Reverse-engineering production volumes, realized prices and margins per asset from royalty payments (royalty rate × value is known per regime), giving a near-real-time 'asset-level P&L nowcast' for mines and oil fields worldwide, including private and state-owned operators. Secondary uses: transfer-pricing and under-declaration detection for tax authorities, and sovereign revenue forecasting.
all.buyer_and_market: Commodity traders and hedge funds (alternative data, a ~$2-3B/yr data-spend market overall), host-country tax authorities and development banks (IMF/World Bank), and sovereign credit analysts. A realistic slice is <$100M unless folded into a broader commodity-supply alt-data platform (where Kpler, Vortexa and Spire monetize at $100M+ ARR).
all.why_now: The US 13q-1 filings only began in 2024-25, adding the US majors with XBRL tagging. Ten years of ESTMA/EU data now make an actual panel. LLMs can reconcile messy project names across registries.
all.novelty_risk: Low crowding, but the signal is annual and lagged (filed 5-6 months after fiscal year-end), which makes it weak alt-data for traders. Most value goes to tax authorities, who are a slow and small buyer. It is a supporting dataset more than a company on its own.

all.name: MSHA Mine Data Retrieval System / Open Government Data (US mine inspections, violations, accidents, employment)
all.jurisdiction: United States (Federal Mine Safety and Health Act of 1977; 30 CFR Part 50 reporting)
all.legal_basis: Mine operators must report every accident, injury and illness (Part 50) and quarterly employment and hours. MSHA must inspect underground mines 4x/yr and surface mines 2x/yr. All inspections, citations, assessed penalties and contests are public through MSHA Open Government Data. There is no confidentiality period.
all.dataset: Clean bulk downloadable flat files covering about 13,000 active mines since 1983/2000: accidents with free-text narratives, about 100k+ violations/yr historically, inspections, assessments, operator/controller history, and quarterly hours. It is large and structured, and already easy to use.
all.current_users: Heavily mined by academics (NIOSH, University of Arizona, University of Kentucky and Marshall theses on ML leading-indicator classifiers), Apify scrapers, ai-analytics.org writeups, MSHA's own Pattern of Violations screening, and safety-software vendors (e.g., Intelex, Cority, Benchmark Gensuite) that do generic EHS work. It is not differentiated.
all.ml_unlock: Predicting serious or fatal accidents per mine per quarter for workers'-comp and liability pricing and for MSHA inspection targeting, plus NLP on accident narratives for root-cause clustering.
all.buyer_and_market: Workers' comp insurers writing mining risk, mine operators' safety departments and MSHA. US mining employs only about 200k people, so the comp premium pool is a few $B and the addressable data/software market is small (tens of $M).
all.why_now: Nothing specific. The data has been open for over 20 years.
all.novelty_risk: High. The data is well known, academically saturated and in a small market. Included only for completeness; not recommended.

all.name: Non-Saskatchewan statutory exploration open-file regimes (noted only: Terranox-clone territory)
all.jurisdiction: Western Australia (WAMEX), Queensland (GSQ Open Data Portal/QDEX), other Australian states, Quebec (SIGEOM/Examine GM reports), Ontario (OAFD), British Columbia (ARIS), Manitoba, Finland (GTK), Brazil (ANM), Chile (SERNAGEOMIN)
all.legal_basis: Tenure laws require annual exploration expenditure reports that become public after a confidentiality period. In WA (Mining Regulations 1981 r.96) the report is open-filed after a compulsory 5 years, extendable 5 years at a time on objection; about 1,600 reports were released in 2025 under the 'sunset clause'. Other Canadian provinces and Australian states run similar regimes with roughly 1-5 year confidentiality.
all.dataset: Hundreds of thousands of reports going back 50-100 years. WAMEX alone holds tens of thousands (many scanned, with drillhole and geochem appendices), and Quebec GM, Ontario OAFD and BC ARIS each hold tens of thousands. Bulk access varies: WAMEX and GSQ have open download, and GSQ ran an 'Industry Report Value Extraction' ML project with FrontierSI.
all.current_users: Crowded: KoBold Metals ($1B+ raised), Earth AI, OreFox, GoldSpot/ALS GoldSpot, VRIFY (DORA), Fleet Space ExoSphere, Minerva Intelligence, Geological Survey of Queensland/FrontierSI, plus Terranox itself in Saskatchewan.
all.ml_unlock: Prospectivity mapping and targeting, the same thesis as Terranox. Excluded as a winner per the brief.
all.buyer_and_market: Explorers and majors' exploration budgets, about $12-13B/yr global non-ferrous exploration spend.
all.why_now: Annual open-file releases keep growing, and LLM extraction from legacy scans now works.
all.novelty_risk: Very high, and per the brief it is a Terranox clone. Listed only for completeness and as an expansion map for Terranox.

all.name: Regulator dossier corpus: EMA Policy 0070 clinical reports + Health Canada PRCI + FDA approval packages/CRLs (an 'AI regulatory reviewer')
all.legal_basis: EMA Policy 0070 (proactive publication of the clinical reports filed with marketing-authorisation applications). It was suspended, then relaunched in September 2023 for new active substances and extended to all application types in 2024. Redacted reports are published within 120 days of the CHMP opinion. Health Canada's Public Release of Clinical Information rests on Food and Drugs Act s.21.1(3) and s.30(1.2)(d.1)/(d.2) plus Food and Drug Regulations / Medical Devices Regulations amendments in force since 2019. Once a regulatory decision is made, CTD Modules 2.5, 2.7 and 5 (full CSRs with section 16 appendices, but no CRFs) stop counting as confidential business information. FDA adds Drugs@FDA review packages (FDAAA) and, since July 2025, Complete Response Letters (see the separate candidate).
all.dataset: Several hundred thousand pages of redacted clinical overviews, clinical summaries and full clinical study reports: the documents sponsors actually submit, not journal papers. They are released per product as redacted PDFs, many of them image-based and needing OCR. Access is a free registered portal (EMA clinical data portal; clinical-information.canada.ca). There is no bulk API, and the terms of use restrict commercial use: Health Canada says the data are 'non-commercial use' and may not be used to support a marketing authorisation anywhere. EMA has similar registered-user terms. It can be paired with the regulator's side of each decision (EPARs, FDA medical/statistical reviews, CRLs).
all.current_users: Mostly academic meta-researchers (e.g., Herder at Dalhousie, Cochrane reviewers) and disclosure/anonymisation vendors (Privacy Analytics/IQVIA, Certara Synchrogenix, Real Life Sciences). AI medical-writing tools (Certara CoAuthor, Yseop, Weave Bio, Formation Bio, Instem) target CSR drafting but train on sponsors' own documents. I found nobody training on the cross-sponsor corpus of submissions paired with regulator decisions.
all.ml_unlock: A 'pre-submission FDA/EMA reviewer' model. It is trained on paired data (submitted dossier, then the regulator's questions, objections, review memos, approval or CRL), predicts which deficiencies a reviewer will raise, red-teams the dossier before filing, and auto-drafts Module 2 summaries in the style that passed. As far as I found, this is the only place where both the private submission and the regulator's judgement are public at scale.
all.buyer_and_market: Pharma/biotech regulatory affairs and medical writing groups, and CROs. Regulatory-affairs outsourcing is about $7-8B/yr and medical writing about $4-5B/yr (my rough analyst-report estimates, not verified this session). A CRL or major objection typically costs 6-18 months of delay, worth $100M+ for a blockbuster, so per-submission value is very high. There is a path to a large company if the product becomes the regulatory 'operating system'.
all.why_now: EMA fully relaunched Policy 0070 in 2023-24, Health Canada's portal has been building a back-catalogue since 2019, and FDA began publishing CRLs in 2025. LLMs can now read 1,000-page scanned CSRs. Regulators themselves are adopting AI reviewers (FDA's Elsa), so sponsors need to anticipate machine-assisted review.
all.novelty_risk: Medium. Medical-writing AI is getting crowded (Certara, Yseop, Weave, Formation Bio, plus Veeva, IQVIA and Medidata adding LLM features), but they use sponsor-internal data. The big blocker is legal: Health Canada's non-commercial clause, and EMA terms that bar use to support MAAs, may forbid training a commercial model or selling outputs based on these documents. Get a legal opinion before betting on it. The FDA documents (reviews, CRLs) have no such restriction.

all.name: FDA Complete Response Letters (CRLs): newly forced-public rejection letters
all.legal_basis: FDA's 'radical transparency' initiative under the Commissioner's discretionary disclosure authority. It published more than 200 CRLs on 10 July 2025 and 89 more on 4 September 2025, and committed to near-real-time publication with company names kept and confidential information redacted. That was paused in April 2026 after a citizen petition and resumed in July 2026. A rulemaking (RIN 0910-AJ16) to codify CRL release is targeted for a proposed rule around October 2026. Before this, sponsors could spin CRLs in press releases and FDA's actual reasons stayed confidential.
all.dataset: 458 CRL records in the openFDA API as of August 2026 (covering 2020-2024 plus new releases): a searchable table on open.fda.gov, bulk PDF zip download, and the api.fda.gov endpoint. Small (hundreds of letters) but extremely high signal: FDA's exact reasons for rejecting NDAs/BLAs (CMC, clinical, statistical, facility). Joinable with ClinicalTrials.gov results, Drugs@FDA reviews, 483s and PDUFA dates.
all.current_users: Law-firm and consultancy write-ups (DLA Piper, FDA Law Blog / Hyman Phelps, RAPS) and manual dashboards (prvwatch, Auria). An IntuitionLabs review of the dataset found nobody using it for ML or prediction. Biotech hedge funds very likely read it by hand.
all.ml_unlock: A PDUFA-outcome and CRL-reason predictor. Given a sponsor's public trial results, manufacturing site history (483s), modality and division, predict approval probability and the most likely deficiency category before the PDUFA date. It could also feed the regulatory-reviewer product above.
all.buyer_and_market: Biotech event-driven hedge funds and specialist investors (each PDUFA moves a stock 30-80%), plus sponsors and their regulatory consultants. Alt-data for healthcare investors is a few hundred million dollars a year. On its own this is closer to a $100-200M niche, so it works best as the wedge into a broader regulatory-intelligence or reviewer platform.
all.why_now: The regime is brand new (2025-26) and still changing. Real-time publication means a growing, timely label set, and the data did not exist publicly before July 2025.
all.novelty_risk: Low today, but the label set is tiny, a classifier on hundreds of examples is easy to copy, and the policy could be reversed (it was already paused once). Incumbents (Evaluate, Citeline/Norstella, BioMedTracker) will add CRL fields quickly. Weak as a standalone company.

all.name: FAERS + MAUDE + recalls as a mass-tort / product-liability early-warning system
all.legal_basis: 21 CFR 314.80/314.81 and 600.80 (mandatory manufacturer reporting of drug and biologic adverse events, giving FAERS). 21 CFR Part 803, Medical Device Reporting (mandatory manufacturer, importer and user-facility reports of device deaths, serious injuries and malfunctions, giving MAUDE). 21 CFR Part 806 (corrections and removals) and recall databases. FDA publishes all of it under FOIA/openFDA.
all.dataset: FAERS has more than 30M reports. MAUDE adds millions of device reports a year, with free-text event narratives and manufacturer narratives. Both have quarterly bulk downloads and openFDA APIs. The data is messy (duplicates, stimulated reporting, unstructured text), which suits LLM extraction. It can be joined with 510(k)/PMA files, recalls, PubMed and court dockets (PACER/JPML).
all.current_users: Pharmacovigilance incumbents (Oracle Argus/Empirica, ArisGlobal, IQVIA, Clarivate) run signal detection for manufacturers. Darrow ($35M raised) mines public documents for class-action leads, and Bloomberg Law reports AI entering mass-tort intake. Small MAUDE alerting tools (Innolitics MAUDE Alerts) and Basil Systems ($11.5M; 510(k)/MAUDE regulatory intelligence for medtech) exist. I found no dedicated model that forecasts which drug or device signal turns into an MDL, and when.
all.ml_unlock: A 'next mass tort' forecaster. Trained on historical FAERS/MAUDE signal trajectories that later became MDLs (talc, Roundup-adjacent, hernia mesh, CPAP foam, 3M earplugs, Zantac, GLP-1 gastroparesis, hair relaxers), it predicts 12-36 months ahead which products will become multi-billion-dollar liabilities and estimates claimant pools. Sold two-sided: to plaintiff firms and litigation funders (offense), and to manufacturers, product-liability insurers and short sellers (defense).
all.buyer_and_market: US mass torts produce settlements of tens of billions of dollars (3M earplugs about $6B, Bayer Roundup about $10B+, J&J talc multi-billion; from memory). The litigation-finance industry has roughly $15-20B AUM in the US. Plaintiff-firm advertising for mass torts is over $1B/yr in TV alone. Product-liability insurers and pharma/medtech general counsels are also buyers. A large company is credible if it becomes the underwriting layer for mass-tort finance.
all.why_now: LLMs can finally parse MAUDE/FAERS narratives at scale, mass-tort volume is at record highs (GLP-1 and hair-relaxer MDLs), and litigation funding is professionalizing and wants quantitative underwriting.
all.novelty_risk: Moderate. Darrow is adjacent and well funded, and lead-gen marketing firms already watch FDA signals by hand. Reputational and ethical optics (being seen as 'ambulance chasing') may limit enterprise buyers. Labels (which signals became MDLs) number only around 100, so the model needs careful design.

all.name: EU Clinical Trials Regulation / CTIS: member-state assessment reports and requests for information
all.legal_basis: Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 (Clinical Trials Regulation), Art. 81, and the EMA transparency rules. Every trial authorised in the EU since 31 January 2023 (with all legacy trials transitioned by January 2025) must go through CTIS. Protocols, investigator brochures (with deferrals), the member states' assessment reports, requests for information (RFIs) and sponsor responses, results summaries and lay summaries are published, subject to deferral rules revised in 2024.
all.dataset: Tens of thousands of trial applications, each with structured fields plus PDF documents: protocols, assessment conclusions, RFI letters raising regulator objections, results. Accessed through the CTIS public portal (euclinicaltrials.eu), which has search and download but a weak API, many PDFs, and 24 languages. It complements ClinicalTrials.gov (FDAAA 801 results mandate, 42 CFR Part 11).
all.current_users: Registry aggregators (Citeline/Norstella Trialtrove, GlobalData, Evaluate) ingest the structured fields. Certara and others give regulatory guidance. Trial probability-of-success ML is crowded: Intelligencia AI, Unlearn, Phesi, Medidata, ZS. I found no one mining the RFI and assessment-report text to predict regulator objections to trial designs.
all.ml_unlock: A 'trial application co-pilot' that predicts which member-state RFIs and objections a protocol will draw, and which design choices delay authorisation. It would be trained on RFI-and-response pairs across thousands of trials, and could extend to protocol optimisation (amendment avoidance; amendments cost about $0.5M each per Tufts CSDD, from memory).
all.buyer_and_market: Sponsors' clinical operations and regulatory teams, and CROs (CRO market around $80B; EU trial start-up is a known bottleneck). Software capture is perhaps a $300M-1B slice. A trial-design AI could plausibly reach a large company if it extends beyond the EU to FDA IND feedback.
all.why_now: CTIS became mandatory for all EU trials in 2025, so the back-catalogue of assessment and RFI text is only now complete. The 2024 transparency-rule revision changed what is published, and the EU's ACT EU programme pushes faster start-up.
all.novelty_risk: Medium-high for generic trial-success prediction (crowded). Lower for the RFI-prediction angle, but the 2024 revision cut publication of some documents (RFIs and assessment reports may now be published only at decision, or deferred). Check how much RFI text is actually public before building.

all.name: FDA inspection record: Form 483s, EIRs, warning letters, import alerts
all.legal_basis: FD&C Act s.704 (inspections; Form FDA 483 observations) and FOIA (5 USC 552) with the FDA electronic reading room's 'frequently requested' proactive posting. Warning letters are published by FDA policy. The FDA Data Dashboard publishes inspection classifications and citations.
all.dataset: Hundreds of thousands of inspection records with classifications, thousands of 483s and EIRs obtained by FOIA (scanned and redacted PDFs), and all warning letters and import alerts. Covers drug, device, food and API manufacturers worldwide, including India and China.
all.current_users: Crowded. Redica Systems ($30M Series B) is built exactly on 483/EIR/FOIA data with NLP for supplier-quality risk. FDAzilla/Govzilla, Clarivate Cortellis, and the FDA Data Dashboard itself also serve this market.
all.ml_unlock: Predicting which manufacturing sites will fail their next inspection or trigger a shortage, for supplier qualification and drug-shortage forecasting.
all.buyer_and_market: Pharma quality and supply-chain teams, generic-drug purchasers and GPOs. A few hundred million dollars a year in quality-intelligence software.
all.why_now: Drug shortages and onshoring policy, and FDA's expanded unannounced foreign inspections in 2025.
all.novelty_risk: High. Redica owns this niche, with a FOIA backlog moat. Not recommended.

all.name: CMS price transparency: hospital MRFs + Transparency in Coverage payer files
all.legal_basis: 45 CFR Part 180 (Hospital Price Transparency, effective 2021; tightened 2024-25) and the Transparency in Coverage final rule (26 CFR 54.9815-2715A, 29 CFR 2590.715-2715A, 45 CFR 147.212; payer in-network rate files since July 2022), reinforced by a February 2025 executive order. They force disclosure of privately negotiated payer-provider rates.
all.dataset: Petabyte-scale monthly JSON in-network rate files from every US payer, plus hospital standard-charge files. Huge, duplicative and messy, with many 'zombie rates'.
all.current_users: Crowded: Turquoise Health (Series A+ about $20M+, Adams Street), Serif Health, Trilliant Health, Clarify Health, Payerset, Gigasheet, H1, MultiPlan/Claritev, and large data firms (Komodo, Definitive Healthcare).
all.ml_unlock: Rate benchmarking, network design and negotiation-leverage prediction, and direct-contracting marketplaces.
all.buyer_and_market: Payers, providers, self-insured employers and TPAs. Healthcare price-intelligence is a several-hundred-million-dollar market, potentially larger via contracting marketplaces.
all.why_now: Enforcement tightening and the 2025 executive order.
all.novelty_risk: Very high; well mined by funded startups. Score low.

all.name: Orange Book / Paragraph IV certifications: generic-entry prediction
all.legal_basis: Hatch-Waxman Act (21 USC 355(j)(2)(A)(vii)(IV)): ANDA filers certify that listed patents are invalid or not infringed. FDA publishes the Orange Book patent and exclusivity listings and the Paragraph IV certification list. Litigation follows in district courts and at PTAB.
all.dataset: Orange Book bulk files (structured), FDA's Paragraph IV list, PACER dockets and PTAB decisions. The data is clean and structured, not messy.
all.current_users: Crowded: DrugPatentWatch (publishes ML/prediction content), IPD Analytics, Lex Machina, Evaluate, Clarivate, Unified Patents, and academic work (Stanford empirical studies).
all.ml_unlock: Predicting the date of generic or biosimilar entry and the outcome of each Paragraph IV suit, for revenue forecasting.
all.buyer_and_market: Pharma business development and forecasting, generic companies, PBMs and equity investors. Mid-hundreds of millions of dollars in competitive-intelligence spend.
all.why_now: The IRA and loss-of-exclusivity wave for 2025-2030 blockbusters.
all.novelty_risk: High. Structured data that incumbents have long used. Score low.

all.name: EMMA muni continuing disclosures (audited financials and event notices for about 50k issuers)
all.legal_basis: SEC Rule 15c2-12 bars underwriters from selling a muni bond unless the issuer commits to file annual financial information (audited financials, operating data) and event notices with the MSRB's EMMA system. These filings are public at once; there is no confidentiality period. MSRB rule G-32 covers primary-offering documents. MSRB said it received about 12k primary-market submissions (official statements) last year and still reviews each one by hand.
all.dataset: Official statements, ACFRs and audited financials, and event notices (defaults, draws on reserves, rating changes) for roughly 1M CUSIPs across about 50k issuers (hospitals, senior living, charter schools, small cities, conduit and project deals), plus trade-level prices on EMMA. Almost all of it is heterogeneous, often scanned PDF. MSRB says nearly half of its $45M budget goes to technology and data, and it is only now using supervised ML to normalize dates and tables. Documents can be downloaded one by one from EMMA; bulk access comes through MSRB paid data subscriptions. Filings are frequently late or incomplete, and lateness itself is a signal.
all.current_users: Bloomberg, ICE and S&P evaluated pricing; Moody's, S&P and Fitch ratings; Merritt Research and Lumesis/Solve (DIVER); BondView; Morgan Stanley's internal 'robot' that reads muni documents; Spline Data (AI muni pricing). Predictive-AI startups profiled by the Bond Buyer in June 2026: Munibonds.ai (claims 1-2 year default warning) and MuniPro (internal rating model for unrated deals; no product released yet). No dominant ML-native player.
all.ml_unlock: A machine 'shadow rating agency' and evaluated-pricing engine for the long tail: unrated and stale-rated munis, especially high-yield conduit deals (senior living, charter schools, hospitals, project finance), where nearly all defaults happen. It would read every ACFR and event notice, extract normalized financials, and output a probability of default, a fair spread and an early-warning feed. Later it could issue NRSRO-style ratings or underwrite muni bond insurance.
all.buyer_and_market: Muni SMAs and mutual funds, high-yield muni funds, broker-dealers, bond insurers and issuers. The US muni market is about $4T outstanding. Revenue pools to displace: the public-finance rating fees of Moody's, S&P and Fitch (on the order of $1B/yr, my estimate) and evaluated-pricing and data subscriptions (several hundred $M/yr, my estimate). A credible path to $100M+ ARR exists if the model becomes the de facto price and credit source for the unrated tail. The SMA and direct-indexing boom is creating many small accounts that need automated credit work.
all.why_now: LLMs can finally parse scanned, heterogeneous ACFR PDFs at scale. MSRB is itself experimenting with AI and pushing toward machine-readable data, and the Financial Data Transparency Act requires machine-readable muni financial data in the coming years, which would cut extraction costs. SMA growth and analyst shortages leave unrated credits uncovered.
all.novelty_risk: Moderate. Several small startups (Munibonds.ai, MuniPro, Spline, BondView) and the incumbents are circling, but none has won. The Financial Data Transparency Act could commoditize the extraction layer, so the moat must be the default and price model plus distribution, not parsing.

all.name: NAIC statutory statements: insurer Schedule D/BA holdings as a private-credit price and credit oracle
all.legal_basis: State insurance codes, based on the NAIC model laws, require every insurer to file a statutory annual statement with quarterly updates. The filings list each holding line by line: Schedule D bonds and stocks, Schedule BA other invested assets, NAIC designation, book and fair value, and acquisition date. They are public records once filed. Securities without public ratings, including private letter ratings, get NAIC SVO or filing-exempt designations. In 2025-26 the NAIC is reworking its private credit treatment: a new principles-based bond definition, SVO discretion over private letter ratings, and new task groups.
all.dataset: Holdings of about 800 life and several thousand P&C insurers, covering several trillion dollars of invested assets, increasingly private credit, private placements (PPN identifiers), ABF/CLO and BA-schedule funds. The same private instrument often appears across several insurers with different carrying values and designations, so the data contains repeated observations of otherwise unpriced assets. Access: per-company PDFs and some data from state departments; clean bulk data is sold by NAIC, S&P Capital IQ and AM Best. That access cost is part of the friction.
all.current_users: S&P Global Market Intelligence and AM Best (statutory data products), the NAIC itself (capital-markets special reports on private credit), rating agencies, Empirasign (private credit data blog), sell-side insurance analysts, and asset managers selling to insurers. I found no startup doing ML cross-sectional reconstruction of private-credit marks from these filings.
all.ml_unlock: An independent marking and shadow-rating engine for private credit. The model would match the same private instrument across insurers' filings (entity resolution on PPN/CUSIP and descriptions), treat the dispersion in their carrying values and designations as noisy labels, and combine them with issuer fundamentals to predict a fair value and default probability for each private loan or private placement. It would also flag insurers that over-mark or rating-shop. That is the 'Bloomberg BVAL for private credit', built from data no single party sees whole.
all.buyer_and_market: Buyers: insurers, LPs and pension funds holding private credit, regulators and the NAIC, reinsurers, banks lending NAV/back-leverage, and secondary buyers. Private credit is roughly $1.7-2T in AUM and growing (my estimate); life insurers are among the largest holders, and private credit now dominates life insurer bond portfolios (Insurance Business, 2026). Independent valuation and ratings for private assets is a multi-billion-dollar pool (Kroll Bond Rating, Houlihan valuation, Lincoln, Egan-Jones). There is a credible path to a large company if it becomes the trusted third-party mark.
all.why_now: Regulators (the NAIC, the Fed, the BIS) are publicly worried about private-credit valuation opacity and private letter rating inflation. The NAIC is rewriting its rules in 2025-26, and the 2026 S&P coverage describes regulators 'pulling back the curtain'. Demand for an independent mark is acute.
all.novelty_risk: Moderate-low for this exact angle. S&P, AM Best and KBRA have the data but sell it as raw tables and ratings, not as an ML cross-insurer marking oracle. Risks: entity resolution is hard, private instruments are partly anonymized, and the incumbents own the clean data feed.

all.name: Form 5500 / EFAST2: every private employer benefit plan's insurance contracts, broker commissions and fees
all.legal_basis: ERISA sections 103-104 require annual Form 5500 filings from employee benefit plans, including pension plans and welfare plans with 100+ participants or that are funded. Schedule A discloses insurance contracts, premiums and broker commissions; Schedule C discloses service-provider compensation; Schedule H discloses financials; large plans attach audited financial statements as PDFs. Filings are public and posted through EFAST2.
all.dataset: Structured bulk datasets for 1999-2025 (Form 5500, 5500-SF and schedules) on the DOL site, plus the filed PDFs and attachments (auditor reports, insurer contract details) through EFAST2 search. That is about 800k filings a year. The structured fields are clean, but the attachments are heterogeneous PDFs.
all.current_users: Judy Diamond Associates (ALM), BrightScope (ISS), FreeERISA, and Fiduciary Benchmarks. Newfront uses LLMs on 5500s internally for plan-design benchmarking. Many benefits-broker prospecting tools exist. ERISA plaintiff firms mine 401k fee data for excessive-fee lawsuits.
all.ml_unlock: A predictive engine for the roughly $1T+ employer health-benefits market (my estimate), not just prospecting. It would join Schedule A premiums, stop-loss contracts and broker commissions with Transparency-in-Coverage price files and company signals to predict each employer's renewal increase, the probability that it switches to self-funding or changes broker, and the fair stop-loss price. Stop-loss carriers and MGUs could quote without an RFP, and an AI-native broker could win accounts with predicted savings. A second use: auto-flag plans likely to face ERISA fiduciary litigation.
all.buyer_and_market: Benefits brokers and consultants (US benefits brokerage commissions about $30B+/yr, my estimate), stop-loss carriers and MGUs (US medical stop-loss premium about $30B+, my estimate), and plaintiff and defense ERISA firms. The large outcome is an AI-native broker or MGA, not a data tool.
all.why_now: Employer health costs are rising about 8-9% a year (my estimate). The CAA 2021 broker-compensation disclosure rules, fiduciary lawsuits over health plans (J&J, Wells Fargo cases) and Transparency-in-Coverage price data together make predictive benefits underwriting newly feasible.
all.novelty_risk: The data-access layer is crowded (Judy Diamond, BrightScope). The ML-underwriting and AI-broker angle is less crowded but competes with funded insurtechs (Newfront, Nayya, Curative-style plans). Thin moat on the data itself.

all.name: FERC Electric Quarterly Reports (EQR): every wholesale power contract and transaction
all.legal_basis: Federal Power Act section 205(c) requires public utilities, including power marketers, to file rates and contracts. FERC Order 2001 (2002) replaced tariff filings with quarterly EQRs listing contract terms and transaction-level sales. EQR data is public with no confidentiality period.
all.dataset: Quarterly filings since 2002 from about 2,000+ sellers: contract terms (counterparty, product, term, pricing basis) and transactions (volumes, prices, delivery points). Tens of GB, notoriously messy, with inconsistent naming and units. Bulk download from FERC; Catalyst Cooperative's open-source PUDL has cleaned parts of it.
all.current_users: Yes Energy (commercial EQR dataset), Catalyst Cooperative (PUDL, open data), S&P Global, Enverus, consultants, and FERC market surveillance. Moderately used for compliance and market research; little predictive ML.
all.ml_unlock: A price-discovery and valuation engine for bilateral power contracts and PPAs. It would infer fair prices and terms for any node, tenor and shape from the full history of disclosed bilateral deals, plus ISO prices and interconnection data. Hyperscalers, data-center developers and IPPs signing 24/7 clean-power PPAs, and lenders financing them, would use it.
all.buyer_and_market: Hyperscalers and data-center developers (tens of GW of new contracting), IPPs, utilities, and banks and tax-equity investors. The power-market analytics market is a few hundred $M (Yes Energy, Enverus power, LevelTen, about $100M+ each, my estimates). A path to large outcomes exists only if the product becomes the transaction layer, as LevelTen did for the PPA marketplace.
all.why_now: The AI data-center power rush has made bilateral power contracting the hottest procurement market in energy, and price opacity is a real pain point.
all.novelty_risk: Medium. Yes Energy and LevelTen (PPA price indices) are close incumbents, and Catalyst offers cleaned open data. The EQR's direct predictive value is limited because many PPA prices are hidden in ISO-settled or non-jurisdictional deals.

all.name: State PUC utility rate-case dockets (cost-of-service studies, testimony, orders)
all.jurisdiction: US (50 state public utility commissions), similar regimes in Canada, UK and Australia
all.legal_basis: State public-utility statutes require regulated utilities to justify rates in public, adjudicated proceedings. Rate-base, cost-of-service and capex plans, testimony, discovery responses and final orders go on public dockets. Narrow trade-secret redactions are possible.
all.dataset: Hundreds of rate cases a year and millions of pages of heterogeneous PDFs across 50 different e-filing systems, along with discovery and data responses. They hold utilities' internal capex plans, load forecasts and data-center load requests. Access is per state, with no bulk API.
all.current_users: S&P Global Regulatory Research Associates (the incumbent rate-case database), Insight Engine and AEE PowerSuite (docket search), consultancies (EY, WWT and HCL selling GenAI for preparing rate filings), and utility-equity analysts.
all.ml_unlock: A model that predicts each pending rate case's outcome (allowed ROE, revenue requirement granted, timing) and extracts every utility's disclosed load-growth and capex pipeline, including data-center interconnection requests, as a leading indicator. Buyers would be investors and grid-equipment suppliers. A secondary product: AI drafting of rate cases for utilities.
all.buyer_and_market: Utility-equity and credit investors, utilities (about $200B+/yr in capex, my estimate), equipment OEMs and data-center site selectors. Direct analytics spend is small (RRA-scale, under $100M, my estimate). Big outcomes need a pivot to grid-capex demand intelligence or to selling to utilities.
all.why_now: There is a record wave of rate cases driven by data-center load and wildfire and grid hardening, and dockets are the only public source of utilities' forward load and capex plans.
all.novelty_risk: Medium-high. S&P RRA owns the investor use case, and the Big 4 and integrators are selling GenAI filing preparation. The market is likely too small on its own, given the user's rejection threshold.

all.name: SERFF insurance rate/rule/form filings (insurers' pricing algorithms made public)
all.jurisdiction: US (state insurance departments via NAIC SERFF)
all.legal_basis: State prior-approval and file-and-use rating laws require P&C (and some life/health) insurers to file rates, rating rules, rating factors and actuarial support. Filings become public once approved or filed, with trade-secret redaction available in some states. This is the closest analogue to SMAD in this lane: proprietary pricing models forced into the open.
all.dataset: About 517,571 SERFF transactions in 2023 (500k+ a year). Packages contain rate tables (some scanned images), rating algorithms, GLM factors, actuarial memos and regulator objection letters. The largest homeowners filing package reached 346k pages in 2024. Access through SERFF Filing Access per state, with bulk access fragmented.
all.current_users: CROWDED. Akur8 Discover, after acquiring Matrisk in Jan 2026, extracts rate tables, rules and new variables for every P&C line and state on a biweekly refresh. Also: ZestyAI ZORRO Discover, Insuraviews, Quadrant Information Services, Perr&Knight, and Milliman (LLM filing analysis).
all.ml_unlock: Reconstruct every competitor's full rating engine to simulate any quote, and predict regulator objections and approval. This is already being productized.
all.buyer_and_market: P&C pricing actuaries and product teams at about 2,500 carriers. US P&C premium is about $900B+ (my estimate), but the filing-intelligence software market is likely $100-300M (my estimate).
all.why_now: LLM table extraction plus regulators' scrutiny of homeowners and auto rate hikes.
all.novelty_risk: High. Well-funded incumbents (Akur8, ZestyAI) shipped products in 2025-26. Listed as a calibration point; not recommended.

all.name: Chapter 11 bankruptcy dockets (schedules, claims registers, monthly operating reports)
all.legal_basis: 11 USC section 107 makes bankruptcy filings public. Section 521 and Rules 1007 and 2015 require debtors to file schedules of assets and liabilities, statements of financial affairs, and monthly operating reports. Claims agents publish claims registers.
all.dataset: Every Chapter 11 case: per-creditor claim amounts, MOR financials, DIP budgets, and plan valuations. Heterogeneous PDFs on PACER (paid per page) and on claims-agent sites (Kroll, Stretto, Epiq).
all.current_users: Octus (formerly Reorg), Debtwire, Chapter11Dockets, Bloomberg Law, V7 Labs agents, claims-trading desks (Cherokee, Xclaim marketplace), and Glade.ai (consumer bankruptcy prep).
all.ml_unlock: A recovery-prediction and claims-pricing engine: predict ultimate recovery per claim class, then make markets in and buy trade claims automatically. In effect, an AI-native claims-trading fund or marketplace.
all.buyer_and_market: Distressed funds and claims traders. Trade-claims market volume is several $B a year; Octus-type data is about $100-200M ARR (my estimates).
all.why_now: Elevated private-credit and middle-market default cycle in 2025-26.
all.novelty_risk: High. Octus, Debtwire and established claims traders dominate, and the data use case is well mined.

all.name: Large-load (data center) interconnection requests and large-load tariff dockets
all.jurisdiction: US: ERCOT/Texas PUC, PJM, MISO, SPP, Georgia, Arizona, Ohio, Virginia and other state PUCs
all.legal_basis: State PUCs require large-load tariffs and filings (for example the Ohio AEP data center tariff and Georgia PSC large-load rules). Texas SB 6 (2025) made ERCOT large-load interconnection reporting and forecasting a regulatory process. Utilities must file load forecasts, IRPs and large-load queue summaries in public dockets, and ERCOT publishes monthly large-load interconnection status reports. Utility filings have no confidentiality window, though customer names are often redacted.
all.dataset: ERCOT monthly large-load queue reports (about 233 GW of requests per press reports), utility IRP and load-forecast testimony, large-load tariff filings, substation and transmission CPCN applications, local zoning and water permits, and county tax abatements. These are heterogeneous PDFs and Excel files spread across 50 PUC e-filing systems, ISOs and counties. Bulk download needs scraping; there is no API.
all.current_users: Halcyon ($21M Series A, March 2026, led by Energize Capital) sells a Large Load Tariff Tracker and a New Substation Development Tracker. Wood Mackenzie, Enverus and Grid Strategies publish phantom-load analyses. Sell-side and hedge-fund analysts track this by hand. No one is known to sell a per-project probability that a load request is real.
all.ml_unlock: A phantom-load model: for every announced or queued data center load request, predict the probability it energizes, the MW and the date. It would fuse queue filings, duplicate requests across utilities (the same developer shopping several sites), land and permit records, turbine and transformer orders, and hyperscaler capex signals. This yields a bottom-up US load forecast that is better than utility IRPs.
all.buyer_and_market: IPPs and gas-turbine developers deciding where to build, utilities and ISOs doing capex planning, hyperscalers scouting rival sites, energy and utility equity investors, and transformer and turbine OEMs. The relevant decisions involve hundreds of billions of dollars a year in data center and grid capex. Plausible spend is $1-5B/yr on energy market intelligence (S&P, Wood Mackenzie and Enverus revenue pools); a winner could be a $1B+ data company.
all.why_now: Data center load requests (more than 200 GW in ERCOT alone) far exceed what is buildable, and Wood Mackenzie and others flag the gap as phantom demand. In 2025-26 regulators began forcing large-load disclosure and financial-commitment tariffs, which created a fresh, fast-growing filing corpus.
all.novelty_risk: Medium-high. Halcyon is directly adjacent and well funded; Enverus and Wood Mackenzie have the distribution. The defensible angle is the predictive per-project resolution model rather than aggregation, but incumbents could add it.

all.name: State PUC dockets (rate cases, IRPs, distribution system plans, discovery responses)
all.jurisdiction: US, all 50 state PUCs plus FERC eLibrary
all.legal_basis: Under state public utility acts, investor-owned utilities must justify rates in contested public proceedings. All pre-filed testimony, exhibits, data requests and responses, staff and intervenor testimony and orders are public record, apart from narrow confidential designations. FERC Form 1 is mandatory under 18 CFR 141.1. There is no confidentiality period.
all.dataset: Millions of PDFs in each state's e-filing system, some scanned, in heterogeneous formats, holding utility capex plans, asset age and condition data, load forecasts, vegetation and storm costs, cost of capital, and settlement terms. FERC Form 1 is structured XBRL since 2021.
all.current_users: Halcyon (AI search and trackers over all 50 PUCs, FERC and ISOs, including a Rate Case/Cost-of-Capital Tracker; $21M Series A in 2026). S&P Global Regulatory Research Associates (the incumbent rate case database), Docket Alarm, and consultancies (EY and HCLTech GenAI rate-case tools for utilities). Catalyst Cooperative (PUDL) cleans FERC Form 1 and EIA data openly.
all.ml_unlock: Predict rate case outcomes (authorized ROE, allowed capex, disallowances and timing) and, more valuably, extract a bottom-up national asset-condition and capex pipeline: which feeders, substations and transformers each utility plans to replace and when. That becomes a demand forecast for grid equipment and a regulatory-risk score for utility securities.
all.buyer_and_market: Utility equity and credit investors (US IOU market cap is about $1T), grid equipment OEMs and distributors (US T&D capex is about $100B+/yr), and utilities themselves for benchmarking. S&P RRA-type subscriptions are a niche of tens of millions of dollars; the equipment-demand angle is larger but unproven.
all.why_now: LLMs make the PDF corpus parseable at scale for the first time. Utility capex is at record highs (grid hardening and data center load), which raises the stakes of regulatory outcomes.
all.novelty_risk: High. Halcyon has raised money to do exactly the aggregation layer, and S&P owns the rate-case data incumbency. A newcomer would need a sharply different predictive product.

all.name: Distribution hosting capacity maps plus Distribution System Plan grid-needs filings
all.jurisdiction: US: California (ICA maps under CPUC D.17-09-026), New York, Minnesota, Illinois, New Jersey, Maryland, Massachusetts, Virginia (Dominion), Nevada and others; EU via Ember/RAP advocacy
all.legal_basis: State PUC orders require IOUs to publish feeder-level hosting capacity (integration capacity analysis) and grid-needs assessments in distribution planning proceedings. These are public by mandate and refreshed monthly or annually. Coverage is a patchwork: many states and all co-ops and municipal utilities publish nothing.
all.dataset: Feeder- and line-segment-level GIS layers (ArcGIS REST services) with load and DER hosting capacity in MW, feeder voltage, substation bank loading and planned upgrades, plus DSP PDFs. Large and machine-readable in leading states, absent elsewhere. NREL's Distribution Grid Atlas and the RAP/Ember 'Transparent Grids' work catalogue gaps.
all.current_users: Kevala (grid assessment platform for utilities and regulators), Pearl Street/Enverus Interconnect (injection capacity maps), Paces (developer siting), EV charging and BESS developers who scrape the maps by hand, and NREL research.
all.ml_unlock: Train on states that publish feeder-level hosting capacity and upgrade costs, then infer a national distribution grid model. Inputs would be OSM and satellite-detected lines and substations, EIA-861 utility stats and load proxies. The model would predict where 1-50 MW loads or batteries can connect without upgrades, and at what cost and wait, including in the roughly 60% of territory with no published map. Effectively a learned national grid digital twin.
all.buyer_and_market: EV fleet depot and truck charging developers, distributed BESS and community solar developers, edge data centers and industrial electrification sites. The direct siting-tool spend is probably a few hundred million dollars a year in the US, but it could be the wedge into a grid-data platform. On its own it risks being the $100-200M niche the founder rejected.
all.why_now: Load connections, not just generation, now face multi-year waits; EV depots, electrified industry and small data centers all need distribution capacity. More states are mandating maps, which grows the labelled training set.
all.novelty_risk: Medium. Kevala and Enverus/Pearl Street are adjacent, but no one is known to sell an inferred map for unmapped utilities. Ground truth outside mandated states is thin, so validation is hard.

all.name: California utility wildfire mitigation plans and Energy Safety data submissions
all.jurisdiction: US: California (OEIS/Energy Safety, CPUC); spreading to Oregon, Utah, Colorado, Washington and other Western states that now require WMPs
all.legal_basis: SB 901 (2018) and AB 1054 (2019) require California electrical corporations to file multi-year Wildfire Mitigation Plans with Energy Safety. These come with quarterly data reports including GIS asset data, ignition tracking, outages, PSPS events, vegetation and inspection findings, and risk-model documentation. They are public apart from limited critical-infrastructure redactions. Several other Western states adopted WMP statutes after 2020.
all.dataset: WMP filings (thousands of pages), quarterly data reports with spatial asset and ignition data, PSPS post-event reports, CPUC fire incident reports and intervenor critiques. A mix of structured GIS and large PDFs, accessible from the energysafety.ca.gov and CPUC document sites.
all.current_users: Technosylva (risk modeling used by California IOUs), Overstory ($43M Series B, Nov 2025, vegetation AI), AiDash, Rhizome (climate risk planning for utilities), Buzz Solutions, and utilities' in-house risk models. Insurance and cat modelers (Verisk, Moody's RMS) model wildfire, but focus less on utility-caused ignition liability.
all.ml_unlock: Train an asset-level utility ignition-probability model on California's mandated ignition and asset data, then transfer it to non-California utilities (PacifiCorp, Xcel, Hawaiian Electric-type exposures). It would price utility wildfire liability for insurers, reinsurers, credit investors and state wildfire funds, as an underwriting and securities product rather than a utility operations tool.
all.buyer_and_market: Utility liability insurers and reinsurers, utility bond and equity investors, and state wildfire funds (California's AB 1054 fund is $21B). Utility wildfire liabilities have run to tens of billions of dollars (PG&E, Hawaiian Electric, PacifiCorp, Xcel), so the underwriting decisions are large, but the buyer count is small.
all.why_now: Utilities beyond California face catastrophic liabilities (Maui, the Oregon PacifiCorp verdicts, Xcel's Smokehouse Creek fire), new state WMP mandates are creating more data, and insurers are pulling capacity.
all.novelty_risk: High on the utility-operations side, which is crowded (Overstory, Technosylva, AiDash, Buzz, Rhizome). The liability-underwriting angle is less crowded but the buyer pool is concentrated.

all.name: ISO/RTO interconnection queues and cluster/facilities study reports (FERC Order 2023)
all.jurisdiction: US: FERC-jurisdictional transmission providers (PJM, MISO, SPP, CAISO, NYISO, ISO-NE, and non-RTO utilities via OASIS); ERCOT GINR
all.legal_basis: FERC Order No. 2023/2023-A (2023-24) amended the pro forma LGIP. Transmission providers must post queue information, cluster study and facilities study results, and a public heatmap of available capacity. The rule imposes 150-day cluster study deadlines with penalties, and withdrawal penalties. Earlier orders (Order 845) already required posting of study results.
all.dataset: Queue spreadsheets (more than 2 TW active nationally) and thousands of study-report PDFs listing network upgrade costs per project and constraint, plus power-flow cases (often restricted under CEII), heatmaps and withdrawal histories. Mostly public, but PDFs are heterogeneous by ISO.
all.current_users: Very crowded. Pearl Street Technologies (SUGAR study automation and Interconnect maps; acquired by Enverus in 2025), Piq Energy ($5M seed for study automation), Paces, Interconnection.fyi, GridStatus, Nira Energy, LevelTen, Tyba, Berkeley Lab 'Queued Up', and the ISOs' own AI pilots (for example the Google/PJM work).
all.ml_unlock: A surrogate power-flow model that predicts the network upgrade cost, timeline and completion probability for any hypothetical project at any point of interconnection. It would learn from historical study PDFs plus withdrawal outcomes, and could extend to co-located large loads.
all.buyer_and_market: Renewable, storage and gas developers, plus tax-equity and M&A investors pricing queue positions. Software TAM is perhaps a few hundred million dollars a year.
all.why_now: Order 2023 cluster studies and data center demand make queue position extremely valuable, and the 2025-26 study cycles are producing new labelled outcomes.
all.novelty_risk: Very high. This is already well mined by funded startups and now by Enverus through the Pearl Street acquisition. Not recommended unless there is a sharp new angle.

all.name: PHMSA pipeline incident, annual and integrity data
all.jurisdiction: US (49 CFR Parts 191/195; PHMSA), with analogues at the Canadian Energy Regulator
all.legal_basis: Operators must file incident reports and annual reports under 49 CFR 191 and 195, covering mileage by material, decade, diameter, coating and cathodic protection, plus leaks repaired. The 2019 Gas Transmission 'Mega Rule' requires MAOP reconfirmation and record traceability; those records are filed with PHMSA but mostly not public. NPMS geometry is restricted to operators and officials.
all.dataset: About 600 incident reports per year since 1986 and operator-by-state annual reports, all in structured CSV/ZIP bulk downloads. They are clean but coarse: no segment-level in-line inspection data is public.
all.current_users: Academic ML papers (ASCE, AIChE, Springer, MDPI) predicting incident causes. Commercial integrity analytics: OneBridge (Cognitive Integrity Management), Dynamic Risk, Irth, Rosen, Baker Hughes and Entegra/OneSoft, which use private ILI data. Insurers use the data informally.
all.ml_unlock: An operator- and system-level pipeline failure and regulatory-risk score for acquirers, lenders and insurers, combining PHMSA filings with enforcement actions and satellite methane data. Limited by the lack of public segment-level data.
all.buyer_and_market: Pipeline insurers, midstream M&A and credit investors, and operators. Pipeline integrity management services are a multi-billion-dollar market, but owned by ILI vendors with private data; the public-data analytics niche is small.
all.why_now: New PHMSA rules (the gas gathering rule, the 2025 leak detection and repair rule) and EPA methane fees raise the value of risk scoring.
all.novelty_risk: Low-to-moderate crowding on public-data analytics, but the public data is too coarse to make anything revolutionary. Valuable data stays private.

all.name: Market transparency feeds: EPA CEMS hourly stack data, FERC EQR, EIA-860/923, EU REMIT inside-information (UMMs)
all.jurisdiction: US (Clean Air Act Part 75; FERC 18 CFR 35.10b; EIA statutory surveys) and EU (REMIT Regulation 1227/2011, amended 2024)
all.legal_basis: Part 75 requires hourly CEMS reporting of gross load and emissions per unit. FERC EQR requires every seller with market-based rates to report contracts and transactions quarterly. EIA forms are mandatory. REMIT Article 4 forces immediate public disclosure of plant outages and capacity changes as urgent market messages (UMMs), and ACER launched a central inside-information tool in 2025.
all.dataset: Large, structured and clean: CEMS hourly per unit since 1995, EQR transaction-level contract prices, EIA plant-level generation and fuel use, and EU-wide outage messages via ENTSO-E, the EEX transparency platform, Nord Pool and ACER.
all.current_users: Saturated: Enverus, Hitachi Velocity Suite, S&P, Wood Mackenzie/Genscape, Montel (REMIT data product), Kpler, Aurora, energy trading desks and quant hedge funds, plus open projects (Catalyst PUDL, GridStatus, Open Grid Emissions).
all.ml_unlock: Outage-aware price forecasting and plant dispatch and heat-rate inference for trading. These are well-established uses with incremental, not revolutionary, gains.
