all.buyer_and_market: Power and gas traders, utilities and IPPs. Energy trading analytics is a multi-billion-dollar market but highly contested.
all.why_now: Volatile power prices from data center load and renewables, plus the 2024 REMIT revision expanding disclosure.
all.novelty_risk: Very high. These are clean, structured feeds that every trading shop already ingests, with none of the 'messy and under-exploited' edge that makes SMAD-type data valuable.

all.name: California GeoTracker ESI plus other state remediation and LUST case files: a parcel-level subsurface contamination model
all.jurisdiction: US: California first, then NJ (SRP/NJ-GeoWeb), TX (TCEQ), FL (OCULUS), WA and other states with UST/LUST and voluntary cleanup files
all.legal_basis: In September 2004 the CA State Water Resources Control Board adopted Electronic Submittal of Information (ESI) regulations, which added data dictionaries to Title 27 CCR. Since Jan 1 2005, every responsible party in the UST, Site Cleanup, Military and Land Disposal programs must upload all groundwater lab data (EDF format), surveyed well locations, boring and well logs, depth-to-water readings and full PDF copies of every report. The data is public as soon as it is filed, with no confidentiality period. Other states require paper or PDF filing under their UST and RCRA corrective action rules, and those files are public records.
all.dataset: GeoTracker alone holds about 66,900 contaminated sites, about 925k field points, more than 230 million analytical results, about 2.6M documents and about 2.3M ESI submittals. It grows by about 400 regulator uploads a day. Access is a public portal with flat-file and ESI bulk downloads. The documents are mostly consultant-written PDF reports with boring logs, many of them scanned. Other states are messier and mostly PDF case files. Together this is a large, heterogeneous record of paid subsurface investigation, roughly the environmental counterpart of SMAD.
all.current_users: Incumbent data aggregators resell regulatory-database lookups for Phase I ESAs: LightBox/EDR and ERIS. They report that a parcel is near a listed site. They do not predict what is in the ground. AI players so far only summarize documents: V7 Go has an agent that extracts RECs from Phase I reports for environmental-impairment underwriters, and several consultancies use LLM report writers. Academic ML work exists on plume and fuel-leak prediction (for example the RMIT fuel-loss work and patents on forecasting contamination migration). I found no funded startup that trains a predictive model on the GeoTracker lab-data corpus.
all.ml_unlock: A 'subsurface contamination foundation model'. It would be trained on the 230M lab results, plus well logs and geology parsed out of the 2.6M PDFs, plus land-use history (Sanborn maps, aerials, business directories). For any parcel it would predict the probability and expected concentration of petroleum, chlorinated solvent, metals and PFAS contamination, along with plume extent and expected remediation cost and duration. Uses: (1) underwriting and pricing pollution legal liability insurance, (2) a risk score that comes before the Phase I and decides whether a $3-50k Phase II is needed, (3) predicting time to closure and cost to finish for cleanup-fund administrators and remediation buyers, (4) brownfield acquisition sourcing: finding sites where predicted cleanup cost is far below the market discount. The Terranox playbook, with contamination in place of uranium.
all.buyer_and_market: Environmental and pollution liability insurers (AIG, Chubb, Beazley, Sompo, Ironshore). US environmental insurance premiums are commonly estimated at about $4-5B a year (my estimate; not verified this run). CRE lenders and SBA/agency lenders, which require ASTM E1527-21 Phase I ESAs on most commercial loans: a market of several hundred thousand reports a year at about $2-4k each, roughly $1B. The US remediation services market is usually quoted at about $30B+ a year. State UST cleanup funds: GeoTracker itself is 60% funded by the CA UST Cleanup Fund. A path to a large company: become the 'Verisk of subsurface risk', priced per parcel across every commercial real estate transaction and insurance policy.
all.why_now: Current VLMs can finally turn decades of scanned boring logs and consultant reports into structured data. PFAS is creating a new wave of contamination liability that insurers cannot price. ASTM E1527-21 now formally expects PFAS to be considered. California has 20 years of mandated machine-readable lab data that nobody has modeled at scale.
all.novelty_risk: Moderate-low. LightBox/EDR (PE-owned) and ERIS own distribution and could build this, but their product is a database lookup, not a prediction. Document-AI startups (V7 and others) only extract and summarize. A risk: the model is California-heavy at first, and other states need heavy PDF ingestion, though that is also the moat. The Phase I market by itself is mid-size, so the big outcome depends on insurance and remediation-economics buyers.

all.name: PFAS forced-disclosure stack (TSCA 8(a)(7) one-time PFAS report, UCMR 5 drinking-water results, state PFAS-in-products filings): PFAS liability attribution
all.jurisdiction: US federal (EPA) plus states (Minnesota Amara's Law, Maine PFAS-in-products)
all.legal_basis: TSCA section 8(a)(7), added by the FY2020 NDAA, requires every entity that has manufactured or imported PFAS, or PFAS-containing articles, since Jan 1 2011 to report uses, volumes, byproducts, exposure and disposal. EPA has delayed it repeatedly. Under the 2026 delay rule the submission period opens Jan 31 2027, or 60 days after a forthcoming final rule on scope, whichever comes first. The window is 6 months, or 12 months for small article importers. Non-CBI data is expected to be published, but how much of it is CBI is uncertain. Under SDWA, UCMR 5 requires utilities to monitor 29 PFAS, with results posted publicly by EPA. Minnesota and Maine require manufacturers to disclose PFAS in products.
all.dataset: UCMR 5: national PFAS occurrence for public water systems, bulk-downloadable now. TSCA 8(a)(7): coming in 2027-28 through CDX/ChemView; a first-ever census of PFAS manufacturers, importers and uses back to 2011, likely tens of thousands of submitters with heterogeneous free-text use descriptions. State product registries: messy portal data. Can be joined with TRI PFAS release data and GeoTracker or state PFAS sampling.
all.current_users: Moody's (through Praedicat) models PFAS as a top emerging casualty risk from scientific literature. Milliman publishes PFAS reserving analyses. Plaintiff firms and the EWG map contamination. Environmental consultancies (Jacobs, Arcadis) do source tracing site by site. I found no startup doing statistical source attribution that links contamination to specific manufacturers and users at scale.
all.ml_unlock: A PFAS liability graph. The model would link each detected contamination site (drinking water, groundwater) to probable upstream sources, using disclosed PFAS uses and volumes, facility locations, hydrogeology and chemical fingerprints (isomer and chain-length profiles). It would then estimate each company's expected PFAS liability. In effect, an actuarial and litigation engine for the largest toxic-tort wave since asbestos.
all.buyer_and_market: Casualty insurers and reinsurers setting reserves and exclusions, litigation funders and plaintiff and defense firms, water utilities pursuing cost recovery, and M&A diligence teams. The 3M settlement with water utilities was $10.3B+ and DuPont/Chemours/Corteva about $1.2B. Total PFAS liability estimates run to hundreds of billions (widely reported; not verified this run). Analytics sold into this could be a $100M+ ARR business, but the buyer set is concentrated.
all.why_now: The TSCA dataset lands in 2027-28, so a startup founded now could be ready on day one. EPA PFAS drinking-water MCLs and CERCLA hazardous-substance designations create legally actionable liability.
all.novelty_risk: Moderate. Moody's/Praedicat and Verisk are the obvious incumbents, though they model at the literature level, not the site level. Several regulatory risks: EPA keeps narrowing scope and delaying (exemptions for articles, R&D and de minimis amounts were proposed in Nov 2025), CBI claims may gut the dataset, and the 2025-26 rollback of the drinking-water MCLs adds uncertainty.

all.name: CCR Rule coal-ash groundwater monitoring disclosures
all.legal_basis: 40 CFR 257.107 (2015 CCR Rule) requires every coal-ash landfill and impoundment owner to post its annual groundwater monitoring and corrective action reports, location restriction demonstrations, structural stability assessments and closure plans on a 'CCR Rule Compliance Data and Information' public website, kept for at least 5 years. The 2024 legacy-impoundment rule extends this to inactive sites.
all.dataset: About 700+ units at about 300 plants. Each utility posts its own PDFs (for example Luminant, Dominion, Basin Electric, Black Hills), mostly tables of groundwater results inside PDFs. There is no central database: Earthjustice compiled one by hand. Messy and under-exploited.
all.current_users: Earthjustice and the Environmental Integrity Project (advocacy mapping), utility engineering consultants (Geosyntec, AECOM), and academics. No ML startup found.
all.ml_unlock: Predicting plume growth and corrective-action and closure cost for each ash unit, and choosing between closure-in-place and excavation. Could also serve as a benchmark for utility asset-retirement-obligation reserves.
all.buyer_and_market: Utilities and their engineering firms, rating agencies and utility investors (ARO exposure), and state PUC intervenors. Coal-ash closure liabilities total tens of billions of dollars, but this is a one-time clean-up wave with few buyers. It looks like a niche consulting tool, probably under the $100-200M/yr bar.
all.why_now: Legacy-impoundment rule deadlines in 2026-2028 and coal plant retirements are driving closure spending.
all.novelty_risk: Low crowding, but the market is too small and shrinking as coal retires. It is a good feature for candidate 1, not a company.
sources: https://www.luminant.com/documents/ccr/Texas/Martin-Lake/2019/2019-Martin Lake-SWR 31277-2019 Annual Groundwater Monitoring and Corrective Action Report-Ash Pond Area.pdf

all.name: EU REACH registration dossiers (ECHA dissemination / IUCLID)
all.legal_basis: REACH Regulation (EC) 1907/2006, under the 'no data, no market' rule, requires registrants of substances above 1 t/yr to submit dossiers of physchem, tox and ecotox studies. Non-confidential study summaries are disseminated publicly under Art. 119. Industry has spent billions of euros on the underlying animal and in-vitro studies.
all.dataset: About 23k+ substances and about 100k+ registration dossiers containing robust study summaries in IUCLID structured format. Available through the ECHA dissemination portal and ECHA CHEM. Bulk reuse has licence restrictions. Some fields are messy (free-text study results, read-across justifications).
all.current_users: Already well mined. Luechtefeld and Hartung (Johns Hopkins / ToxTrack) built RASAR read-across models on the REACH data (Toxicological Sciences 2018), commercialized through UL. Academic QSAR groups, the OECD QSAR Toolbox and EPA CompTox also use it. Many regulatory consultancies use it for read-across.
all.ml_unlock: Predictive toxicology that replaces animal tests for new registrations or the coming REACH revision, and safe-by-design screening of chemicals.
all.buyer_and_market: Chemical companies and registrants, consumer goods makers, and regulatory consultancies. The in-silico tox market is a few hundred million dollars, and competitive.
all.why_now: The REACH revision (polymer registration, MAF) and the EU and US push away from animal testing.
all.novelty_risk: High crowding. The headline ML idea has been done and commercialized since 2018. Score low.

all.name: EPA ECHO / NPDES Discharge Monitoring Reports and enforcement history
all.legal_basis: Under the Clean Water Act section 402 and 40 CFR 122.41(l)(4), NPDES permittees must self-report effluent monitoring on DMRs. The NPDES eRule (2015) requires electronic reporting, and EPA publishes the data through ECHO along with CAA and RCRA inspection and enforcement histories.
all.dataset: Monthly DMRs for about 300k+ permittees, plus inspections, violations and penalties across CWA, CAA and RCRA. Clean, bulk-downloadable structured data from ECHO.
all.current_users: Academic and government ML for inspection targeting: Hino, Benami and Brooks (Nature Sustainability 2018) and the UChicago Energy & Environment Lab EPA-targeting project. NGOs (EIP) and ESG data vendors use ECHO violations as signals. Sales-intelligence tools also scrape ECHO.
all.ml_unlock: Predicting permit violations, or forecasting facility-level compliance risk for lenders, insurers and ESG investors. Also predicting which facilities will be inspected or face enforcement.
all.buyer_and_market: Mainly regulators, which buy little and slowly, plus ESG data vendors. Commercial value is modest and the data is too clean and too available to be a moat.
all.why_now: Little urgency: federal enforcement is declining in 2025-26, which lowers demand.
all.novelty_risk: Clean public data, already studied in academia, low willingness to pay. Score low.

all.name: NEPA EIS/EA corpus
all.legal_basis: NEPA (42 USC 4332) and agency NEPA procedures require EISs and EAs for major federal actions. These are published (through the EPA EIS database and agency sites), and they contain extensive privately funded environmental baseline studies (wetlands, species, cultural resources, hydrology).
all.dataset: Tens of thousands of EIS and EA PDFs since 1970, plus comment-response records. PNNL has built the NEPATEC corpus.
all.current_users: PNNL PolicyAI and PermitAI (DOE-funded, partnered with OpenAI), CEQ permitting-tech efforts, and permitting and siting startups (Transect, Paces and others).
all.ml_unlock: Predicting time and cost to permit and litigation risk for infrastructure projects. Generating draft EIS sections automatically.
all.buyer_and_market: Developers of energy, transmission and data-center projects, and federal agencies. Permitting is a real pain point, but the government is building the tooling and giving it away.
all.why_now: Permitting-reform momentum and the Seven County (2025) Supreme Court ruling. But both shrink the scope of NEPA analysis.
all.novelty_risk: Crowded: national labs plus several funded startups. The government is supplying the tools. Score low.

all.name: GHGRP / EU Methane Regulation (2024/1787) MRV reporting
all.legal_basis: Under GHGRP, facilities above 25kt CO2e must report emissions annually, and the data is public through FLIGHT. The EU Methane Regulation 2024/1787 requires operators to measure and report source-level methane, and from 2027 requires importers to show MRV equivalence.
all.dataset: Structured facility-level emissions data (GHGRP). EU operator reports are starting now. Both are often paired with satellite data.
all.current_users: Very crowded: Kayrros, GHGSat, Carbon Mapper, MethaneSAT (ended 2025), Highwood Emissions, Project Canary, Bridger Photonics, and others.
all.ml_unlock: Reconciling reported emissions against measured ones, and certifying importer gas as low-methane.
all.buyer_and_market: LNG importers and buyers in the EU, and oil and gas operators. Large market, but saturated with funded players.
all.why_now: EU import requirements phase in from 2027-2030. Meanwhile the US federal GHGRP is being rolled back in 2025-26.
all.novelty_risk: Very crowded. Score low.

all.name: Statutory borehole and well-log archives as a pre-drilled ground model (BGS NGDC + US/Canada water-well logs + NZ Geotechnical Database + state DOT boring logs)
all.jurisdiction: UK (GB), plus US states, Canadian provinces and New Zealand as expansion
all.legal_basis: UK: Mining Industry Act 1926 s.23 says anyone sinking a borehole deeper than 30 m to search for or extract minerals must notify BGS beforehand and deposit the drilling records when finished (NI: Mineral Development Act (NI) 1969). Water-well notification and records go to BGS's National Well Record Archive under the Water Resources Act 1991 (section numbers from memory, not checked). Canada: every province legally requires drillers to submit well logs (BC was last, around 2016). US: varies by state; California holds about 1M well completion reports. NZ: the NZGD was created after the Christchurch earthquakes and councils push consultants to upload site-investigation data. Some commercial mineral logs at BGS can be held confidential; the length of that period is not confirmed.
all.dataset: BGS Onshore GeoIndex: more than 1.8 million borehole records, many with scanned hand-written or typed logs that can be viewed free per borehole, plus water-well records in the NWRA. A digital deposit portal handles new submissions. US/Canada: millions of driller logs, many scanned PDFs (e.g. Mississippi DEQ 'DrillScans' PDFs per county) or semi-structured databases; coverage is 5-100% depending on state. NZGD: tens of thousands of CPTs and boreholes in structured form (exact count not checked). Data is heterogeneous: lithology free text, SPT blow counts, water strikes, depth to rockhead. Coverage and quality are messy and hard to exploit, which is the opportunity.
all.current_users: Academic ML papers (3D stratigraphy, generative AI for subsurface models from boreholes). BGS's own 3D geological models (GeoSure, etc.). Groundsure/Landmark sell desk-study reports that cite BGS data. GroundedAI (Vancouver, $2M, July 2026) does AI for tunnelling ground risk. Terra AI ($20M Series A, Khosla) does AI subsurface modelling, mainly for mining/energy (focus not verified). I found no funded company building a national-scale 'predicted site investigation' product from statutory borehole archives.
all.ml_unlock: A 'virtual site investigation' foundation model: OCR and LLM-parse millions of scanned logs into a standard schema, then train a spatial model (borehole logs + geology maps + LiDAR + InSAR + CPT) that predicts, for any parcel, a probabilistic ground profile: depth to rock or bearing stratum, groundwater, soft or compressible layers, contamination flags, piling length and foundation cost, with uncertainty. Products: (1) pre-acquisition ground-risk scores and foundation cost estimates for developers, data-center and battery/solar site selectors, and housebuilders; (2) optimal placement of the few real boreholes (active learning), cutting SI spend; (3) ground-risk underwriting for contractors' all-risk insurers and for subsidence home insurance; (4) ground-source heat pump and aquifer thermal storage sizing.
all.buyer_and_market: Developers and housebuilders, data-center and renewable site selectors, tier-1 contractors, engineering consultancies, construction and subsidence insurers. Global geotechnical site-investigation services are roughly a $10B+/yr market (rough estimate, not sourced in this search). Unforeseen ground conditions are a leading cause of construction claims and overruns, a multi-billion-dollar pain. UK subsidence claims alone run to hundreds of millions of GBP in bad years (ABI, from memory). A path to a large company: become the default 'ground truth' layer bought before every land deal, and expand country by country wherever drillers are forced to file logs.
all.why_now: LLM/vision OCR can finally read millions of heterogeneous hand-written logs cheaply. The data-center, grid-battery and housing build-out (UK target of 1.5M homes) needs fast site screening. Heat pump mandates need subsurface thermal data. BGS has just modernised digital deposit.
all.novelty_risk: Moderate. BGS itself and desk-study vendors (Groundsure, Landmark) are incumbents but not ML-native. GroundedAI and Terra AI are adjacent. Academics publish on the problem. The key risk is that ground-truth quality and coverage are patchy and engineers are liable for the final design, so the product must be pitched as screening and decision support, not a replacement for SI.

all.name: Post-Surfside Florida condo disclosure regime (SIRS reporting + milestone inspections), with copycat state laws
all.jurisdiction: Florida, US (expansion: New Jersey 2023 structural inspection/reserve law; California SB 326/SB 721 balcony inspections, which are not public; other states considering)
all.legal_basis: SB 4-D (2022), HB 1021 (2024) and HB 913 (2025) after the Surfside collapse. Condo and co-op buildings of 3+ stories need milestone structural inspections at 30 years (25 near the coast; HB 913 changed timing) and every 10 years after. Phase 1/2 reports go to the local building official, who reports to DBPR. Associations had to complete a Structural Integrity Reserve Study by 31 Dec 2025 and must electronically file a SIRS Reporting Form with DBPR within 45 days of completion. DBPR publishes submissions in public databases 'exactly as submitted'. Full SIRS and inspection reports must be given to unit owners and buyers, and many must be posted on association websites (25+ unit associations).
all.dataset: (a) DBPR public SIRS-reporting viewers (two: pre- and post-July 2025): per-association reserve components, funding status, study dates. Unclear whether bulk download exists, so scraping may be needed. (b) Milestone inspection Phase 1/2 reports: engineer PDFs held by ~400+ local building departments, obtainable via Florida's very broad public-records law (Ch. 119). Heterogeneous scanned PDFs with photos, crack and spalling descriptions, and repair cost estimates. (c) Repair permits: OPPAGA's first statewide report (26-04, 2026) counted 903 repair permit applications ($1k-$30M) and 54 unsafe or uninhabitable buildings. Reporting gaps are large: only 64-71% of jurisdictions reported, and Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach have big holes. Florida has roughly 1.5M+ condo units in tens of thousands of associations (estimate).
all.current_users: Reserve-study firms and software (e.g. ReservesPro and traditional reserve-study engineers), engineering firms (Rimkus, SOCOTEC) that sell the inspections, condo-insurance MGAs, and Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac condo project review (Fannie's 'unavailable' list of condo projects with critical repairs). I found no funded startup aggregating and ML-scoring the DBPR SIRS data plus the milestone reports at state scale (not exhaustively verified).
all.ml_unlock: A building-level 'condo structural and financial distress' model. Parse every SIRS filing and milestone report, link them to permits, insurance, HOA financials, sales and listing data. Predict, 12-36 months ahead, the probability and size of a special assessment, a structural deficiency or unsafe order, insurance non-renewal and price collapse for every condo building. Sell a feed to mortgage lenders and GSE-style condo project review (automating eligibility), title and condo insurers, iBuyers and investors, and buyers' agents and brokerages. Expand to a national 'building health record' as other states copy Florida.
all.buyer_and_market: Lenders and servicers of the roughly $300B+ Florida condo mortgage stock (rough), condo master-policy insurers, HOA managers, and buyers. A data feed for lenders and insurers could be a $100M+ ARR niche in Florida alone, which risks being too small unless it generalises nationally. The national path is condo and HOA risk across ~75M Americans in community associations (CAI figure from memory) plus multifamily structural risk.
all.why_now: First full SIRS cycle was due 31 Dec 2025. DBPR public portal went live 2024-25. First statewide milestone data (OPPAGA, July 2026) shows huge reporting gaps. The Florida condo price slump driven by special assessments is in the news now. LLMs make the heterogeneous engineer PDFs parseable.
all.novelty_risk: Low to moderate. Incumbents (reserve-study engineers, CoreLogic/ICE condo data, Fannie's condo review) could add it. Data access to local inspection reports is laborious. The main risk is market size: it must expand beyond Florida (NJ has a similar law) to be YC-large.

all.name: NYC Facade Inspection & Safety Program (Local Law 11/FISP) reports + DOB complaints/violations
all.jurisdiction: New York City, US (similar ordinances in Chicago, Boston, Philadelphia, San Francisco, Cincinnati, Detroit, Milwaukee, Columbus, St. Louis, Cleveland)
all.legal_basis: NYC Admin Code §28-302 / 1 RCNY 103-04 (Local Law 11 of 1998). Buildings over six stories must have a licensed Qualified Exterior Wall Inspector inspect and file a technical report on facades and appurtenances every 5 years, classifying them Safe / SWARMP / Unsafe. Filed with DOB and public through DOB NOW and BIS.
all.dataset: About 14-16k buildings per 5-year cycle (figure from memory). Decades of PDF technical reports with photos plus structured filing status in NYC Open Data (DOB NOW: Safety Facades compliance filings). Plus DOB complaints, violations, ECB and permit datasets as bulk APIs.
all.current_users: In May 2024 NYC DOB hired Thornton Tomasetti + T2D2 (an AI facade-inspection startup) to use AI on decades of facade reports and incident data to predict failures, so it is already being mined. Drone and AI facade-inspection startups (T2D2 and others) and sidewalk-shed analytics also exist.
all.ml_unlock: A predictive facade-failure and unsafe-condition model for every tall building, and a sidewalk-shed lifetime predictor, sold to insurers and owners; extend to multi-city facade ordinances.
all.buyer_and_market: Building owners, property insurers, facade contractors. NYC facade repair is roughly a $1-2B/yr spend (rough). Multi-city expansion still makes this a mid-size niche.
all.why_now: Cycle 10 is underway. DOB is pushing to shrink 'sidewalk shed' blight (400+ miles of sheds). AI drone inspection is maturing.
all.novelty_risk: High: DOB's own AI study with T2D2/Thornton Tomasetti covers the obvious product, and the market is a local niche.

all.name: UK planning application document archives (incl. embedded geotech, flood, ecology, heritage, viability reports)
all.legal_basis: Town and Country Planning (Development Management Procedure) (England) Order 2015, art. 40: local planning authorities must keep a public planning register, including applications and accompanying documents. Applicants must submit supporting technical reports (Flood Risk Assessments, Phase 1/2 geo-environmental reports, ecology and BNG assessments, viability appraisals), which are then publicly viewable on ~330 council portals (Idox, etc.).
all.dataset: Millions of applications per decade (~400-500k decisions a year in England). Each has PDFs: drawings, consultant reports, officer reports, decision notices. Spread across ~330 heterogeneous portals with no bulk API. Mostly scrapable.
all.current_users: LandTech (LandInsight), Searchland, Nimbus, PlanningAlerts-style services, Glenigan/Barbour ABI (construction leads), and UK government AI tools ('Extract' to digitise old plans, 'Consult'). Many seed-stage 'AI planning consultant' startups (approval prediction, auto-drafting). Crowded.
all.ml_unlock: An approval-probability and conditions predictor for any site and scheme, trained on officer reports and decisions. Also mining the embedded consultant reports (e.g. geotech) as a secondary subsurface data source.
all.buyer_and_market: Housebuilders, land promoters, planning consultants, councils. UK planning consultancy is roughly a £1B+ market (rough). Mostly UK-local.
all.why_now: Labour government's planning reform and 1.5M homes target, plus government AI planning tools.
all.novelty_risk: High: LandTech, Searchland and many AI-planning startups, plus government tools, already target this.

all.name: UK EPC register (domestic, non-domestic, DEC)
all.legal_basis: Energy Performance of Buildings (England and Wales) Regulations 2012 (implementing EU EPBD). An EPC is required on sale, let or construction and lodged on the central register. The data is published under the Open Government Licence by MHCLG.
all.dataset: About 25M+ certificates since 2008 (the new service says certificates since 2012 are included). Fields are structured: fabric, heating, floor area, ratings, recommendations. Bulk CSV download (after GOV.UK One Login) and a developer API via the new 'get-energy-performance-data' service, which replaced epc.opendatacommunities.org.
all.current_users: Heavily mined: retrofit and heat-pump platforms (Kamma, Parity Projects, Furbnow, Sero, Hestia), mortgage lenders' green-mortgage tools, AVMs and proptech (Chimnie, Zoopla, Rightmove), many academic ML papers, and API resellers (Apify scrapers, MCP bundles).
all.ml_unlock: Predicting the EPC rating, retrofit cost and heat-pump readiness for uncertified homes. Already done by many.
all.buyer_and_market: Lenders (MEES and green-mortgage targets), landlords, retrofit installers. A decent market, but commoditised.
all.why_now: Proposed MEES EPC C for rentals by 2030 and the new EPC methodology (HEM) reform.
all.novelty_risk: Very high: saturated by funded proptech, lenders and academics.

all.name: US building permits (municipal permit records)
all.legal_basis: State and municipal building codes require permits for construction, which become public records under state open-records laws. Many cities publish them as open data.
all.dataset: Hundreds of millions of permits across thousands of portals, heterogeneous free-text descriptions, contractor IDs and valuations.
all.current_users: Shovels ($5M seed, AI-normalised national permit data), BuildZoom, Construction Monitor, ATTOM, Cherre, Dodge/ConstructConnect, HouseCanary/CoreLogic for AVMs, and insurers (roof-age inference). Well mined.
all.ml_unlock: Property condition and roof-age inference for insurers, contractor-quality scoring, construction lead-gen. Mostly already built.
all.buyer_and_market: P&C insurers, building-products manufacturers (lead gen), lenders. Large, but the market is contested.
all.why_now: LLM normalisation of free-text permits lowers cost, which helps incumbents equally.
all.novelty_risk: Very high: Shovels and others raised specifically to do this.

all.name: Land registries and deed/mortgage records (HM Land Registry Price Paid, US county recorder deeds/mortgages)
all.legal_basis: Land Registration Act 2002 (open register; Price Paid Data under OGL). US state recording statutes make deeds, mortgages, liens and lis pendens public at ~3,600 county recorders.
all.dataset: UK: about 30M price-paid transactions since 1995 (bulk CSV, monthly), plus title registers sold per title. US: billions of scanned recorded documents, mostly OCR'd by aggregators.
all.current_users: Saturated: CoreLogic, ICE/Black Knight, ATTOM, First American DataTree, Cherre, Reonomy, and every AVM (Zillow, HouseCanary, Hometrack, Zoopla). Title-automation startups (Doma, Spruce, Qualia, etc.).
all.ml_unlock: AVMs, title automation, distress prediction. All largely built.
all.buyer_and_market: Large (title insurance is roughly $20B+/yr in the US) but dominated by incumbents.
all.why_now: No specific new forcing event.
all.novelty_risk: Extremely high.

all.name: NHTSA defect-signal corpus (ODI complaints + EWR + manufacturer communications/TSBs + Part 573 recall filings)
all.legal_basis: TREAD Act 2000 / 49 USC 30166(m) and 49 CFR 579 (Early Warning Reporting): OEMs and tire/equipment makers must file quarterly death/injury claims, property damage, warranty claims, field reports and consumer complaint counts. 49 CFR 512 Appendix C makes warranty, field-report and complaint counts confidential by class; death/injury incident data and production counts are public (from memory, not confirmed on the NHTSA page fetched). 49 USC 30166(f) and MAP-21 2012 require OEMs to send NHTSA all dealer and owner communications about defects, including TSBs, and these are published. 49 CFR 573 recall defect reports and chronologies are public. ODI owner complaints are public. No confidentiality delay applies except the CBI fields.
all.dataset: About 2M+ free-text ODI owner complaints with VIN prefix, component and narrative, as bulk flat files from NHTSA. Recall 573 reports and chronologies, which are heterogeneous PDFs. Manufacturer communications/TSBs, hundreds of thousands of PDFs, many scanned. Investigation (PE/EA) files. Public EWR quarterly death/injury and production data. All free via nhtsa.gov datasets and API, with large unstructured PDF portions.
all.current_users: We Predict (UK analytics startup, small; supplied 'DeepView' to NHTSA in 2019 and markets warranty-reserve prediction). Legacy SAS and IBM TREAD compliance tools. Academics (Virginia Tech, MSI topic-model work on complaints). Plaintiff firms and Recall Masters (consumer recall notification) use the recall data. No funded startup is visibly doing cross-OEM defect forecasting from the full PDF corpus.
all.ml_unlock: A cross-OEM 'defect early-warning' model. It reads complaints, TSB PDFs, recall chronologies and EWR to predict which components or suppliers will be recalled 6-18 months ahead. It also maps defects to the shared tier-1 supplier part (e.g., Takata or ARC inflators, ZF/TRW), and forecasts recall population and cost. A second product is warranty-reserve calibration for OEMs and suppliers.
all.buyer_and_market: Buyers: OEM and tier-1 supplier quality and warranty teams, product-liability and recall insurers, auto lenders and fleet owners, and possibly hedge funds (supplier exposure). US automakers pay roughly $15-20B/yr in warranty claims per Warranty Week (from memory); global auto warranty spend is about $50B+. Recall costs run to tens of billions per year. A realistic software TAM is $0.5-2B. It is a land-grab against incumbent quality-analytics vendors (SAS, Siemens, Tavant).
all.why_now: LLMs can finally read the heterogeneous TSB and recall PDFs and owner narratives at scale and link them by component and supplier. EV, ADAS and software defects (OTA recalls) are driving recall counts to record highs. In 2025 NHTSA amended the SGO and pushed more AV and ADAS reporting.
all.novelty_risk: Moderate. OEMs have far richer private warranty and telematics data, so the public-data edge is the cross-OEM view and the supplier linkage. We Predict exists but appears small. Sales cycles into OEM quality organizations are slow. The recall-prediction 'alpha' angle is niche.

all.name: FAA Service Difficulty Reports + Airworthiness Directives + NTSB dockets
all.jurisdiction: USA (with analogues: EASA ADs and Transport Canada CADORS/SDR)
all.legal_basis: 14 CFR 121.703, 125.409, 135.415 and 145.221: air carriers and repair stations must report failures, malfunctions and defects to the FAA (SDRS), which publishes them. ADs under 14 CFR 39 are public rules. NTSB dockets under 49 CFR 831/837 publish investigation evidence (maintenance records, metallurgy, interviews). Reports are public immediately; there is no confidentiality period.
all.dataset: SDRS: on the order of 1-2M free-text defect reports since the 1970s (count from memory, unverified), with ATA chapter, part number, aircraft make/model/serial and narrative. Queryable and exportable online. ADs are thousands of PDFs (FAA DRS). NTSB CAROL and docket: tens of thousands of investigations with PDF exhibits, many digitized scans. All are free, but part numbers are noisy and narratives are terse.
all.current_users: Mostly research: NLR (Netherlands) automated defect risk analysis, Georgia Tech, MITRE, and SKYbrary-featured ML classification of depressurization events. Commercial MRO and predictive-maintenance players (Airbus Skywise/Palantir, Boeing AnalytX, GE, ePlaneAI, Aerogility) run on proprietary airline data. I found no startup built primarily on SDR, AD and docket data.
all.ml_unlock: A fleet-wide 'next AD and part-reliability' forecaster. It predicts which components and part numbers will get ADs or SBs and drive unscheduled removals, by tail number and serial. It feeds lessor residual-value and maintenance-reserve pricing, used-serviceable-material (USM) and PMA parts demand forecasting, and aviation insurance underwriting.
all.buyer_and_market: Buyers: aircraft lessors (AerCap and others; about $300B+ of leased assets, where maintenance reserves are key), USM and PMA parts traders (USM about $6-8B/yr), MROs (global MRO about $90-100B/yr), and aviation insurers. A credible software and data business is $300M-1B. A larger path is to become the trading and pricing layer for used parts.
all.why_now: LLMs can normalize terse SDR narratives and link part numbers across SDRs, ADs, SBs and NTSB exhibits. Supply-chain shortages have made parts forecasting and USM valuable. Engine durability crises (GTF powder metal, LEAP) show the value of early defect signals.
all.novelty_risk: Medium. OEMs and Skywise hold vastly better data, and SDR reporting is inconsistent and under-reported. The edge is cross-OEM, cross-fleet public signal aimed at lessors and traders, who lack OEM data access. The space has few public-data startups, but buyers are concentrated.

all.name: EU MRV per-ship CO2/fuel disclosures (+ AIS) for EU ETS/FuelEU liability
all.legal_basis: Regulation (EU) 2015/757 (MRV), amended by 2023/957: ships over 5000 GT calling at EU ports must monitor and report verified annual fuel, CO2 (now also CH4/N2O), distance and time. EMSA publishes per-ship annual data, as of 30 June of the following year. EU ETS has covered shipping since 2024, with 100% surrender phased in by 2026 emissions. FuelEU Maritime applies from 2025. The IMO DCS equivalent is not public.
all.dataset: About 12,000+ ships per year, from 2018 onward. Per-IMO-number annual fuel and CO2 per distance/transport work, verifier and company. Bulk XLSX download from EMSA THETIS-MRV. Annual granularity only, so it needs fusion with AIS (which is not forced-disclosure public data and is sold by Spire, exactEarth and others) to model voyages.
all.current_users: Heavily used: Kpler, Spire, Windward, MarineTraffic, RightShip (GHG rating), ZeroNorth, Siglar Carbon, Marine Benchmark, Signal Ocean, classification societies, and NGOs (T&E). Many academic ML ship-fuel models are calibrated on MRV (PolyU, Fraunhofer CML EmissionSEA).
all.ml_unlock: A ground-truth-calibrated voyage-level fuel and emissions model for every ship worldwide. It feeds an ETS/FuelEU liability engine for charter parties, compliance pooling and surplus trading, and green-premium freight pricing.
all.buyer_and_market: Buyers: shipowners, charterers, commodity traders, ETS and FuelEU compliance desks. EU ETS shipping allowances are worth several €B per year (roughly 90-100 Mt CO2 × €70-80). The software layer is likely a few hundred $M at most.
all.why_now: Full ETS surrender phase-in (2026), FuelEU pooling markets, and the IMO Net-Zero Framework negotiations make per-voyage emissions a money number.
all.novelty_risk: High. The space is crowded with well-funded maritime data incumbents, and MRV is widely known and easy to use (clean XLSX). The 'messy, under-exploited' advantage is low.

all.name: FMCSA carrier safety data (MCMIS inspections/crashes, Census, L&I insurance filings, SMS)
all.legal_basis: 49 USC 31106, 49 CFR 350/385/387 and FOIA. Roadside inspection results (about 3M+ per year), reportable crashes, the motor-carrier census (MCS-150) and insurance and authority filings are published via SAFER/QCMobile, the Socrata datasets and the Data Dissemination Program. SMS percentiles were partly hidden from public view after the FAST Act 2015.
all.dataset: Millions of inspection and violation records, crash records and about 2M+ carrier census records, plus daily authority, insurance and revocation feeds. Structured CSV and API. Clean and well known.
all.current_users: Very crowded. Nirvana Insurance (Series D, $100M, Dec 2025, about $1.5B valuation; mainly telematics but underwrites with FMCSA data), Highway (carrier identity and fraud; FTV growth round Aug 2025), Carrier Assure, RMIS, Carrier411, Cover Whale, Inshur, Loadsure, Motive, Samsara, Truckstop, and plaintiff 'nuclear verdict' analytics. USDOT itself is exploring AI for carrier identity.
all.ml_unlock: Carrier risk, fraud and double-brokering detection, plus a crash-likelihood score for underwriting, brokers and shippers. Most of this is already built.
all.buyer_and_market: US commercial auto insurance is about $60B+ in premiums. Freight brokerage vetting and cargo-theft losses run to billions. The market is large but taken.
all.why_now: The freight-fraud surge and the nuclear-verdict crisis. These are already priced in by incumbents.
all.novelty_risk: Very high. Multiple funded companies, including one unicorn, are in the space.

all.name: US CBP vessel manifests / bills of lading
all.legal_basis: 19 USC 1431(c) and 19 CFR 103.31: inbound vessel manifest data (shipper, consignee, goods description, weights, ports) is publicly disclosable to the press and public unless the importer files for confidentiality, which is renewable every 2 years. There is no delay; the data is released near-daily via CBP AMS to licensed press subscribers.
all.dataset: About 15-20M+ US import bills of lading per year with free-text goods descriptions and party names. Bulk distribution goes through CBP to data resellers. Messy entity names. Air and truck manifests are not public.
all.current_users: Saturated: Altana ($200M Series C, about $1B valuation, 2024), S&P Panjiva, ImportGenius, ImportYeti, Descartes Datamyne, Sayari, Exiger, Kharon, Flexport and Project44 analytics, and hedge-fund alt-data vendors.
all.ml_unlock: Supply-chain graph and forced-labor/UFLPA/sanctions exposure, plus tariff-evasion and transshipment detection. Altana and others already do this.
all.buyer_and_market: Customs, enforcement, compliance and procurement. The trade-data and supply-chain-risk market is about $1-3B. It is large but owned.
all.why_now: The 2025-26 tariff regime and transshipment enforcement increase demand, but incumbents capture it.
all.novelty_risk: Very high. It is the canonical example of a forced-disclosure dataset already turned into a unicorn.

all.name: NHTSA Standing General Order ADS/ADAS crash reports
all.legal_basis: NHTSA Standing General Order 2021-01 (amended 2021, 2023 and April 2025, effective 16 June 2025) under the Safety Act defect authority. Named ADS and L2 ADAS makers and operators must report crashes in which automation was active within 30s and that meet severity criteria. Penalties are up to $27,874 per day per violation. Monthly public CSV releases. Narrative, ODD flag and software version can be claimed as CBI; VIN digits and exact dates are withheld.
all.dataset: Thousands of crash rows across ADS, ADAS and other CSVs (from 2021) plus a data element definitions PDF. Small and partly redacted; narratives are often CBI.
all.current_users: Journalists, safety researchers, plaintiffs' bar (Tesla Autopilot litigation), state legislatures and AV companies benchmarking each other.
all.ml_unlock: An AV/ADAS crash-rate benchmark for insurers and cities, normalized by exposure. Exposure data is not in the dataset, and the data is too small and redacted to support a big ML product.
all.buyer_and_market: AV insurers and municipal permitting are niche today. Potentially large later as robotaxi liability grows, but the dataset alone will not carry a company.
all.why_now: Robotaxi scale-up (Waymo, Zoox, Tesla) and reporting rule changes in 2025-2026.
all.novelty_risk: Low crowding but also low value. The redactions and small n limit it.

all.name: Port State Control inspections (Paris MoU THETIS / Tokyo MoU APCIS / USCG PSIX)
all.legal_basis: EU Directive 2009/16/EC (Port State Control) and the MoU regimes require inspection of foreign ships and publication of inspection, deficiency and detention results. In practice, Paris MoU has restricted bulk download since 31 Dec 2018, reportedly after a dispute between the Netherlands and the vetting company RightShip. The data remains viewable record by record.
all.dataset: Hundreds of thousands of inspections with deficiency codes and detention flags. Bulk access is now restricted for Paris MoU; Tokyo MoU and USCG are partially queryable; Equasis aggregates.
all.current_users: RightShip (owned by BHP, Rio Tinto and Cargill), Q88 and vetting platforms, P&I clubs, classification societies, and many academic detention-prediction ML papers (PolyU, LJMU).
all.ml_unlock: Detention, casualty and vetting risk scoring per ship. This is already RightShip's core product.
all.buyer_and_market: Charterer vetting and marine insurance. RightShip-scale, roughly $100M-class.
all.why_now: Nothing new. Access is getting worse, not better.
all.novelty_risk: High crowding with restricted access. Poor candidate.

all.name: ETSI/ITU standard-essential patent (SEP) declarations x patent claims x technical specs: automated essentiality and FRAND royalty-stack engine
all.jurisdiction: Global (ETSI in France; also IEEE, ITU-T); patents in US, EP, CN, KR
all.legal_basis: ETSI IPR Policy Art. 4.1 requires members to disclose, in a timely way, any IPR they believe is or may be essential to a standard. Declarations go into the public ETSI IPR database. The 3GPP technical specs and change requests are also public. Declaring is self-serving and goes unchecked, so studies find only about 20-40% of declared families are actually essential. No confidentiality period applies. (The EU SEP Regulation, which would have created a register and essentiality checks, was withdrawn in 2025, so no public verifier exists.)
all.dataset: ETSI IPR database: hundreds of thousands of declared patents (5G alone has 60k+ families). It can be bulk exported but is messy, with inconsistent patent numbers and family-level declarations. 3GPP specs are versioned Word/PDF, tens of thousands of documents, plus every meeting contribution on the 3GPP FTP. The patent full text and prosecution histories come from USPTO, EPO and CNIPA. The core ML task, matching each claim element to a spec clause, needs heterogeneous text alignment at scale.
all.current_users: IPlytics (bought by LexisNexis IP) and PatSnap Eureka SEP offer declaration analytics and some AI essentiality scoring. Consultancies such as Analysis Group and TT Consultants, and patent pools such as Avanci, Sisvel and Via LA, pay human experts roughly $5-20k per patent for essentiality checks. Court-appointed experts in Unwired Planet and InterDigital v Lenovo did manual counts. I found no well-funded startup that owns an automated claim-to-spec essentiality verdict trusted in court or arbitration.
all.ml_unlock: A model that reads each declared patent's claims against the exact 3GPP spec version and outputs a defensible essentiality probability with a claim chart. Rolled up per licensor, that gives a 'true essential share' for 5G/6G, Wi-Fi 7, video codecs and cellular IoT. This number drives FRAND royalty rates (the top-down method in court) and decides who should pay whom. It also lets implementers such as car OEMs, IoT makers and handset makers push back on over-declared portfolios, and lets licensors price litigation.
all.buyer_and_market: Buyers are implementers (automotive, IoT, handset makers), licensors (Nokia, Ericsson, InterDigital, Qualcomm), pools (Avanci, Sisvel), litigation funders and courts/arbitrators. The money at stake is large: Qualcomm's licensing arm alone takes about $5-6B/yr, and Nokia Technologies about EUR 1.4B/yr. Total cellular SEP royalties are commonly estimated at $20B+/yr (my estimate, not verified in this run). Essentiality and valuation services today are probably a $200-500M niche, but the realistic path to a large company is to become the neutral rate-setter or to take a share of licensing deals and disputes, like a FRAND clearinghouse.
all.why_now: 6G declarations are starting. The EU's withdrawal of the SEP Regulation leaves no public essentiality check. IoT and automotive implementers are flooding into licensing. LLMs can now do claim-element-to-spec alignment that was previously too costly to automate. UK, German and UPC courts are setting global FRAND rates and need top-down counts.
all.novelty_risk: Medium. IPlytics/LexisNexis and PatSnap sell analytics and some AI scoring, and academic work exists (Baron & Pohlmann). There is no dominant, court-grade automated essentiality product yet. The main risk is credibility: courts and licensors may not accept a model's verdicts, and incumbents with IP data could add the feature.

all.name: Hatch-Waxman forced disclosures (Orange Book listings + Paragraph IV certifications + ANDA litigation dockets + PTAB IPRs + prosecution histories): generic-entry date prediction
all.legal_basis: 21 U.S.C. 355(b)(1) and 21 CFR 314.53 require brand companies to list patents covering a drug in FDA's Orange Book. Under 21 U.S.C. 355(j)(2)(A)(vii)(IV), a generic applicant must certify invalidity or non-infringement (Paragraph IV) and notify the brand, and filing suit within 45 days triggers a 30-month stay. FDA publishes the Paragraph IV list (drug, date, first-filer). The resulting district court cases (mostly D. Del. and D.N.J.) are on PACER. Patent-settlement agreements must be filed with the FTC under MMA 2003, and the FTC publishes aggregate reports. USPTO file wrappers and PTAB IPR records are public. No confidentiality period applies, though settlement terms stay private.
all.dataset: Orange Book (structured, monthly), the FDA Paragraph IV list (about 1,500+ entries), thousands of ANDA cases on PACER (complaints, claim-construction orders, expert reports, sealed and unsealed opinions) and PTAB trial records. The patent prosecution histories (USPTO ODP file wrappers) are scanned PDFs of office actions. FDA also publishes approval letters, tentative approvals and Competitive Generic Therapy (CGT) designations. Data is spread across 5+ sources and partly paywalled (PACER at $0.10/page). The prediction target is labeled by history: the actual generic launch date.
all.current_users: DrugPatentWatch and Evaluate Pharma offer loss-of-exclusivity (LOE) dates. IQVIA, Citeline and Clarivate (Cortellis) track patents and litigation. Docket Navigator and Lex Machina provide ANDA litigation analytics. Hedge-fund specialists and expert networks do this by hand. I found no ML startup that produces a probabilistic generic-entry date curve per molecule from the full forced-disclosure record; my search turned up only law-firm commentary and blogs.
all.ml_unlock: A probabilistic generic and biosimilar entry-date model per product, combining patent strength (from prosecution history, claim scope and PTAB outcomes), judge and venue base rates, the number and identity of Paragraph IV filers, settlement likelihood and forfeiture rules. It would update in real time as dockets move and would produce a revenue-at-risk curve for each brand.
all.buyer_and_market: Buyers are long/short healthcare hedge funds, generic and biosimilar makers deciding which ANDA to file (each costs millions), brand lifecycle teams, PBMs, payers and pharma M&A/BD. More than $200B of branded revenue faces loss of exclusivity in 2025-2030 (industry estimate, not verified here). Market for the data and models: the healthcare investing data market (Evaluate, Citeline) is worth several hundred million dollars a year. Taking it further toward 'which ANDA to file' decision support, or principal investing, could make it a larger company.
all.why_now: A large patent cliff is coming (Keytruda, Eliquis, Opdivo and others, roughly 2026-2030). The biosimilar 'patent dance' under the BPCIA adds similar disclosures. USPTO's Open Data Portal (2025) makes file wrappers easier to get by API. The FTC is challenging improper Orange Book listings (2023-25), which changes the patent mix. LLMs can read claim-construction orders and expert reports.
all.novelty_risk: Medium. Incumbent LOE databases exist and buy-side analysts are sophisticated, so differentiation has to come from measurably better entry-date accuracy. The core buyer set (healthcare hedge funds plus generic makers) is concentrated.

all.name: Open court records (PACER federal + 3,000+ fragmented state trial-court dockets): casualty 'litigation catastrophe' model for insurers and reinsurers
all.legal_basis: The common-law and First Amendment right of public access to court records (Nixon v. Warner Communications, 1978) and the Judicial Conference's PACER access policy make filings public. States have their own public-access rules. Pleadings, verdicts, expert designations and settlements approved by the court become public records. PACER fees bring in over $150M/yr. The Open Courts Act of 2026 would replace PACER and remove fees but is not law yet.
all.dataset: PACER: hundreds of millions of documents across 94 districts. Free Law Project's RECAP/CourtListener mirrors a subset, with bulk data. State courts are a patchwork of portals, many requiring scraping or paid access, with scanned complaints, verdict forms and jury instructions. The data is very messy, mostly unstructured PDF, which is a moat for whoever normalizes it. It can be joined to MDL dockets (JPML), FDA MAUDE, EPA and scientific literature.
all.current_users: State dockets: Trellis ($14.1M Series A, 2021), UniCourt, Docket Alarm (Fastcase/vLex/Clio). Federal: Lex Machina (LexisNexis) and Bloomberg Law. Litigation prediction: Theo Ai ($4.2M seed), Pre/Dicta, Premonition. Insurance claims: CLARA Analytics. Emerging mass-tort modeling: Praedicat (now with Verisk; works with Lloyd's, Convex and Cytora). Plaintiff-side demand letters: EvenUp (unicorn). The data is fairly well mined for legal research. It is less well mined for insurer reserving and pricing at the portfolio level.
all.ml_unlock: A 'casualty cat model' that does for liability what RMS/AIR do for hurricanes. It would read every new complaint and docket event nationwide to (a) catch emerging mass torts early (PFAS, social media addiction, GLP-1, ultra-processed food) by tracking filing velocity, plaintiff-firm advertising and science, and (b) predict verdict and settlement severity by venue, judge, plaintiff firm and defendant. The output is portfolio-level tail-loss curves for casualty reinsurers and excess and surplus (E&S) carriers.
all.buyer_and_market: Buyers are casualty reinsurers (Swiss Re, Munich Re, Gen Re), E&S and umbrella carriers, Lloyd's syndicates, ILS investors entering casualty, and litigation funders. US commercial casualty premiums run to hundreds of billions of dollars, and 'social inflation' has added tens of billions of dollars in adverse reserve development (Gen Re and Swiss Re report this; figures approximate). Cat-model analogue: Moody's RMS and Verisk catastrophe modeling earn roughly $0.5-1B/yr each, which shows a credible path to a large company.
all.why_now: Record nuclear verdicts in 2023-25 forced casualty reserve hikes. Reinsurers are pulling back and want any modeled view of liability tail risk. LLMs can finally parse heterogeneous state dockets cheaply. Free-PACER legislation could cut data costs.
all.novelty_risk: Medium-high. Praedicat/Verisk owns the emerging-risk framing. Trellis, UniCourt and the big legal-data vendors own docket access. Theo Ai and Premonition do case-level prediction. The open space is the integrated, actuarially credible portfolio model sold to reinsurers. Getting insurer claims data as labels will be essential and slow.

all.name: UCC Article 9 financing statements (plus state tax liens and judgments): private-credit liens graph for SMB and private-credit risk
all.jurisdiction: US (50 Secretary of State offices plus county filing offices); analogues are Canada's PPSA registries, UK Companies House charges and Australia's PPSR
all.legal_basis: UCC 9-310 requires a filed financing statement to perfect most security interests. Lenders must file publicly or risk losing priority, so every secured loan, equipment lease, merchant cash advance (MCA) and inventory facility to a private business leaves a public trace. Filings are public at once, with no confidentiality period, and lapse after 5 years unless continued.
all.dataset: Tens of millions of active UCC-1/UCC-3 filings across 50+ state systems. Formats differ: some offer bulk XML/CSV subscriptions, many offer only per-record PDF images, and collateral descriptions are free text. Join keys are fuzzy (debtor-name normalization). Combinable with state tax liens, judgments, Secretary of State entity data, and the CFPB 1071 small-business lending data (rule delayed).
all.current_users: Data resellers include LexisNexis, Dun & Bradstreet, Experian, Equifax, CSC and Wolters Kluwer CT Lien Solutions. MCA stacking tools include Cobalt Intelligence and CRS Credit API. AI SMB lending tools include Kaaj ($3.8M seed), Middesk, Enigma and Baselayer. Lead-gen scrapers resell 'just-financed' leads. Heavily used for compliance and leads. Less used as a full ML credit graph.
all.ml_unlock: A national graph of who has lent to whom against what collateral, rebuilt from collateral free text. It would predict SMB default and distress months ahead (stacking velocity, lender mix shift to MCA, tax liens), size private-credit exposure to sectors, and flag fraud such as double-pledged collateral and lien-hiding. In effect, a credit bureau for private business debt built only from forced public filings.
all.buyer_and_market: Buyers are SMB lenders and MCA funders (about $20B+/yr in MCA originations), equipment lessors, private-credit and asset-based lending (ABL) funds, trade-credit insurers, suppliers setting net terms, and banks. Commercial credit data is a multi-billion-dollar market (D&B and Experian Business are each about $1-2B in revenue), which is a credible large-company path if accuracy beats the bureaus.
all.why_now: Private credit has grown past $1.5T with little transparency, and regulators (Fed, IMF, BoE) are flagging it. MCA stacking losses are rising. LLMs can parse free-text collateral descriptions and fuzzy-match entities at scale.
all.novelty_risk: Medium-high. Big bureaus already ingest UCC data, and several small API vendors and AI underwriters exist. The edge would be the graph/ML layer and private-credit exposure analytics, not data access.

all.name: USPTO / EPO patent file wrappers (prosecution histories, examiner citations, office actions, PTAB trials)
all.jurisdiction: US, EU (EPO Register), plus WIPO PATENTSCOPE
all.legal_basis: 35 U.S.C. 122(b) requires publication of applications at 18 months, and the full file wrapper becomes public under 37 CFR 1.11/1.14. EPC Art. 93 (publication) and Art. 128 (file inspection) open the EPO Register, including examiner search reports and citations. PTAB trial records are public under 35 U.S.C. 316.
all.dataset: Millions of applications with full prosecution histories: office actions, responses, examiner interviews and citations. Formats are a mix of XML, text and image PDFs. The USPTO Open Data Portal replaced PEDS in 2025 with API and bulk access. The EPO Register is accessible via OPS.
all.current_users: Very crowded. Juristat, LexisNexis PatentAdvisor and Patent Bots offer examiner analytics. Patlytics raised a $40M Series B (2026). Solve Intelligence raised a $40M Series B (Dec 2025). Others include IPlytics, PatSnap, Clarivate/Derwent, Anaqua, Ankar, Unified Patents and Docket Navigator for PTAB.
all.ml_unlock: Examiner-specific allowance and claim-scope prediction, automated prior-art and invalidity charts, patent valuation from prosecution estoppel. Mostly built already.
all.buyer_and_market: Buyers are law firms, corporate IP departments and litigation funders. The IP analytics and software market is perhaps $2-5B, but the well-funded incumbents and fast-growing AI entrants above are already in it.
all.why_now: The ODP API launch in 2025 and LLM drafting. But many others have already acted on this.
all.novelty_risk: High. Already well mined by funded startups and incumbents. Not recommended unless paired with a non-legal buyer, as in the SEP and Hatch-Waxman candidates above.

all.name: Chapter 11 bankruptcy dockets (claims registers, monthly operating reports, Rule 2015.3 reports, DIP and plan documents)
all.legal_basis: 11 U.S.C. 107 makes papers filed in a bankruptcy case public records. Debtors must file schedules of assets and liabilities (FRBP 1007), monthly operating reports (US Trustee guidelines), Rule 2015.3 reports on non-debtor affiliates, and Rule 2019 disclosures of creditor-group holdings. Claims agents (Kroll, Stretto, Epiq) host the claims registers for free.
all.dataset: Thousands of large chapter 11 cases, each with tens of thousands of docket entries: scanned schedules, claims (proofs of claim as PDFs) and financial reports. Free through claims-agent sites; otherwise PACER.
all.current_users: Crowded. 9fin raised a $50M Series B (2024) and was reported raising a $170M Series C at a $1.3B valuation. Octus (formerly Reorg) and Debtwire have long covered this. Bloomberg Law, BankruptcyData and Bloomberg/PitchBook also serve the space.
all.ml_unlock: Recovery-value prediction by claim class, prediction of trading prices for claims, and an early-warning model for which suppliers' receivables are at risk.
all.buyer_and_market: Buyers are distressed-debt funds, claims traders and restructuring advisers. A few hundred million dollars a year in data spend, and much of it is already captured by 9fin and Octus.
all.why_now: Elevated chapter 11 filings and liability-management exercises in 2024-26.
all.novelty_risk: High. Well mined by richly funded 9fin and Octus. Score low.

all.name: Public procurement award disclosures (EU TED, US FPDS/SAM.gov/USAspending, UK Contracts Finder/Find a Tender)
all.legal_basis: EU Directive 2014/24/EU Arts. 49-51 require contract notices and award notices in TED above set thresholds, and eForms have been mandatory since Oct 2023. The US FFATA/DATA Act and FAR Part 4.6 require FPDS reporting of awards over $10k, published on USAspending. The UK Procurement Act 2023, in force Feb 2025, extends transparency notices and contract publication.
all.dataset: TED: about 700k+ notices/yr in 24 languages, with a bulk XML/eForms API. FPDS/USAspending: tens of millions of structured award records. The source tender documents are often linked PDFs on national portals, which is messy.
all.current_users: Crowded. US players include GovDash, Govini, GovSpend, Deltek GovWin and Sweetspot. EU/UK players include Tendium, Stotles, Tendios, Hedda (EUR 1.5M, 2025), Cato (EUR 6M) and many TED-screening tools.
all.ml_unlock: Bid/no-bid win-probability and price-to-win models trained on award notices with bidder counts and prices, and agency demand forecasting.
all.buyer_and_market: Buyers are government contractors. Public procurement is about $750B+/yr federal in the US and about EUR 2T/yr in the EU, but the software is already contested.
all.why_now: EU eForms standardization (2023) and the UK Procurement Act (2025) improve data quality.
all.novelty_risk: High. Many funded startups and incumbents. Score low.

all.name: Kansas WIMAS (plus Nebraska NRD and Colorado) mandatory per-well annual metered water-use reports, combined with western water-rights registries
all.jurisdiction: US (Kansas first; also Nebraska NRDs, Colorado, Idaho, Texas GCDs, and western state water-rights databases)
all.legal_basis: Kansas Water Appropriation Act (K.S.A. 82a-732): every water-right holder must file an annual water-use report each year. Not filing can bring civil penalties, and meters are mandated in most groundwater management districts. Western prior-appropriation states keep public registries of rights (priority date, place of use, quantity) because adjudication law requires it. There is no confidentiality period: the reports are public records as soon as they are filed.
all.dataset: WIMAS / KDA water-use database: about 30k+ points of diversion, with annual pumped volume, acres irrigated and crop type per well, from about 1990 to now. KGS publishes bulk downloads. Western water rights are harmonized in HarDWR (11 states, millions of rights, figshare). Adjudication decrees and transfer files are mostly scanned PDFs at the state engineer and court level, and that is the messy part nobody has pulled out.
all.current_users: Academic hydrologists (KGS, USGS, PSU HarDWR team). Water-market brokers and appraisers such as WestWater Research, which mostly works by hand. I found no ML startup that prices water rights or farmland water security at the parcel level from these records. Farmland data players (AcreValue/Granular-Corteva, FBN) value soil, not the water right.
all.ml_unlock: A parcel-level 'water-backed farmland value and curtailment risk' model. It would predict, for any western or High Plains parcel, the probability of curtailment or pumping cutbacks over 5-20 years, its sustainable pumping volume, and the implied dollar value of its water right. Inputs: well-level pumping histories, priority dates, aquifer decline, drought forecasts, and adjudication outcomes extracted by LLM from scanned decrees. The output is an underwriting score for farmland lenders and buyers, a missing primitive in a market where water now decides most of a western farm's value.
all.buyer_and_market: Buyers: farmland lenders (Farm Credit System, about $400B+ in ag real-estate loans; Rabobank, MetLife and Nuveen/TIAA farmland funds), farmland REITs, water-market investors, and municipalities and data centers buying water rights. US farmland is worth about $3.5T (USDA land-values report). One data-subscription comparison is CoStar for commercial real estate. 'CoStar for water-backed land' is plausibly a $300M-1B ARR category over time, but that is speculative.
all.why_now: The Ogallala is declining, the Colorado River is being renegotiated (post-2026 guidelines), and Kansas LEMAs and Nebraska allocations are tightening. Data centers are now bidding for western water. LLMs can now read decades of scanned adjudication decrees and transfer orders.
all.novelty_risk: Moderate-low. Water brokers have the domain knowledge but no ML. Climate-risk vendors (Jupiter, First Street) model physical drought, not legal water entitlements. The main risk is a slow-buying customer base: ag lenders are conservative.

all.name: California Pesticide Use Reporting (PUR): every agricultural pesticide application since 1990
all.legal_basis: Full use reporting became mandatory in 1990 under the California Food and Agricultural Code and 3 CCR 6624-6627, after the Food Safety Act of 1989. Growers and licensed applicators must report every agricultural application (product, rate, acres, crop, date, location to the square-mile section) to the county agricultural commissioner. CDPR then publishes it. There is no confidentiality period; the data is published with about a 1-2 year lag.
all.dataset: About 2-3M+ application records per year, more than 30 years in total. Bulk annual downloads in delimited text from CDPR (CalPIP), at section level (about 1 sq mi) with grower and site IDs. Since 2022 the data is linked to permits, and SprayDays notifications began in 2025. It is clean and well structured, not scanned.
all.current_users: Heavily used in academic epidemiology (Parkinson's, autism and cancer exposure studies) and by UC IPM, USGS (land-use derivation), OPCA, environmental NGOs, and plaintiffs' experts in paraquat and chlorpyrifos litigation. Commercial ag-chemical market intelligence comes mostly from Kynetec surveys. I found no startup building a commercial ML product on PUR.
all.ml_unlock: Use 30 years of field-level spray history as a pest-pressure and resistance sensor. Train a model that forecasts outbreaks, insecticide or fungicide resistance emergence, and demand by product and section, and infers crop rotations and yields. Sell it as (a) demand forecasting and competitive intelligence to ag-chemical makers and distributors and (b) exposure reconstruction for toxic-tort litigation and insurers.
all.buyer_and_market: Ag-chemical and biologicals companies (Bayer, Corteva, Syngenta, BASF, Nutrien Ag Solutions) buy market data through Kynetec; Kynetec's total revenue is reported in the low hundreds of millions of dollars. Mass-tort exposure analytics is a niche. Realistically this is a $50-200M niche, which the founder considers too small, unless it becomes a broader ag-intelligence play.
all.why_now: California's 2025 SprayDays rollout and the push for real-time reporting, the boom in biological crop protection, and a growing pesticide mass-tort docket.
all.novelty_risk: Low competition, but also limited size. It is one state and one data stream, and the buyers are few and consolidated.

all.name: EPA UCMR 5 and Consumer Confidence Reports: PFAS, plus mandatory Lead Service Line Inventories
all.jurisdiction: US (federal SDWA; every community water system)
all.legal_basis: Safe Drinking Water Act 1445(a)(2): the Unregulated Contaminant Monitoring Rule. UCMR 5 (2023-2025) required all systems serving 3,300+ people, plus a sample of smaller systems, to test for 29 PFAS and lithium, with results published by EPA. The CCR rule requires annual public water-quality reports. The Lead and Copper Rule Revisions required every system to publish a service-line material inventory by Oct 16, 2024, and the LCRI requires replacing them within 10 years.
all.dataset: UCMR 5: about 10k systems' sampling results, bulk downloads from EPA. CCRs: about 50k annual PDF reports in heterogeneous formats, never centralized. LSL inventories: about 9.2M estimated lead lines, with system-level inventories published in heterogeneous spreadsheets and PDFs. Also SDWIS violations data.
all.current_users: BlueConduit (funded by Google.org and Rockefeller; ML that predicts lead service-line locations for hundreds of utilities) dominates the lead-line angle. Academic and RTI/Mathematica ML models exist for PFAS in private wells. Engineering firms (Jacobs, Arcadis) and PFAS plaintiffs' firms use UCMR data. EWG's Tap Water Database aggregates it.
all.ml_unlock: A 'PFAS liability graph'. Join UCMR, CCRs, state well data, industrial discharge (TRI/NPDES) and fire-training sites. Predict PFAS concentration for every untested system and every private well, attribute the likely source (polluter), and estimate the utility's treatment cost. Buyers would use it for litigation allocation, insurer exposure, and utility capital planning.
all.buyer_and_market: PFAS remediation and treatment is a $10B+/yr US market. 3M's settlement with utilities was $10.3B, and DuPont/Chemours/Corteva's was $1.19B. Buyers would be utilities, insurers and reinsurers pricing PFAS exclusions, plaintiffs' and defense firms, and industrial companies with exposure. The software slice is plausibly $200-500M.
all.why_now: The UCMR 5 dataset is complete (sampling ended 2025), the federal PFAS MCLs are on a 2029-2031 compliance clock (partly rolled back or extended in 2025), and litigation waves continue against downstream industrial users.
all.novelty_risk: Medium. BlueConduit owns lead lines. PFAS prediction is crowded with academics, environmental consultancies, and NGOs, but there is no dominant venture-backed ML player. The regulatory rollback risk is real.

all.name: State-mandated water well driller logs (well completion reports)
all.jurisdiction: US (nearly every state, e.g. CA DWR well completion reports, TX TWDB SDR, MN CWI) plus many countries
all.legal_basis: State water-well construction statutes require licensed drillers to file a completion log for every well within a set period (e.g. 60 days in California), covering lithology, depth, static water level and yield. California made the logs public in 2017 (SB 83 / Water Code 13752). Most are public with no confidentiality period.
all.dataset: Tens of millions of logs nationally (about 1M+ in California). Many are scanned handwritten PDFs, and lithology descriptions are free text: exactly the messy, under-exploited format.
all.current_users: DrillerDB launched an 'AI Geology Estimator' in Aug 2025 that extracts lithology and water levels from well-log PDFs nationwide and predicts depth to water at any address. USGS and state surveys use the logs for hydrogeologic models. Academic ML papers exist (Stanford, water-well success predictors).
all.ml_unlock: 3D national subsurface lithology and aquifer-yield model built from LLM-parsed driller logs. It would predict dry-well risk, drilling cost and success for any parcel, and serve geothermal-loop and data-center siting.
all.buyer_and_market: Water-well drilling (about $3-5B/yr US industry), geothermal heat-pump installers, homebuilders, and rural land buyers. The software slice is small, about $50-150M.
all.why_now: OCR and LLMs can finally read the handwritten logs, and SGMA well-permit restrictions are tightening.
all.novelty_risk: High overlap with DrillerDB, which is already doing exactly this. The application is also adjacent to Terranox-style subsurface ML.

all.name: USDA RMA crop insurance Summary of Business and Cause-of-Loss files
all.legal_basis: Federal Crop Insurance Act and FOIA/transparency policy. RMA publishes county- and crop-level policies, premiums, indemnities, and cause of loss by month, from 1989 to now. Policy-level farmer data is protected under 7 USC 1502(c), so the public data is aggregated to county level.
all.dataset: Bulk downloadable delimited files: county x crop x insurance plan x cause-of-loss x month, more than 35 years. Clean and well structured, but aggregated. There is no parcel- or farm-level data.
all.current_users: Heavily used by academics, AgRisk (NMSU), USDA ERS, AIPs and reinsurers. Ag-insurtechs and parametric players (e.g. CropIt, Arbol, Descartes) and big incumbents (Verisk/AIR crop models, Cognizant-powered carriers) already mine it.
all.ml_unlock: Loss-cost prediction and fraud and anomaly detection at county x crop level, or as training labels for satellite-based field-level yield-loss models. That is incremental, not revolutionary.
all.buyer_and_market: Federal crop insurance is about $17-20B in annual premium. Buyers would be the approved insurance providers (about 13 AIPs) and reinsurers. But RMA itself sets rates, so the pricing edge private parties can capture is limited.
all.why_now: Climate volatility, record indemnities, and the 2025-26 farm bill expansion of area-based products.
all.novelty_risk: Well mined, and the data is aggregated, which blocks a real moat. RMA's fixed rate-setting caps the value a private model can capture.
sources: https://www.cfo.gov/wp-content/uploads/scorecards/FY24-Q4/Risk Management Agency (RMA) Federal Crop Insurance Corporation (FCIC).pdf

all.name: FDA inspection classifications, Form 483s, and food recalls
all.legal_basis: FDA posts inspection classifications and compliance actions under its transparency initiative and FOIA. Form 483s become public through FOIA and proactive posting. Recalls are published in the Enforcement Report.
all.dataset: Inspection classification database (about 300k+ inspections), 483 PDFs (released partially, often redacted), warning letters, and the weekly recall enforcement report. Mixed structured data and PDFs.
all.current_users: Crowded. Redica Systems (venture-funded, built on FOIA'd 483s), Govzilla/FDAzilla, Leucine FDA Tracker, and commercial datasets on HuggingFace. FDA itself began an AI-informed inspection-targeting pilot in 2026.
all.ml_unlock: Predict which supplier facility will get a recall or OAI next, as supplier-risk scoring for food and pharma procurement.
all.buyer_and_market: Pharma and food QA and supply-chain teams. The market for regulatory intelligence is a few hundred million dollars and contested.
all.why_now: FMA Section 204 food traceability rule (compliance delayed to 2028) and FDA's own AI targeting.
all.novelty_risk: High. Multiple funded incumbents already do this.

all.name: EU CAP payment beneficiary publication
all.legal_basis: Regulation (EU) 2021/2116 Art. 98-99 requires member states to publish every beneficiary of EAGF/EAFRD funds annually. That covers name (for legal persons and above de minimis), municipality, amounts per measure, and group membership. Data stays online for 2 years.
all.dataset: About 6M beneficiaries per year, roughly EUR 55B per year in payments. It is published on 27 separate national websites in heterogeneous formats, and older years are deleted after 2 years, so continuous archival is required. The EU now collects data centrally via the ARACHNE/data-mining tool for audit.
all.current_users: Journalists (farmsubsidy.org, investigative consortia), the European Commission's ARACHNE fraud-risk tool, and academics. I found no commercial ML company.
all.ml_unlock: Pan-EU farm-entity graph: link beneficiaries to corporate registries and land parcels (LPIS where public). Predict farm consolidation and land-transaction candidates, credit risk, and subsidy-fraud networks. Sell to ag lenders, input companies, and land investors.
all.buyer_and_market: EU ag lenders (Rabobank, Crédit Agricole), agri-input sales teams, and anti-fraud bodies (OLAF, EPPO). The likely market is $50-150M, and GDPR limits it for natural persons.
all.why_now: The 2028+ CAP reform debate, EPPO fraud cases, and the 2-year deletion rule, which makes an early archive a moat.
all.novelty_risk: Low competition, but small market and GDPR constraints.

all.name: NHTSA defect-disclosure stack (manufacturer communications, TSBs, complaints, SGO crash reports, Part 573 recalls)
all.legal_basis: TREAD Act (2000) and 49 CFR Part 579. Under 579.5, manufacturers must send NHTSA copies of every notice, bulletin and communication they send to dealers or owners about defects, malfunctions or repairs; NHTSA publishes these as 'Manufacturer Communications' and TSBs. Part 573 recall reports are public. Standing General Order 2021-01 (amended 2023/2025) requires crash reports for ADS/L2 ADAS vehicles, which NHTSA publishes. Consumer complaints (VOQs) are public. Early Warning Reporting warranty-claim and field-report counts are mostly confidential; only aggregate death/injury counts are released.
all.dataset: Bulk downloads from NHTSA/ODI on data.gov: recalls, complaints (about 2M+), investigations, TSBs and manufacturer communications. The communications are hundreds of thousands of heterogeneous PDFs: dealer bulletins, warranty extensions, repair procedures, often scanned. SGO crash CSVs are refreshed monthly. The data is messy and spans many document types, and the communications PDFs are under-exploited.
all.current_users: Plaintiff and lemon-law firms, CarComplaints-type consumer sites, and academic text-mining papers (ESV, Virginia Tech, Ajou). Acerta Analytics (Canadian, ML on in-plant/telemetry data, small). Predii and Tavant use OEM-internal repair and warranty data rather than the public PDFs. Some hedge funds use complaint counts as alt data. A search found no funded startup building a recall- and warranty-cost forecaster on the full public communications corpus.
all.ml_unlock: A 'recall and warranty-liability forecaster': an LLM reads every TSB, dealer communication and complaint narrative, links them to components and suppliers (Tier-1/Tier-2), and predicts which component or supplier will hit a recall or warranty extension, with the expected campaign cost, months before the Part 573 filing. Silent warranty extensions in dealer bulletins are a leading indicator of recalls.
all.buyer_and_market: Product-recall insurers and reinsurers pricing auto-supplier recall cover, OEM and supplier quality and procurement teams, credit and equity investors in suppliers, and plaintiff firms. Global auto warranty spending is about $50B/yr (Warranty Week). US recalls run 25-35M vehicles/yr, often costing $100M-$1B+ per campaign.
