Each buyer segment looks like a few hundred $M of SaaS and data spend. The insurance/underwriting wedge could be larger if the model shows predictive lift.
all.why_now: LLMs can finally parse hundreds of thousands of unstructured dealer bulletins and complaint narratives at low cost. EVs and software-defined vehicles are driving record recall counts (OTA/software recalls). SGO ADAS crash data is a new feed, and NHTSA recently moved to make manufacturer communications more searchable.
all.novelty_risk: Moderate. The data is famous but mostly mined in aggregate (complaint counts). OEMs have far better private warranty data, so OEM quality teams may not value it. The best buyers are outsiders (insurers, investors, suppliers' counterparties). S&P Mobility, J.D. Power or Verisk could enter. No clear funded direct competitor was found.

all.name: OSHA Injury Tracking Application case-level data (Forms 300/301) plus OSHA and MSHA inspection records
all.legal_basis: 29 CFR 1904.41, as amended by OSHA's 'Improve Tracking of Workplace Injuries and Illnesses' final rule (July 2023, effective 1 Jan 2024). Establishments with 100+ employees in high-hazard industries (Subpart E, Appendix B) must electronically submit case-level 300 log and 301 incident report data each year. Establishments with 20+ employees in listed industries, and all with 250+, submit 300A summaries. OSHA publishes the data with PII removed. Political risk: a similar Obama-era rule was rescinded in 2019. OSHA inspection and violation data and MSHA mine-level data (Mine Act) are also public.
all.dataset: OSHA ITA downloads: 300A establishment summaries for 2016-2025, and case-detail (300/301) files for CY2023, 2024 and 2025 in CSV/ZIP, now with OIICS codes on the five narrative fields (what happened, injury, object/substance). Coverage is establishment-identified (name, address, EIN-like IDs, NAICS) across tens of thousands of establishments and hundreds of thousands of cases per year. It can be joined to OSHA enforcement (IMIS/OIS), severe injury reports, MSHA, and the EPA/PHMSA incident databases.
all.current_users: Academics and journalists. Safety-tech companies (Voxel, Intenseye, Protex AI, Benchmark Gensuite) sell computer vision or EHS software on customers' private data and do not mine the public data. Verisk/ISO and NCCI hold proprietary workers' comp claims data. No startup was found doing establishment-level risk scoring on the new case-level public data.
all.ml_unlock: An establishment-level 'injury-risk score' for every US worksite with 100+ employees in high-hazard industries. It would combine injury narratives, injury-rate trends, inspection and violation history, and hiring and turnover signals to predict future lost-time and severe injuries and the expected workers' comp loss cost. Two products follow: (1) underwriting and pricing tools for workers' comp carriers and MGAs, which today rely on experience mods lagging 2-4 years; (2) supplier and contractor safety pre-qualification for procurement. A full-stack ML-native workers' comp MGA is possible.
all.buyer_and_market: US workers' comp premium is about $55-60B/yr (NCCI), and a few points of loss-ratio improvement are worth billions. Contractor pre-qualification (ISNetworld, Avetta, about $1B+ combined revenue) is a second buyer. The full-stack MGA route makes the market the premium pool itself.
all.why_now: Case-level 300/301 data has been public only since 2024, so there are just three years of it. LLMs can turn free-text injury narratives into risk features. Workers' comp carriers are under pressure from rising medical severity.
all.novelty_risk: Low to moderate. Incumbents (Verisk, NCCI, large carriers) hold better claims data but not timely establishment-level narratives. Regulatory risk is real: the current administration could narrow or rescind the case-level submission rule (2019 precedent). Coverage is limited to 100+ employee establishments in Appendix B industries.

all.name: EU Pay Transparency Directive employer gender-pay-gap reports (plus UK gender pay gap)
all.legal_basis: Directive (EU) 2023/970. Member states had to transpose it by 7 June 2026, but many are late. Article 9 requires employers with 250+ workers to report pay-gap indicators annually, and those with 150-249 every 3 years from June 2027 (100-149 from 2031). Reports cover mean and median gaps, bonus gaps, quartile distribution, and gaps by category of workers. Article 29 requires a national monitoring body to collect and publish the data in a user-friendly way that allows comparison between employers. Job applicants get pay-range rights, and pay-secrecy clauses are banned. UK Equality Act (Gender Pay Gap Information) Regulations 2017: 250+ employers publish to gov.uk (about 10k employers/yr, public since 2017).
all.dataset: From 2027, employer-level pay-gap and quartile data for tens of thousands of EU employers, published by about 27 heterogeneous national bodies in different formats and languages, some only as employer-posted PDFs. The UK set is a clean CSV/API, about 10k employers × 8 years. Combined with mandatory salary ranges in job ads, this becomes a quasi-public pay dataset.
all.current_users: Compliance software companies are well funded: Figures (France), Syndio, Trusaic, Ravio, Payscore, beqom, PayAnalytics (acquired by beqom), and Mercer/WTW/Korn Ferry. UK GPG data is used by journalists and ESG raters. Compliance tooling is crowded; nobody yet owns a pan-EU harmonized employer pay graph built from the mandatory publications, because they do not exist until 2027.
all.ml_unlock: A harmonized 'pan-European employer pay graph'. ML ingests 27 national publications plus legally mandated salary ranges in job postings and infers role-level pay bands per employer. It also predicts which employers face joint pay assessments (gap above 5%) and equal-pay litigation exposure. Buyers: compensation teams (benchmarking without surveys), employment plaintiffs and litigation funders, ESG and asset managers.
all.buyer_and_market: The comp benchmarking and survey market is about $3-5B/yr globally (Mercer, WTW, Radford/Aon, Payscale, Ravio). Equal-pay litigation exposure in the EU is new and could be large. A credible path to a big company exists if the 'Levels.fyi/Radford for Europe from public data' framing works.
all.why_now: Transposition deadline June 2026, first mandatory reports June 2027, and the salary-range-in-job-ad rules start now. The data appears in a fragmented, multilingual, messy form exactly when it starts to matter.
all.novelty_risk: High competition for compliance software. Medium for the data-aggregation play: Ravio, Figures and Mercer are positioned to build it. Transposition delays and divergent national publication rules are a risk (some states may publish only aggregates, not per-employer data). The ML is mostly extraction and imputation, which is less defensible.

all.name: Health-plan Transparency in Coverage machine-readable files (negotiated rates)
all.legal_basis: Transparency in Coverage final rule (45 CFR 147.210-212, 29 CFR 2590.715-2715A; CMS/DOL/Treasury, 2020), enforced from July 2022. Every group health plan and issuer must publish monthly machine-readable files of in-network negotiated rates for every provider and service, plus out-of-network allowed amounts. A companion rule (45 CFR 180) requires hospitals to publish standard charges. 2025-2026 executive actions tightened enforcement and standardization.
all.dataset: Petabyte-scale JSON files published monthly by about 1,000+ payers and TPAs. They are huge, duplicative and inconsistent, with phantom rates for services providers never perform. Hospital MRFs come in many formats.
all.current_users: Crowded and well funded: Turquoise Health (about $55M+ raised), Serif Health, Trek Health, Payerset, Clarify Health, Gigasheet, H1 / Ribbon, PolicyReporter, plus Milliman/Optum internally.
all.ml_unlock: Payer-provider contract negotiation intelligence and network design: predict the 'true' effective rate per provider and payer, and simulate renegotiation outcomes. Self-insured employers get plan-level network cost modeling.
all.buyer_and_market: Providers' revenue-cycle teams, payers, self-insured employers and benefits consultants. US commercial health spending is about $1.4T; the plausible software and data TAM is in the billions.
all.why_now: The data has been mature for 3+ years, CMS keeps tightening standards, and LLMs help clean it.
all.novelty_risk: Already well mined by funded startups (Turquoise, Serif and others). Late entry; score low for novelty.

all.name: State insurance rate and form filings (SERFF public access)
all.legal_basis: State rate-regulation laws (prior-approval or file-and-use) require P&C, health and life insurers to file rates, rating rules, actuarial memoranda and forms with each state DOI. Most states make filings public once disposed (via SERFF Filing Access or DOI portals). Trade-secret redaction is allowed for some model components. California Prop 103 makes filings public and allows intervenor challenges.
all.dataset: SERFF processed about 518k transactions in 2023. Individual homeowners filing packages reach 346k pages, including scanned rate tables, GLM factor exhibits and actuarial memos. Access is per-state, mostly by web portal and PDF, with no bulk API in many states.
all.current_users: Crowded: ZestyAI (filings analysis product), Insuraviews (VC-backed), S&P Global Market Intelligence RateWatch, Perr&Knight, Quadrant Information Services (rate comparisons), Earnix Filing Accelerator, Verisk/FilingRamp. NAIC is itself piloting AI for SERFF review.
all.ml_unlock: Reconstruct each competitor's full rating algorithm from filed factor tables and predict competitors' next rate moves and market exits by state and line. An auto-generated filing copilot is another option.
all.buyer_and_market: P&C carrier pricing and product teams and MGAs. The intelligence market is a few hundred $M/yr, so it is a niche.
all.why_now: The homeowners crisis (CA/FL withdrawals), record rate filings, and LLMs able to parse 300k-page packages.
all.novelty_risk: High. Multiple funded startups and incumbents are already doing this, and the market looks like the $100-200M niche the user rejected.

all.name: OpenFEMA NFIP redacted claims and policies
all.legal_basis: FEMA publishes NFIP data via the OpenFEMA program under the OPEN Government Data Act (2019) and FEMA open-data policy. Data is redacted (no addresses; census-tract or rounded lat/long) to satisfy the Privacy Act.
all.dataset: About 2.7M NFIP claims (1978-present) and about 70M+ policy transaction records, available as bulk CSV/Parquet and an API. Clean and well documented.
all.current_users: Heavily used: First Street, Fathom (Swiss Re), ICEYE, Cotality (CoreLogic), Verisk, ZestyAI, Neptune Flood, Kettle, plus many academic ML papers.
all.ml_unlock: Property-level flood loss prediction for private flood insurance. This is already done.
all.buyer_and_market: Private flood insurers and MGAs, mortgage lenders. Flood premium is about $4-5B; the NFIP itself is about $3.5B.
all.why_now: Risk Rating 2.0 and growth of private flood cover. Little that is new.
all.novelty_risk: Very crowded and clean public data, so there is no edge. Score low.

all.name: DOL ERISA Form 5500 (Schedule A insurance) and LCA/PERM labor disclosures
all.legal_basis: ERISA §§103-104 require annual Form 5500 filings for employee benefit plans, including Schedule A carrier premiums and broker commissions and audited financial attachments. These are public via EFAST2 bulk downloads. The INA and 20 CFR 655/656 require H-1B LCA and PERM disclosures, which DOL OFLC publishes quarterly.
all.dataset: About 800k+ Form 5500 filings/yr with PDF attachments. LCA/PERM: millions of records with employer, job and wage, as CSV/XLSX.
all.current_users: Very crowded. Form 5500: Judy Diamond, Benefeature, Larkspur, BenefitFlow, Freeerisa, Apify scrapers. LCA/PERM: MyVisaJobs, H1BGrader, Levels.fyi, Revelio Labs, Lightcast.
all.ml_unlock: Predict which employers will switch benefits broker or carrier, or estimate role-level pay. Both are incremental.
all.buyer_and_market: Benefits brokers' sales teams and HR-tech. The market is a few hundred $M.
all.why_now: Nothing new.
all.novelty_risk: Already mined by many incumbents. Not a winner.

all.name: FCC Equipment Authorization exhibits (FCC ID internal photos, RF test reports, manuals), plus foreign analogs (ISED REL, Korea RRA, Taiwan NCC, Anatel)
all.jurisdiction: US (analog regimes in Canada, Korea, Taiwan, Brazil, Japan MIC)
all.legal_basis: 47 CFR Part 2 Subpart J (2.1033 application exhibits) with confidentiality under 47 CFR 0.457/0.459 and OET KDB 726920. Every intentional radiator sold in the US (phones, IoT, cars, wearables, servers with radios, drones) needs a grant. Short-term confidentiality (STC) on internal and external photos, test setup photos and user manuals runs for a maximum of 180 days from grant. After that, the exhibits become public automatically. Schematics, block diagrams, BOM/parts lists and operational descriptions can stay permanently confidential. Long-term confidentiality for internal photos and manuals needs a special justification plus an NDA or limited-access arrangement, so most devices end up with public internal photos.
all.dataset: Millions of grants since the late 1990s. Each grant includes PDFs: high-resolution internal PCB photos (chip markings are often legible), external photos, RF exposure (SAR) and emissions test reports with measured power by band, antenna specs, label locations and user manuals. Access is through the FCC EAS/OET search (apps.fcc.gov/oetcf/eas), with no clean bulk API. Third-party mirrors such as fccid.io and device.report scrape it. The data is heterogeneous: scanned and generated PDFs from hundreds of test labs and TCBs. Grants often surface 1-6 months before product launch, and internal photos follow within 6 months of grant.
all.current_users: Mostly hobbyists, journalists who spot pre-launch devices (Apple, Google, Samsung leaks), RF engineers, and patent/SEP analysts working by hand. fccid.io and device.report are scraped mirrors without analytics. TechInsights (and formerly IHS/Omdia teardown services) sells teardown, BOM and design-win intelligence based on physical teardowns, not systematic ML over FCC exhibits. I found no funded startup doing ML BOM/design-win extraction at scale from FCC/ISED exhibits; my searches returned only TechInsights.
all.ml_unlock: An automated 'virtual teardown' of every radio-equipped product on the market: vision plus OCR models read chip top-markings and module IDs from internal photos, link them to SAR and RF test data, and output a continuously updated design-win and BOM graph (which chip, PMIC, memory and modem is in which device, by OEM and ODM, over time). Uses: (1) semiconductor competitive intelligence and sales targeting; (2) SEP licensing enforcement, identifying every unlicensed cellular, Wi-Fi or UWB device for pools like Avanci/Sisvel and licensors like InterDigital, Qualcomm and Nokia; (3) supply-chain and sanctions compliance, flagging Section 889/entity-list components (Huawei/HiSilicon, Hikvision modules) in devices sold in the US; (4) investor alt data on design-win share shifts (for example, Qualcomm versus MediaTek versus in-house Apple modem).
all.buyer_and_market: Buyers are semiconductor vendors' strategy and sales teams, SEP licensors and patent pools, hedge funds, and compliance teams at retailers and carriers. Comparables: TechInsights is a multi-hundred-million-dollar-revenue teardown/IP intelligence firm (my estimate, not verified in this search). SEP licensing is a market worth tens of billions of dollars a year in royalties, where finding infringers is a costly bottleneck. Enforcement-linked revenue (share of recovered royalties) gives a path past $1B.
all.why_now: Vision-language models can now read noisy chip markings and messy multi-lab PDF layouts that defeated older OCR. The number of devices with cellular, Wi-Fi 7 and UWB radios is exploding, cellular IoT royalty enforcement (Avanci 5G vehicle, IoT pools) is ramping, and US enforcement of the Section 889/covered list (FCC 2022 ban on authorizing Huawei, ZTE, Hikvision and Dahua equipment) gives compliance buyers urgency.
all.novelty_risk: Moderate. TechInsights could add this but relies on physical teardowns for a few hundred flagship devices a year, while the long tail (tens of thousands of IoT grants a year) is unmined. FCC terms and scraping are fine because the data is public. The main risks are a buyer base that is concentrated in semis and SEP, and chips sometimes hidden under shields or epoxy, which limits recall.

all.name: FAA OE/AAA obstruction evaluation filings (Form 7460-1) as a leading indicator of physical infrastructure buildout
all.legal_basis: 14 CFR Part 77 requires notice to the FAA (Form 7460-1) for any structure or temporary crane over 200 ft AGL, or near airports above certain slopes. That covers wind turbines, MET towers, cell towers, transmission structures, tall buildings, and construction cranes for large projects such as data centers and fabs. Filings and determinations (Determination of No Hazard) are public at oeaaa.faa.gov, typically months to years before the project is announced or built. There is no confidentiality period; filings are public on submission or circularization.
all.dataset: Hundreds of thousands of aeronautical study cases since the 2000s. Each has lat/long, height AGL/AMSL, structure type, sponsor name (often an LLC shell), filing and expiry dates, and determination letters (PDFs). There are bulk download interfaces and per-case PDFs. Sponsor names are obfuscated through LLCs and consultants, which is the messy, under-exploited part.
all.current_users: The US Fish and Wildlife Service and USGS (wind turbine database), wind developers and consultants (Capitol Airspace, etc.), and tower companies. Construction lead-gen firms (Dodge Construction Network, ConstructConnect) mostly rely on permits and bids. My search found no evidence that anyone systematically uses OE/AAA with ML to track data center, fab or energy pipelines.
all.ml_unlock: An 'infrastructure precognition' engine. It fuses OE/AAA crane and structure filings with entity resolution (LLC to parent, for example a hyperscaler shell), utility interconnection queues and permits to predict where and when data centers, wind farms, transmission lines and fabs will be built, months before announcement. Outputs include probability of construction, MW load, and timing.
all.buyer_and_market: Buyers are power traders and utilities (load forecasting), data center REITs and land developers, equipment vendors (transformers, switchgear, turbines), construction lead-gen firms, and hedge funds tracking AI capex. The construction intelligence market (Dodge, ConstructConnect) is roughly $1B+ in combined revenue (my estimate, not verified). Data center market intelligence is a fast-growing niche. As a standalone dataset this is narrow; it needs fusion with other forced disclosures to be a large company.
all.why_now: The AI data center buildout is the largest capex wave in decades, every buyer is desperate for early site intelligence, and LLM entity resolution of shell sponsors and consultants is now cheap.
all.novelty_risk: Moderate-to-high crowding in data center tracking generally (several datacenter-intel firms use permits, satellite imagery and interconnection queues). OE/AAA specifically seems underused, but it is a feature, not a company, unless combined with other sources.

all.name: FCC experimental licenses (Part 5), ULS, and ECFS ex parte disclosures as a corporate R&D and regulatory 'leak' feed
all.legal_basis: 47 CFR Part 5 requires any company testing unlicensed radio tech (new devices, satellites, drones, 6G, mmWave) to apply for an experimental license. Applications are public, with limited confidentiality, and narrative exhibits are often confidential while location, frequencies and the applicant are public. 47 CFR 1.1206 ex parte rules require written disclosure of every lobbying meeting in permit-but-disclose proceedings, posted in ECFS. ULS and IBFS/ICFS licensing are public by statute.
all.dataset: Tens of thousands of experimental license applications (OET ELS), millions of ECFS filings (comments, ex parte letters, PDFs), and the ULS licenses database with bulk weekly downloads. The PDFs are heterogeneous and unstructured. ECFS has an API.
all.current_users: Journalists (who found Amazon's disguised experimental tests, Apple and Google pre-launch tests), telecom lawyers and lobbyists, and a few policy-intelligence services (FiscalNote, Bloomberg Government, Policy-tracking tools). Hedge-fund alt-data use is ad hoc. My search found no dedicated ML startup.
all.ml_unlock: A model that predicts corporate product launches and FCC regulatory outcomes. It classifies experimental filings by technology and parent company (seeing through the shells companies use), and models ex parte meeting patterns to forecast rulemaking votes (spectrum reallocations worth billions to carriers and satellite operators).
all.buyer_and_market: Hedge funds (telecom, satellite, semis), corporate strategy teams, telecom law firms. This is a slice of alternative data spend (several billion dollars a year industry-wide), but the addressable part here is likely under $100M a year. Too small alone.
all.why_now: The spectrum pipeline is being restored (FCC auction authority returned in 2025 with mandated auctions of 800 MHz), a direct-to-device satellite boom is driving filings, and LLMs make unstructured ECFS PDFs tractable.
all.novelty_risk: Low crowding, but the market is small and it overlaps with policy-intelligence incumbents (FiscalNote, Bloomberg Gov). Probably a feature, not a $1B company.

all.name: ITU Space Network filings (BR IFIC / SNS) and FCC Space Bureau Part 25 filings
all.jurisdiction: International (ITU Radio Regulations) plus US FCC
all.legal_basis: ITU Radio Regulations Articles 9 and 11 require administrations to file advance publication, coordination requests and notifications for every satellite network, which the ITU publishes in the biweekly BR International Frequency Information Circular (BR IFIC). Filings get priority by date, which creates 'paper satellite' incentives. FCC Part 25 requires public applications with orbital debris mitigation showings, EPFD analyses, and milestone and deployment reports.
all.dataset: Tens of thousands of satellite network filings with orbital parameters, frequency assignments, power and antenna patterns (SRS database, BR IFIC; partly subscription or DVD, with some free access). FCC ICFS filings are public PDFs including debris analyses and interference studies.
all.current_users: Spectrum coordination consultants and software vendors (Transfinite Visualyse, ITU's own tools), satellite operators' regulatory teams, and national administrations (for example, the Netherlands' algorithmic ITU database analysis). This is a small professional niche, and I found no ML startup.
all.ml_unlock: Interference and coordination-outcome prediction for mega-constellations, an automated 'paper satellite' detector, and forecasts of which filings will actually be built (combined with launch manifests and FCC milestones).
all.buyer_and_market: Satellite operators, national regulators, insurers and investors. The market is small: coordination tooling and consulting is probably under $100M a year globally (estimate). Fails the market-size filter.
all.why_now: There are 100k+ satellites proposed in filings, direct-to-device spectrum fights are under way, and WRC-27 preparations are ongoing.
all.novelty_risk: Low crowding, but a niche market and a slow, regulator-centric buyer base. Score low on size.

all.name: EU DSA Article 39 advertising repositories (VLOP ad libraries)
all.legal_basis: Digital Services Act Article 39 requires very large online platforms and search engines (Meta, Google, TikTok, X, LinkedIn, Snap, Pinterest, Amazon, etc.) to keep public repositories of every ad shown in the EU. Each ad is kept for 1 year after its last impression and includes content, advertiser, payer, dates, targeting and exclusion parameters, and reach by member state. Spend is not disclosed for commercial ads; spend bands are disclosed only for political ads.
all.dataset: Every ad served in the EU on VLOPs: billions of creatives with targeting and per-country reach. Meta has an official API (ads_archive), and TikTok has the Commercial Content API (application required). Google, LinkedIn, Snap and Pinterest have no official API (web UI only), and X offers CSV exports.
all.current_users: This space is crowded. adlibrary.com (11-platform API with estimated spend), Foreplay, Atria, Creatify, Superscale and many Apify scrapers sell creative and competitor intelligence. Incumbents Pathmatics/Sensor Tower and MediaRadar estimate ad spend. Mozilla and academic researchers audit the repositories.
all.ml_unlock: Reverse-engineering spend and ROAS: inferring commercial ad spend and creative performance from reach, run-length and targeting (DSA reach data is a quasi ground truth that pre-DSA ad-intel lacked). Plus generative creative optimization trained on what competitors keep running.
all.buyer_and_market: DTC brands, agencies and hedge funds (ad spend as a revenue proxy). The ad intelligence market is several hundred million dollars a year, but crowded.
all.why_now: EU per-country reach data since 2023 is new, and AI creative generation drives demand for 'what works' data.
all.novelty_risk: High. Many funded tools already exist and the barrier is low. Score low.

all.name: EU DSA Transparency Database (statements of reasons for content moderation)
all.legal_basis: Digital Services Act Article 24(5) requires online platforms to submit every content moderation decision and statement of reasons (content per Article 17) to a public, machine-readable Commission database 'without undue delay'.
all.dataset: 2.8 billion+ statements of reasons as of January 2024 (about 12 million a day), now likely tens of billions. There are 33 fields (decision type, ToS versus illegal grounds, automated detection and decision flags, territorial scope, content dates), accessible via the transparency.dsa.ec.europa.eu web interface, API and daily dumps. The data is of low quality: 99.8% cite ToS grounds, free text is templated, and optional fields are mostly null. There is no actual content.
all.current_users: Academic researchers (arXiv audits), the dsatdb Python package, NGOs and regulators. There is no meaningful commercial use.
all.ml_unlock: At most, benchmarking platforms' moderation consistency, or compliance analytics for DSA audits. No high-value prediction is available because the content itself is not included.
all.buyer_and_market: Trust and safety teams, DSA auditors and regulators. Small (well under $100M).
all.why_now: DSA enforcement fines and mandatory audits are ongoing.
all.novelty_risk: Not crowded, because it is commercially weak. Fails the size filter.

all.name: FCC Broadband Data Collection (BDC) / National Broadband Map and challenges
all.legal_basis: The Broadband DATA Act (2020) and 47 CFR Part 1 Subpart V require all ISPs to file location-level availability and speed twice a year, publish them on the National Broadband Map, and run a public challenge process. The map drives $42.45B in BEAD allocations.
all.dataset: Availability claims for every ISP across about 115M+ Broadband Serviceable Locations, with bulk downloads every six months, plus challenge data. Note that the location fabric is licensed from CostQuest and is not fully open.
all.current_users: This space is crowded. CostQuest (fabric vendor), Ookla, Measurement Lab, BroadbandNow, state broadband offices and consultants (CTC, Vernonburg), and dozens of BEAD analytics startups, plus fiber builders' internal teams.
all.ml_unlock: Predicting overstated coverage and optimal subsidy-bid strategy for ISPs in BEAD and state grants.
all.buyer_and_market: ISPs, state broadband offices and fiber investors. This is a one-off, subsidy-driven market that is shrinking as BEAD awards finish in 2025-2026.
all.why_now: The BEAD restructuring ('Benefit of the Bargain', 2025) is shifting awards, but the window is closing.
all.novelty_risk: High crowding and a closing window. Score low.

all.name: India RERA project filings: quarterly progress reports, approvals and financials for every real-estate project
all.jurisdiction: India (each state RERA, about 30 portals; MahaRERA, UP-RERA, HRERA, TNRERA, K-RERA and others)
all.legal_basis: Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act 2016. S.3 requires registration before any project is advertised. S.4 requires sanctioned plans, approvals, land title, a declared completion date and a 70% escrow declaration. S.11 requires public quarterly updates on units booked, construction status and approvals. State rules add QPR financials, photos, and engineer, architect or CA certificates. Penalties for missed filings reach 5% of project cost (S.61/63). Filings are public from registration onward; there is no confidentiality period.
all.dataset: Hundreds of thousands of registered projects, each with a time series of QPRs, plan revisions, extension orders and complaint/adjudication records. Format is heterogeneous: Haryana and MP mostly upload scanned PDF certificates, MahaRERA and UP have structured project pages, and Gujarat has colour charts. Compliance is patchy: about 75-80% of ongoing MahaRERA projects skip QPRs, and only 35-57% of Haryana projects file. That gap is itself a predictive signal. Access is by scraping state portals; there is no bulk API.
all.current_users: Verified.RealEstate sells AI-based monitoring of TNRERA filings (slipping completion dates, stalled progress while collections continue) to buyers and lenders. Generic scrapers sell RERA data extraction (e.g. Actowiz). Proptech portals (Square Yards, Housing, PropEquity, Liases Foras, ANAROCK) show RERA IDs and status. I found no funded startup offering a cross-state, ML-driven project-completion and default score.
all.ml_unlock: A 'credit bureau for under-construction real estate'. A model ingests every state's QPRs, certificates, plan revisions, complaints and missed filings, plus satellite imagery of the site, and outputs a per-project probability of a 12/24-month delay or stall, with a developer-level contagion score. It could also price surety bonds and construction loans, and flag diversion of escrow money.
all.buyer_and_market: Construction-finance lenders (banks, NBFCs, AIFs, the government SWAMIH stressed-housing fund). Insurers writing the IRDAI surety bonds introduced in 2022. Homebuyers via portals (B2B2C). Rating agencies. Stalled housing in India is estimated, from memory and not verified this session, at roughly 0.4-0.5M units worth around INR 4-5 lakh crore (about $50-60B; ANAROCK estimates). Developer and construction lending runs to several INR lakh crore. A 10-50 bps pricing edge, or avoiding a single defaulted loan, is worth a lot to a lender. A SaaS/data business serving India-only lenders likely caps at $100-300M ARR unless it expands into insurance underwriting or lending itself.
all.why_now: RERA is about 8 years old, so there are now enough complete project life cycles (completed vs stalled) to train on. LLM/VLM parsing of scanned certificates and photos is newly cheap. Surety insurance for RERA projects is new and needs underwriting data. Stalled-project stress (Supertech, Jaypee, Amrapali) keeps lenders paying attention.
all.novelty_risk: Moderate. Proptech incumbents and small diligence firms touch the data, but none appears to run cross-state outcome-labelled prediction. Risks: messy multi-state scraping, possible portal access blocks, and India data-business willingness to pay is lower than in the US.

all.name: Chile SEIA / e-SEIA: every environmental impact study and declaration since 1997, extendable to Latin American licensing systems
all.jurisdiction: Chile (SEA). Extensions: Peru SENACE, Colombia ANLA, Brazil IBAMA/state licensing, Mexico SEMARNAT MIA gazette
all.legal_basis: Ley 19.300 (Bases Generales del Medio Ambiente) and the SEIA Regulation (DS 40/2012). Projects above listed thresholds (mining, energy, transmission, ports, water, real estate) must file a DIA or EIA. The full file is public immediately and permanently on e-SEIA: baseline studies, annexes, agency observations (ICSARA), the proponent's responses (Adendas), citizen-participation comments, the evaluation report (ICE) and the RCA resolution. There is no confidentiality period. The Escazú Agreement reinforces access.
all.dataset: Tens of thousands of projects since 1997; figure from memory, not verified this session. Each project carries hundreds to thousands of pages: scanned PDFs, Excel baseline monitoring data, KMZ/shape geometry, and the full regulatory Q&A trail with an outcome label (approved, rejected, withdrawn), duration and imposed conditions. Mining and energy baseline studies hold expensive private field data: hydrogeology, flora and fauna surveys, air quality, archaeology. Access is by web scraping of e-SEIA; there is no bulk dump.
all.current_users: Academic only, as far as I found. A FONDEF-funded UANDES/PUCV project builds NLP plus ML 'approval probability' and regulatory-risk indicators for the Atacama region, expanding to Antofagasta. Environmental consultancies (e.g. GHD, Jaime Illanes, Arcadis) reuse baselines manually. US permitting-AI startups (Paces, Transect, PermitFlow) do not cover Chile or Latin America.
all.ml_unlock: A permitting copilot and oracle for Latin American mining and energy. (1) For a new project, predict the ICSARA questions agencies will ask, the approval probability, the time to RCA and the likely conditions, using all prior files near the site. (2) Auto-generate baseline chapters and the Adenda responses from the public corpus plus nearby prior baselines. That cuts months and millions of dollars per EIA and reduces litigation risk (Tribunales Ambientales reversals are common).
all.buyer_and_market: Mining, lithium, copper, green-hydrogen, transmission and renewables developers, plus environmental consultancies. Chile has tens of billions of US dollars of investment under evaluation at any time; a large EIA costs $1-10M+ and delays cost far more. Chile alone is a niche (well under $100M/yr). The path to scale is to replicate across Peru, Colombia, Brazil, Mexico and Argentina (RIGI), then sell to global miners. Even then this is closer to a $100-300M ARR outcome unless it becomes a full AI environmental consultancy taking a share of the roughly $1B+ Latin American EIA-consulting spend.
all.why_now: Long-document LLMs can finally read 3,000-page EIAs and their Adendas. Chile's 2024-25 'permisología' reform push and the lithium/copper/green-hydrogen pipeline create urgency. US permitting-AI startups have validated the category but ignore Latin America.
all.novelty_risk: Low commercial competition, but a real academic/government effort (FONDEF), and SEA may build its own tools. Market-size risk is the main weakness: it may land in the $100-200M niche category the user already rejected unless it expands across Latin America.

all.name: China mandatory enterprise environmental information disclosure plus pollutant-permit self-monitoring data
all.jurisdiction: China (Ministry of Ecology and Environment and provincial EEBs)
all.legal_basis: MEE 'Measures for the Administration of Legal Disclosure of Enterprise Environmental Information' (issued Dec 18 2021, effective Feb 8 2022), with Format Guidelines. Covered entities are key pollutant dischargers, mandatory clean-production-audit firms, and listed companies/bond issuers penalized in the prior year. They must publish annual reports by March 15 covering permits, emissions, self-monitoring results, hazardous waste, carbon emissions by facility and violations, plus ad hoc reports. A separate Pollutant Discharge Permit regime publishes the permits themselves (capacity, process lines, emission limits) and self-monitoring and execution reports. Many provinces publish online CEMS data. Disclosure is immediate, with no confidentiality period.
all.dataset: Facility-level permits and monitoring for hundreds of thousands of plants (steel, cement, coke, power, chemicals, paper); scale from memory. Data includes stack-level CEMS readings (near real time in some provinces), annual reports and capacity and process data. It is spread across national and provincial platforms with heterogeneous formats, many PDFs, and Chinese-only interfaces. It is free to view; there is no bulk export.
all.current_users: IPE (Ma Jun's NGO) aggregates the data into the Blue Map / China Pollution Map Database and sells supply-chain screening to brands. Academic groups (e.g. the CHIPOMAP project) use it. TransitionZero and others estimate Chinese steel output and CO2 mostly from satellite data. Commodity and quant funds and alt-data vendors use satellite and CEMS-derived indicators, but I found no startup openly productizing permit-plus-CEMS nowcasting.
all.ml_unlock: Plant-level nowcasting of Chinese heavy-industry output and utilization (steel, cement, aluminium, coke, power). Emissions from CEMS and the permit-declared process lines translate into daily production estimates, fused with satellite data. The product would forecast official NBS output and commodity prices weeks earlier, and give a facility-level carbon dataset for CBAM verification.
all.buyer_and_market: Commodity trading houses, quant and macro hedge funds, iron-ore and coal miners (BHP, Rio, Vale), and EU importers facing CBAM (definitive phase from 2026). The alternative-data market is several billion dollars a year and growing, and China industrial nowcasting is among the most valuable verticals. A credible path exists to $100M+ ARR serving funds plus CBAM compliance.
all.why_now: The 2022 measures mandated carbon and facility disclosure. CBAM's definitive period started in 2026 and needs installation-level emissions for Chinese steel and aluminium. LLM translation and parsing of Chinese PDFs is cheap.
all.novelty_risk: High geopolitical and legal risk. China's Data Security Law, the 2023 crackdowns on foreign due-diligence and expert-network firms (Mintz, Capvision), and restrictions on offshore access to Wind and CNKI make systematic export of industrial data by a foreign startup legally dangerous, and platforms can be shut off at any time. Satellite-based competitors (Kayrros, SpaceKnow, TransitionZero) occupy the nowcasting buyer relationships. A US YC company is a poor fit.

all.name: Brazil ANP exploration and production data (BDEP): seismic and well data released after confidentiality
all.legal_basis: Lei do Petróleo 9.478/1997 makes E&P data a national asset. Operators and acquisition companies must deliver all seismic, well and geochemistry data to ANP. Under ANP Resolution 757/2018 that data becomes public after 5 years (exclusive) or 10 years (non-exclusive, i.e. multi-client). A long-pending draft would lengthen this to 10/15 years and 30 years for 'areas of federal exploratory interest'. ANP has also made public data from 23 onshore basins free.
all.dataset: BDEP holds decades of 2D/3D seismic, tens of thousands of wells (logs, cores, reports) and geochemistry, in heterogeneous formats (SEG-Y, LAS, scanned reports). Access is via ANP requests and technical data packages; parts are free onshore.
all.current_users: Oil majors, Petrobras, multi-client seismic firms (TGS, CGG/Viridien, SLB), Brazilian universities via RNP, and many consultancies. More than 9,000 data requests in a decade. ML-on-subsurface vendors (e.g. Bluware, Earth Science Analytics, and the majors' in-house teams) already work on seismic and well interpretation.
all.ml_unlock: A Brazil-wide subsurface foundation model trained on released seismic plus wells to predict prospectivity in open-acreage (Oferta Permanente) blocks, including the onshore and equatorial margin, and hydrogen/helium/CO2-storage potential. It would sell ranked block picks before each permanent-offer cycle.
all.buyer_and_market: Small and mid-cap E&Ps bidding in ANP Oferta Permanente, CCS developers and natural-hydrogen explorers. The bigger prize is a global multi-regime subsurface model (Norway Diskos, UK NDR, Australia NOPIMS, Brazil BDEP), but that enters the crowded subsurface-AI space.
all.why_now: Oferta Permanente is continuously auctioning blocks, equatorial margin exploration is restarting, and interest in natural hydrogen and CCS is rising.
all.novelty_risk: Crowded and structurally a Terranox clone (an ML prospectivity model on mandatorily disclosed exploration data), which the brief says is not a valid winner. Majors and seismic vendors already mine it, and oil is a shrinking-interest sector for VC. Listed for completeness only.

all.name: Brazil CAR (Cadastro Ambiental Rural) plus GTA animal-transit guides plus embargo lists: self-declared boundaries of about 7M rural properties
all.legal_basis: Forest Code Lei 12.651/2012 Art. 29 makes registration of every rural property mandatory. The owner declares the perimeter, permanent preservation areas (APP), legal reserve and remnant vegetation. The geometry is public via SICAR. GTA animal-transit guides are mandatory for cattle movement; some states expose them. IBAMA embargo lists and INCRA SIGEF certified boundaries are public.
all.dataset: Polygons for about 7M properties (count from memory, not verified this session), downloadable as shapefiles by municipality, plus status flags; combined with PRODES/DETER deforestation rasters. GTA data is partially public by state. Messy issues include overlapping self-declared polygons, fraud and unvalidated registrations.
all.current_users: Very crowded. State-run free 'Selo Verde' platforms (Pará, Minas Gerais, Acre, Espírito Santo, built by UFMG) check CAR and PRODES compliance for the EUDR. Agrotools, TerraMagna (agri-credit fintech using satellite plus public registries), Traive, Satelligence, Trase/Global Forest Watch, Imaflora and the big traders' in-house teams are all active.
all.ml_unlock: Indirect-supplier deforestation and land-grab detection: infer cattle laundering chains from GTA flows plus CAR overlaps plus imagery, and price farm credit and EUDR due-diligence risk.
all.buyer_and_market: EU importers and traders under the EUDR (applies from end-2026 after two delays), banks and Brazilian agri-credit (CPR) lenders. The market is large, but it is being commoditised by free government tools and well-funded incumbents.
all.why_now: EUDR enforcement at end-2026, and Brazil's CPR agri-credit boom.
all.novelty_risk: Heavily mined; free state platforms undercut pricing; EUDR delays reduce urgency. Not a good fit.

all.name: India MCA21: mandatory public financial statements of every private company (and the Korea DART equivalent for externally audited unlisted firms)
all.jurisdiction: India (Ministry of Corporate Affairs); analogous regime in Korea (DART, Act on External Audit of Stock Companies)
all.legal_basis: Companies Act 2013 s.137 requires every company, including private ones, to file audited financial statements (Form AOC-4/XBRL) and an annual return (MGT-7: shareholding, directors) with the Registrar of Companies, viewable by anyone for a fee. This is unusual: US private companies disclose nothing. Korea similarly forces unlisted companies above audit thresholds to post audited statements on DART.
all.dataset: Financials and charge (secured-loan) registrations for about 1.5-2M active Indian companies over 10+ years; size from memory. Mixed XBRL and scanned-PDF attachments. Access is via the MCA V3 portal (per-document fees) or resellers.
all.current_users: Crowded: Tofler, Probe42, Zauba Corp, Crisil, CIBIL, Perfios, Lentra and most Indian SME lenders. In Korea, NICE and KED credit bureaus plus fintechs (e.g. Deepsearch).
all.ml_unlock: Private-company default and fraud prediction, and supplier-risk scoring for global procurement teams sourcing from India (China+1).
all.buyer_and_market: SME lenders, trade-credit insurers, and global procurement/KYB platforms. Large in aggregate, but incumbents already sell exactly this.
all.why_now: The China+1 supply-chain shift raises foreign demand for Indian counterparty diligence; LLMs can parse the scanned annexures.
all.novelty_risk: Already well mined by funded data companies and bureaus; low differentiation. Score low.

all.name: EU Data Act: forced sharing of connected-product data (industrial machines, farm equipment, vehicles, HVAC, medical and energy devices)
all.jurisdiction: EU / EEA (27 member states plus EEA)
all.legal_basis: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 (Data Act), applying since 12 Sept 2025. Under Art. 4–5, the user of a connected product can access the product and related-service data free of charge, in machine-readable form and in real time where feasible. The user can also tell the data holder (the OEM) to send that data to a third party of the user's choice. The third party may be charged FRAND compensation. From 12 Sept 2026, products placed on the market must be designed for access (Art. 3). Limits: (1) gatekeepers cannot be recipients; (2) the data cannot be used to build a competing product; (3) a 'trade secrets handbrake' and a safety handbrake let OEMs withhold some data; (4) products made by micro and small firms are exempt. There is no confidentiality period. Access depends on the user's consent, so this is not a public dump.
all.dataset: This is not one public file. Under the law, a third party can obtain raw sensor and telemetry streams (vibration, temperature, fault codes, hours, energy use, GPS) for any connected machine whose owner signs up, whichever OEM made it. Volume is potentially enormous (tens of millions of industrial and agricultural assets in the EU). The data arrives as heterogeneous OEM APIs and exports. Format quality varies widely. Many OEMs are still building portals (Proemion offers a Data Act data portal), and some will resist through the trade-secret clause.
all.current_users: Mostly compliance vendors so far: Proemion, Fiskil, Nortal and consultancies selling OEM compliance. Incumbent predictive-maintenance companies (Augury, Uptake, Cognite, Siemens/Senseye, SparkCognition) mostly fit their own sensors or work through OEM partnerships. I found no well-funded startup positioned explicitly as a 'Data Act-native' multi-OEM aftermarket or underwriting layer.
all.ml_unlock: An OEM-agnostic foundation model for machine health, trained across brands on Data Act-pulled telemetry. Products built on it: (a) independent predictive maintenance and parts forecasting for mixed fleets, breaking the OEM aftermarket lock-in; (b) pricing equipment-breakdown insurance and residual value for lessors and used-equipment marketplaces (an 'asset-level credit score' for machines); (c) verified usage data for equipment-as-a-service financing. The legal novelty is that a third party can get a competitor OEM's machine data with the customer's consent, which was impossible before 2025.
all.buyer_and_market: Buyers: multi-brand fleet operators (construction rental, agriculture contractors, plants), independent service organisations, equipment lessors and insurers. The industrial aftermarket and service market in Europe is worth hundreds of billions of euros. The predictive-maintenance software market is usually estimated at about $10B+ globally (analyst estimates, not verified here). Equipment-breakdown insurance and leasing underwriting is a further multi-billion-dollar pool. A path to a large company is plausible if it becomes the default multi-OEM data intermediary.
all.why_now: The access right only went live in Sept 2025, and the access-by-design obligation starts in Sept 2026. Standards, APIs and enforcement (national authorities such as BNetzA) are being set now. Whoever builds the aggregation layer and the cross-OEM training corpus in 2026–27 gets a data moat.
all.novelty_risk: Medium. The idea is obvious to incumbents, and OEMs (Siemens, Deere, CNH, Caterpillar) will drag their feet and use the trade-secret handbrake and the 'no competing product' clause. Execution needs sales to fleet owners and a lot of integration work. There is legal-uncertainty risk until the first enforcement cases. It is less crowded than the open datasets below because the data is not public: you must earn each user's consent.

all.name: Norway Diskos and Sodir released petroleum, CCS and offshore-wind subsurface data (with the UK NSTA National Data Repository as a twin)
all.jurisdiction: Norway (Norwegian Continental Shelf); a similar regime exists in the UK (NSTA NDR)
all.legal_basis: Under the Norwegian petroleum regulations (Petroleum Act and resource-management regulations), licensees must report all well, seismic and production data to the Norwegian Offshore Directorate (Sodir). Data is confidential for a limited period: Sodir cites a '2/5-year period', roughly 2 years for well data and longer for some seismic, with release on relinquishment. After that it is released via Diskos. Sodir has also loaded CCS data (since 2017) and offshore-wind site data (2023). This is the closest analogue to SMAD in my lane, but it is hydrocarbon and storage subsurface, not mineral assessment.
all.dataset: Petabytes of well logs, cores and core photos, palynology slides (multi-gigapixel), completion reports (many scanned PDFs), 2D/3D seismic and production data, covering 50+ years and thousands of wells. Sodir announced 30,000 more datasets made publicly accessible in 2023. Access: Diskos members download directly. Non-members order through the Diskos Public Portal, and the overview of released data is open to all. FactPages are free for wells more than 20 years old.
all.current_users: Oil majors and Diskos members (Equinor, Aker BP and others). Halliburton runs the Diskos data platform. Earth Science Analytics (Norwegian ML startup, EarthNET) applies ML to Diskos data for prospectivity and rock properties and partners with Rockwash Geodata. Cognite, SLB and S&P (CSM) offer analytics. Petroleum ML is well mined. CCS and geothermal reuse is less so.
all.ml_unlock: A subsurface model that ranks and de-risks CO2 storage sites (capacity, injectivity, caprock and fault leakage risk) and repurposes legacy wells and seismic for geothermal and hydrogen storage. It would cut site characterisation from years and hundreds of millions of dollars to months. It would also check legacy wellbore integrity (leak risk of plugged and abandoned wells crossing storage complexes) by reading scanned completion reports with VLMs.
all.buyer_and_market: Buyers: CCS licensees on the NCS and UKCS (Equinor/Northern Lights, Shell, TotalEnergies; Norway has awarded multiple CO2 storage licences, and the UK has awarded 20+), plus insurers of storage liability. The CCS subsurface characterisation and MMV services market is estimated at low single-digit $B per year globally. That is probably smaller than the founder's bar unless the product expands to global CCS and geothermal.
all.why_now: North Sea CCS is scaling: Northern Lights began injecting in 2025, and EU NZIA requires 50 Mt/yr storage capacity by 2030 from oil and gas producers. Released legacy data is the cheapest characterisation input. Modern VLMs can now read the scanned report backlog.
all.novelty_risk: Medium-high. The data is known to every major, and Earth Science Analytics and the service companies already apply ML to it. The CCS angle is less crowded, but buyers are few and concentrated. It is also close to the founder's existing geoscience lane, so it may feel 'mining-adjacent'.

all.name: German Marktstammdatenregister (MaStR): mandatory register of every generator, storage unit and large consumer
all.legal_basis: Energy Industry Act (EnWG §111e) and the Marktstammdatenregisterverordnung (MaStRV). Every operator of an electricity or gas generation unit (down to balcony solar), every battery storage unit and every large grid-connected consumer must register master data with the Bundesnetzagentur. There is no confidentiality period. Data is published under licence DL-DE-BY-2.0. Exact location is withheld for units under 30 kW (postcode or municipality only).
all.dataset: Several million units, the large majority rooftop PV, plus wind, storage, CHP, etc. Fields include capacity, commissioning date, technology, operator, EEG subsidy data and grid-connection points, linked to grid operators. Bulk download is daily zipped XML, with a SOAP API. The open-mastr Python package and Zenodo CSVs exist. The data is clean-ish but has many operator-entered errors.
all.current_users: Researchers (open-mastr by RLI/fortiss, the eGon project), energy consultancies (enervis and others), and installers and solar-plus-storage companies (Enpal, 1KOMMA5) for lead generation and market sizing. Grid-planning software firms (envelio/Intelligent Grid Platform, gridX) use it alongside DSO data. It is well known in the German energy scene.
all.ml_unlock: Combine MaStR with DSO grid-connection data and power-price data to predict grid-connection and hosting capacity, and which BESS or solar sites will actually get connected and when, at parcel level. Germany has a grid-connection-request backlog of hundreds of GW of storage. Each developer pays heavily for failed applications, and DSOs are drowning. A second product: infer unregistered or misreported assets and forecast behind-the-meter flexibility for VPPs.
all.buyer_and_market: Buyers: BESS and renewables developers, infrastructure investors and DSOs. German grid-scale storage capex is heading into the tens of billions of euros, and siting intelligence could charge per project. A realistic software TAM is probably $100–500M per year in Germany alone, larger only with an EU rollout. That is borderline against the founder's size bar.
all.why_now: A storage connection-request flood (well over 100 GW of requests reported in 2024–25), new EnWG reforms on connection procedures, and the 2025+ requirement for DSOs to publish grid-connection information.
all.novelty_risk: Medium-high. The register is open, well documented and widely used. Grid-capacity analytics startups exist across Europe (envelio, Pexapark adjacent, and others). The differentiator would be the predictive connection-outcome model, not the data.

all.name: Energy Performance Certificate registers (France DPE open data via ADEME, UK EPC register, EU EPBD recast databases)
all.legal_basis: The EU Energy Performance of Buildings Directive requires an energy certificate on every sale or rental. France additionally requires every DPE to be lodged with ADEME, published as open data since the July 2021 reform. The Loi Climat et Résilience bans renting G-rated homes from 2025, F from 2028 and E from 2034, which makes the DPE legally consequential. The UK publishes its EPC register in bulk. The EPBD recast (2024) requires national EPC databases with public, aggregated access and renovation passports. There is no confidentiality period. The certificate is public once lodged.
all.dataset: France: about 10M+ residential DPE records since 2021, plus tertiary (commercial) DPE, on data.gouv.fr with address, surface, heating system, insulation, consumption and class. The data is messy, has known assessor fraud and bias, and is joinable to DVF prices and the BDNB building database. UK: about 30M+ EPC certificates, bulk downloadable.
all.current_users: Heavily used. In the UK: Kamma, Hestia, Sero, PriceHubble, Furbnow. In France: PriceHubble, Yanport, Hellio and the energy-renovation players. BNP Paribas collaborates with ADEME on DPE for green-mortgage analytics. Apify scrapers sell 'DPE F/G leads'. Several seed startups (some Seedcamp-backed) work on retrofit targeting.
all.ml_unlock: A building-level 'true energy and stranding' model that corrects biased and fraudulent DPE ratings using DVF prices, smart-meter aggregates and imagery. It would predict which of a bank's mortgaged or a landlord's assets will become unlettable under the 2028/2034 bans, plus the cheapest retrofit path and its price impact. Sold as transition-risk underwriting for mortgage books and REIT portfolios.
all.buyer_and_market: Buyers: banks (ECB climate-risk supervision, EU Mortgage Credit Directive green-mortgage flows), institutional landlords, insurers and renovation aggregators. EU mortgage stock is about €7T+. Renovation-wave spend is €100B+ per year. Climate-risk analytics software for real estate is roughly a $1B+ category, but crowded.
all.why_now: French rental bans bite in 2025, 2028 and 2034. The EPBD recast must be transposed by May 2026, with national databases and minimum energy performance standards for non-residential buildings. Banks must report Pillar 3 energy-label data.
all.novelty_risk: High. Many funded proptech and climate-fintech companies already ingest these registers. Differentiation would need proprietary fusion (smart-meter data plus imagery) and distribution into banks.

all.name: Swedish/Nordic public-access principle applied to public procurement (winning and losing bids, unit prices, contracts)
all.jurisdiction: Sweden (Tryckfrihetsförordningen ch. 2, offentlighetsprincipen), similar in Finland, Norway (offentleglova, eInnsyn) and Denmark
all.legal_basis: In Sweden, every document received by a public authority is an allmän handling. Once a contract is awarded, the absolute procurement secrecy lifts (Offentlighets- och sekretesslagen 19:3). After that, anyone can request the submitted tenders, including competitors' prices. Only specific business secrets are redacted, under OSL 31:16, after a harm test. Authorities must keep public registers (diarier) of every document. Norway publishes authority journals via eInnsyn.
all.dataset: Sweden runs about SEK 800B+ per year of public purchasing. Every tender, bid, price sheet, evaluation memo and contract is obtainable on request, but mostly as PDFs and spreadsheets obtained one request at a time, unstructured. Norway's eInnsyn journal metadata is searchable online. There is no bulk dump, so this is an under-exploited, labour-intensive corpus. The 2/5-year confidentiality concept does not apply: disclosure is immediate after award.
all.current_users: Tendium (Stockholm, VC-funded, AI tender search and bid writing), Mercell/Visma Opic (tender aggregation), Proku.ai (Denmark). In the UK, Stotles and Tussell use contract notices. Most players work on notices and tender documents. Systematic harvesting of competitors' priced bids via mass FOI requests appears rare.
all.ml_unlock: A 'should-cost and win-probability' engine. Mass-request and parse every awarded bid with its prices in a category (IT consulting, construction, healthcare supplies), then model the winning price per line item and buyer. Suppliers use it to price bids. Public buyers use it to detect overpricing and collusion (cartel detection for competition authorities).
all.buyer_and_market: Buyers: suppliers bidding public contracts, public buyers and competition authorities. EU public procurement is about €2T per year (about 14% of GDP). Bid-management and tender-intelligence software is a market of a few hundred $M to $1B+. Nordic-only is small. EU expansion is limited because most EU states lack Sweden-style bid access.
all.why_now: LLMs can now parse heterogeneous priced bids at scale. EU procurement directive reform (2026 proposal) and eForms standardisation are increasing structure.
all.novelty_risk: Medium-high. Tender-AI is crowded (Tendium, Mercell, Stotles, Tenderbolt and many GPT wrappers). The priced-bid harvesting moat is real but labour-intensive and Nordic-limited, so the TAM is probably below the bar.

all.name: EU Battery Passport (Batteries Regulation 2023/1542)
all.legal_basis: Regulation (EU) 2023/1542, Art. 77. From 18 Feb 2027, every EV battery, LMT battery and industrial battery over 2 kWh placed on the EU market needs a digital passport via QR code. Some data is public. Composition (point 45) and the dismantling manual (point 48) are restricted to persons with a 'legitimate interest', and the implementing act under Art. 77(9) defining that tier is still pending. Art. 14 gives access to battery-management-system state-of-health data for buyers, second-life operators and others.
all.dataset: About 71 data points per battery, of which 56 apply to EVs. Many are static: manufacturer, chemistry, carbon footprint, recycled content. Dynamic state of health is thin: EVs have only 'State of Certified Energy' (point 61), and industrial batteries are 'if applicable'. The format is decentralised (each economic operator hosts its own), not a central registry. There will be millions of passports per year, but the data is shallow.
all.current_users: Passport and traceability vendors: Circulor, Arianee, Minespider, Spherity, Codibly and others. Battery-health analytics firms (TWAICE, Aviloo, Elysia, Volytica) use BMS data directly rather than passports.
all.ml_unlock: Residual-value and second-life grading for used EV and industrial batteries, trained on passport data plus Art. 14 BMS access. Product: an instant underwriting and pricing score for used-EV lenders, insurers and repurposers.
all.buyer_and_market: Buyers: used-EV lenders and lessors, fleet operators, second-life BESS integrators and recyclers. The used-EV finance and battery second-life market is multi-billion, but battery-health analytics is already served.
all.why_now: The passport is mandatory from Feb 2027, and Data Act access overlaps.
all.novelty_risk: High, and the data is thin. TWAICE (well funded), Aviloo and Elysia already do battery health, and passport SaaS is crowded. The passport carries less state-of-health data than advertised.

all.name: Company-registry financial filings (UK Companies House, Danish CVR, Norway Brønnøysund plus public tax lists, Swedish Bolagsverket) and CSRD/ESRS sustainability reports
all.legal_basis: The Companies Act 2006 requires every UK company to file accounts publicly. Danish, Norwegian and Swedish registries publish annual reports (XBRL in DK and NO). Norway publishes every resident's income, wealth and tax (skattelister). The CSRD requires sustainability reports, but Omnibus I (agreed Dec 2025) cut its scope to EU companies with more than 1,000 employees and more than €450M turnover, roughly an 80–90% reduction. The UK ECCTA reform that would have forced small and micro companies to publish full P&L and file in iXBRL from April 2027 was paused in January 2026, with no new date.
all.dataset: Millions of companies. Filings are partly scanned PDFs (UK small companies) and partly iXBRL. Bulk downloads and free APIs exist (Companies House bulk accounts, CVR API, Brønnøysund API).
all.current_users: Very crowded: Dun & Bradstreet, Creditsafe, Beauhurst, Endole, Proff, Moody's/Bureau van Dijk Orbis, Validis, plus many fintech lenders (iwoca, Funding Circle). For CSRD: MSCI, Clarity AI, Briink, Sweep, Persefoni.
all.ml_unlock: SME default and fraud prediction, or an ESG fact-extraction model. These are incremental, not revolutionary.
all.buyer_and_market: Credit-data and KYB is a large market (tens of billions of dollars) but dominated by incumbents. CSRD data demand shrank sharply after the Omnibus.
all.why_now: Weak: the UK P&L disclosure is paused and the CSRD scope has been cut.
all.novelty_risk: Very high. These are among the most mined disclosure datasets in Europe. French DVF property transactions are similarly saturated (Meilleurs Agents, PriceHubble, Yanport). Listed for completeness only.

all.name: Regulator-forced clinical study report (CSR) disclosure: EMA Policy 0070 plus Health Canada PRCI
all.jurisdiction: EU (EMA) and Canada (Health Canada); the US FDA has no equivalent
all.legal_basis: EMA Policy 0070 (publication started Oct 2016) forces publication of clinical overview, clinical summaries, full individual clinical study reports, protocols, sample case report forms (CRFs) and statistical analysis plans (CTD modules 2.5, 2.7, 5.3) for centrally authorised drugs after the CHMP opinion. Publication was suspended in 2023 except for COVID-19 products. It resumed for new active substances with an opinion from Sept 2023, and a Step 2 expansion began April 2025. Canada: Food and Drugs Act s.30(1.2)(d.1/d.2) and the 2019 amendments to the Food and Drug Regulations and Medical Devices Regulations make clinical information stop being confidential business information (CBI) after a final regulatory decision. The rule applies to past submissions too. A new Health Canada search portal launched in Aug 2026 (Torys). There is no proprietary period beyond the decision date.
all.dataset: Hundreds of drug dossiers, each running to thousands to tens of thousands of pages of redacted PDF CSRs: full efficacy and safety tables, patient narratives, protocol amendments, SAPs and anonymisation reports. Heterogeneous scanned and redacted PDFs with no structured export. EMA requires an account login and offers view-only or download access. Health Canada's portal (clinical-information.canada.ca) restricts use to non-commercial purposes. The data is large, messy and almost unused beyond Cochrane-style academic reviews.
all.current_users: Academic meta-researchers (e.g. Doshi, Herder, Cochrane reviewers). Pharma intelligence vendors (Citeline/Norstella, Evaluate, Clarivate Cortellis) mostly use registry and press data, not full CSRs. Trial-design AI startups (Unlearn.AI, Phesi, QuantHealth, Formation Bio internally) train on registries, sponsor data or Medidata rather than on these CSR dumps. I found no startup positioned on structuring the full EMA and Health Canada CSR corpus.
all.ml_unlock: An LLM and vision pipeline that turns every published CSR into a structured trial-level and arm-level database: endpoints, effect sizes, AE tables, dropout reasons, protocol amendments, and the regulator questions that followed. On top of that sits a model that predicts a new protocol's probability of regulatory success, the expected effect size and variance (for sample sizing), and likely amendment and failure modes. It could also supply external or synthetic control arms built from real comparator-arm data.
all.buyer_and_market: Pharma and biotech clinical development, plus CROs. Global clinical trial spend is about $80-100B/yr. Clinical trial analytics and design software is a multi-$B market, and Medidata alone was acquired for $5.8B. Moving phase-transition success by a few points is worth hundreds of millions per program.
all.why_now: EMA restarted publication in 2023-2025 and expanded it in 2025. Health Canada's new portal arrived in 2026. LLM and vision models can now parse 10k-page redacted PDFs cheaply, which was infeasible in 2018.
all.novelty_risk: Moderate. Licensing is the big caveat: Health Canada terms are non-commercial and EMA terms need checking. A business might have to sell insights, not data, or pair with FDA FOIA'd documents and sponsor partnerships. Incumbents (Citeline, Medidata/Dassault, IQVIA) could move in. The corpus is also small in count (hundreds of drugs), so its value lies in depth, not breadth.

all.name: Patent-mandated biological sequence listings (WIPO ST.26), especially antibody and protein sequences
all.jurisdiction: Global (USPTO, EPO, WIPO PCT, JPO, CNIPA)
all.legal_basis: Patent law requires enabling disclosure, and WIPO Standard ST.26 (mandatory since July 2022) requires machine-readable XML sequence listings for any claimed nucleotide or amino-acid sequence. Applications publish 18 months after priority. Patent sequences then flow into the GenBank and ENA patent divisions and into PLAbDab.
all.dataset: Hundreds of millions of patent sequences, including several hundred thousand therapeutic antibody heavy and light chains, each tied to claims, targets, assignees and dates. PLAbDab (Oxford OPIG) holds about 150k+ patent and literature antibodies. Post-2022 data is in ST.26 XML, while pre-2022 listings are messy text or PDF. Functional data (affinity, epitope, developability) is buried in the patent examples.
all.current_users: Incumbent sequence-search vendors: CAS STNext, Clarivate GenomeQuest, Patsnap Bio, Questel. Academic users include OPIG/PLAbDab and the 'Data mining patented antibody sequences' (mAbs 2021) work. AI antibody-design firms (Absci, Generate, BigHat, Chai, Nabla) use the data as training data but do not productize it.
all.ml_unlock: A generative 'patent-aware' antibody and protein design engine. It would map claimed sequence space per target, predict whether a new design infringes claim scope (CDR identity thresholds, genus claims), and generate novel binders in white space. The patent examples' assay tables (extracted by LLM) would serve as functional labels.
all.buyer_and_market: Biologics developers: IP and legal teams plus discovery teams. The patent analytics market is about $1B. Antibody discovery services run about $5-8B, and biosimilar and biobetter FTO is high-value per decision.
all.why_now: ST.26 XML made the post-2022 corpus machine-readable. Generative antibody models make 'design around' a real product.
all.novelty_risk: Crowded on search (CAS, Clarivate, Patsnap). Generative design is crowded (dozens of AI antibody startups). The differentiated wedge is narrow, a FTO+generation hybrid, and probably a feature rather than a company.

all.name: Journal-mandated raw cryo-EM image deposition (EMPIAR and EMDB)
all.jurisdiction: Global (EMBL-EBI, with wwPDB policy and journal mandates)
all.legal_basis: wwPDB and major journals require deposition of cryo-EM maps (EMDB) and models (PDB) for publication. Raw micrograph deposition in EMPIAR is encouraged or required by some journals and funders, such as Wellcome and NIH data management and sharing (DMS) plans. Hold periods are typically until publication (max about 1 year for PDB/EMDB).
all.dataset: EMPIAR holds thousands of entries of raw movies and particle stacks, multiple PB in total. EMDB holds 40k+ maps. Raw data captures full conformational heterogeneity that the single deposited structure discards. Formats are heterogeneous (MRC, TIFF, EER) with inconsistent metadata.
all.current_users: Academic heterogeneity methods: cryoDRGN (Zhong/Princeton), 3DFlex, CryoSPARC (Structura Bio, commercial). Companies: Gandeeva ($40M), MOMA ($236M), Septerna, Shuimu (ByteDance-backed), CryoCloud (EUR 2M, 2025). Most of them generate proprietary data rather than mining EMPIAR at scale.
all.ml_unlock: A foundation model trained on all public raw cryo-EM particles that outputs conformational ensembles, not single structures. It would surface cryptic and allosteric pockets and dynamics for drug design that AlphaFold-class models (trained only on PDB coordinates) miss. It would be sold as an ensemble API or a pocket-discovery engine.
all.buyer_and_market: Structure-based drug discovery at pharma and biotech. The computational drug discovery software market is about $3-5B, and the cryo-EM market is about $1.5B. Partnership-style milestone deals are typical.
all.why_now: EMPIAR growth plus cheap GPUs. Post-AlphaFold, the field's bottleneck is dynamics, and the raw-data-to-ensemble gap is recognized.
all.novelty_risk: Medium-high. Isomorphic, Genesis, Chai and academic labs target dynamics. Raw-data scale (PB) is a moat but also a cost. The labels are noisy.

all.name: Journal-mandated raw mass-spectrometry proteomics deposition (PRIDE / ProteomeXchange)
all.legal_basis: Journals (MCP, JPR, Nature-family) require ProteomeXchange deposition of raw MS files for proteomics papers. NIH DMS policy (Jan 2023) and other funder policies push the same way. Datasets are private until publication.
all.dataset: About 40k+ ProteomeXchange datasets with hundreds of millions of raw spectra, multiple PB in total (PRIDE 2025 update, ProteomeXchange 2026 update). Vendor-specific raw formats, inconsistent sample metadata (SDRF adoption is partial). Huge and under-reanalyzed.
all.current_users: Academic tools: Prosit/MSAID (MSAID acquired by Bruker), Casanovo, InstaNovo, AlphaPeptDeep (Mann lab). Commercial instrument vendors (Thermo, Bruker) and platform startups (Seer, Nautilus) focus on hardware. Some pretraining on PRIDE has happened academically.
all.ml_unlock: A spectral foundation model for de novo peptide and PTM identification across all public raw data. It would let pharma find neoantigens, HLA peptides and post-translational biomarkers without databases, and reanalyze 40k public studies into a pan-disease proteome atlas for target and biomarker discovery.
all.buyer_and_market: Pharma target and biomarker discovery, immuno-oncology (neoantigen vaccines), and diagnostics. The proteomics market is about $30B+ including instruments. The software/informatics slice is about $1-2B.
all.why_now: Instrument throughput is surging (Astral and others). De novo sequencing accuracy crossed usability with transformers in 2023-2025.
all.novelty_risk: Medium-high. Bruker/MSAID, Thermo, InstaDeep (InstaNovo) and academic labs are active. Commercial capture likely goes to instrument vendors.

all.name: DOE Geothermal Data Repository (GDR) mandatory submission for DOE-funded geothermal projects
all.legal_basis: The DOE Public Access Plan and GTO award terms say PIs 'must submit data and metadata' for funded projects to the GDR (OpenEI/NREL). Submission timing follows the Data Management Plan, and a moratorium is possible per submission. The National Geothermal Data System aggregates state survey data.
all.dataset: Well logs, temperature gradients, geophysics, FORGE (Utah) enhanced geothermal system (EGS) test data, play-fairway studies. Heterogeneous files, PDFs and spreadsheets, with no file-size limits.
all.current_users: Zanskar (AI geothermal exploration, $115M Series C 2025, explicitly built on public geologic data). Fervo uses FORGE learnings. Academic play-fairway work.
all.ml_unlock: Hidden-geothermal-resource prediction and EGS siting. This is essentially the Terranox pattern applied to heat.
all.buyer_and_market: Geothermal developers and data-center power buyers. The market is large (firm clean power), but this product is a developer business, not data/software.
all.why_now: AI data-center power demand. Bipartisan geothermal support.
all.novelty_risk: High. Zanskar is well funded and doing exactly this, so this candidate is a Terranox clone in spirit and the user rejected heat-to-power. Low value as a new idea.

all.name: NIH Data Management and Sharing Policy (2023) mandated deposits across generalist and domain repositories
all.jurisdiction: USA (NIH, with similar NSF and Gates Foundation policies)
all.legal_basis: The NIH DMS Policy (effective Jan 25, 2023) requires all NIH-funded research generating scientific data to submit a DMS plan and share data by the time of publication or the end of the award. NIH 2025 Public Access Policy requires zero-embargo publication.
all.dataset: Fragmented across hundreds of repositories (Figshare, Dryad, Zenodo, dbGaP, SRA, GEO, domain archives). Extremely heterogeneous formats, metadata often minimal. About $35B/yr of NIH research now sheds data.
all.current_users: Data aggregation vendors (Elucidata, Bioturing, Genialis) for omics. LLM literature tools (Elicit, Consensus) cover papers, not data. Many pharma internal teams mine GEO/SRA.
all.ml_unlock: An agent that discovers, harmonizes and reanalyzes mandated deposits into a queryable 'all preclinical evidence' graph. It would predict target-disease reproducibility, the chance a preclinical finding replicates, before a pharma in-licensing decision.
all.buyer_and_market: Pharma business development and target validation teams. Bayer/Amgen found about 75-89% irreproducibility, and in-licensing deals are worth billions. The market would be data/analytics subscriptions at the $100M-1B scale.
all.why_now: The mandate took effect in 2023, so the first 3-year deposit wave is accumulating now. LLM agents can harmonize messy metadata.
all.novelty_risk: Medium. Elucidata, Causaly, BenchSci (which pivoted from reagent search and has heavy funding) and Recursion's public data efforts overlap. Data quality is poor.

all.name: Telescope proprietary-period archives (HST/JWST via MAST, ESO, ALMA)
all.legal_basis: Observatory policy: General Observer (GO) data become public after an exclusive access period, typically 12 months (shorter or zero for some JWST programs and all DDT/ERS programs).
all.dataset: PB-scale calibrated imaging and spectra, well curated and fully public through MAST/ESO archives.
all.current_users: Heavily mined by academic astronomers and ML groups (e.g. Polymathic AI's AstroCLIP, Multimodal Universe).
all.ml_unlock: An astronomy foundation model for anomaly and transient discovery.
all.buyer_and_market: Essentially no commercial buyer, only grant-funded science. Possible spillover into space-domain awareness, but that uses different sensors.
all.why_now: Not compelling.
all.novelty_risk: Data is well mined and has no market, so I rejected it as a company.

all.name: Dutch BRO subsurface registry (CPTs and geotechnical boreholes), plus the NZ Geotechnical Database and other mandated ground-investigation archives
all.jurisdiction: Netherlands (main one); New Zealand (NZGD, set up after the Christchurch earthquakes); similar archives exist in Hong Kong (GEO Geotechnical Information Unit) and in US state DOT boring logs
all.legal_basis: Wet basisregistratie ondergrond (Dutch Key Register of the Subsurface Act, in force 2018, phased in through tranches 1-3 by Besluit BRO, Stb 2019-292). Government bodies (Rijkswaterstaat, provinces, municipalities, water boards) must deliver every geotechnical CPT, geotechnical borehole, groundwater well and similar survey they commission to the public BRO. Contractors running government work submit on the client's behalf. The data is open by law. The CPT data comes in through tranche-1 delivery rules. I did not confirm the exact delay and confidentiality rules in this search.
all.dataset: Machine-readable cone penetration tests (CPTs) with full depth profiles of cone resistance, sleeve friction and pore pressure. My unverified estimate is several hundred thousand CPTs nationally, counting the older DINO archive. There are also geotechnical borehole descriptions (BHR-GT), soil-mechanics lab tests, groundwater monitoring wells and the GeoTOP/REGIS 3D models. Access is free: PDOK ATOM bulk download, WMS/WFS, the BRO REST API and DINOloket. Formats are XML and GEF, and the data is open (CC0/public domain). This is unusually clean structured data, not scanned PDFs. NZGD is a similar collection of tens of thousands of CPTs and boreholes, shared by private engineers under a sharing condition and gated behind free registration.
all.current_users: Mostly academic ML work: TU Delft and Deltares CPT soil-classification and stratigraphy papers, ISSMGE NUMGE 2023 papers, and Aron Noordam's KIVI talk on data-driven geotechnics. VIKTOR.ai offers a no-code app that visualises BRO CPTs. Commercial site-investigation firms (Fugro, Wiertsema, Inpijn-Blokpoel) use it as context for their own work. Related startups do not use public borehole archives as a cross-jurisdiction prior: EMerald Geomodelling (Norway) does ML bedrock mapping from airborne EM plus its own drilling; GroundedAI (Vancouver) is a tunnel-logging system of record and raised CAD 2M in July 2026; Groundwork AI is tiny. I found no funded startup building a foundation model of the subsurface from mandated CPT and borehole archives.
