all.ml_unlock: A 'subsurface foundation model': give it a site polygon and get a probabilistic 3D soil profile (stratigraphy, cone resistance, settlement and liquefaction risk, pile-length estimate) before any ground investigation. Then do active learning: tell the engineer where the 2-3 CPTs that most reduce uncertainty should go, instead of a blanket grid. Outputs: (1) pre-bid geotechnical risk pricing for contractors and developers, (2) automated preliminary foundation and pile design, (3) data-center, solar, wind and battery site screening (pile refusal and settlement are big cost-overrun drivers), (4) an underwriting signal for subsidence and foundation-damage insurance. The Dutch archive is the training set; transfer to the US and UK using state DOT and BGS borehole archives.
all.buyer_and_market: Site developers (data centers, renewables, logistics), EPC contractors and geotechnical consultancies. Unexpected ground conditions are widely cited as the largest single source of construction claims and overruns. My unverified estimate is that geotechnical and site-investigation services are a low-single-digit $B/yr market globally, and foundation and piling construction runs to tens of $B. A software layer charging $5-50k per site screen across tens of thousands of utility-scale and industrial sites a year could plausibly reach $300M+ ARR. A bigger outcome is taking ground risk onto the balance sheet (guaranteed pile lengths or insured ground risk), which is how this gets past the $200M niche ceiling.
all.why_now: BRO tranches finished phasing in during 2019-2023, so the archive is now national and machine-readable. The data-center and renewables buildout means huge numbers of greenfield sites need fast geotechnical screening, and interconnection timelines punish slow ground investigation. Generative 3D models (diffusion over voxels, neural fields) now handle sparse conditioning well.
all.novelty_risk: Moderate-low. Fugro or Deltares could build this but are services-first. Academic prototypes exist but nobody sells a product. The main risk is weak transfer: Dutch soft Holocene deltaic soils may not generalise to US glacial till or bedrock. A strong US wedge would need US archives too (state DOT boring logs, which are scanned PDFs and the messy-data moat). The NL market alone is too small, so the company only works if the model generalises across jurisdictions.

all.name: California GeoTracker ESI (mandatory electronic submittal of all contaminated-site investigation data), plus other state cleanup-file archives
all.jurisdiction: California, USA. Analogues include NJDEP SRP DataMiner/EDSA, Texas TCEQ, the Florida DEP OCULUS document archive and state LUST/brownfield files nationwide.
all.legal_basis: From memory, not confirmed on the fetched FAQ page: California Code of Regulations Title 23, Div. 3, Ch. 30 (sections 3890-3895, from AB 2886 of 2001), with Title 27 for landfills. Since about 2002-2005, responsible parties at UST/LUST cleanups, SLIC/site-cleanup sites, DoD sites, landfills and waste-discharge permittees must upload all lab analytical data (EDF format), well and boring coordinates and elevations (GEO_XY/GEO_Z), depth-to-water (GEO_WELL), boring logs and every technical report as PDF to GeoTracker. These consultant-paid investigations then become public records on GeoTracker's public side. Confirmed: GeoTracker has public and secure sections, and uploads go through ESI.
all.dataset: About 20+ years of lab-analytical results, probably tens of millions of rows (my unverified estimate), covering petroleum hydrocarbons, chlorinated solvents, metals and, increasingly, PFAS from 2019+ state orders. Also tens of thousands of sites' boring logs and well data, plus hundreds of thousands of PDF reports (Phase I/II assessments, remedial action plans, closure reports). Partly downloadable as bulk text files of site, analytical and geo data. The PDFs need per-site scraping. The mix of structured analytical data with messy PDFs is the moat.
all.current_users: Environmental due-diligence database vendors (EDR/LightBox, ERIS, GeoSearch) index site lists, not the underlying sample data. AI startups automate the writing of Phase I ESA reports (V7 Labs Phase I agent, Nomic, A.Team templates), which is LLM report-drafting work. I found no startup training a spatial plume and contamination-probability model on the full sample-level data to price unobserved parcels.
all.ml_unlock: A contamination probability map for every parcel in the state, later the nation: predicted concentrations of PFAS, TCE/PCE vapor-intrusion risk, MTBE and benzene in groundwater at depth, from a model trained on 20 years of consultant sampling plus land-use history, hydrogeology and permits. Products: (1) instant Phase I/II triage and estimated remediation cost for CRE lenders and acquirers, (2) PFAS liability estimates for water utilities, insurers and corporate defendants (PFAS liability is very large: the 3M settlement alone was about $10.3-12.5B), (3) site selection for data centers and housing, (4) environmental insurance (pollution legal liability) underwriting.
all.buyer_and_market: About 100k+ US Phase I ESAs per year at $2-5k each (my unverified estimate), so roughly $0.5B/yr for reports alone. Environmental remediation services run about $30B+/yr in the US. Pollution legal liability insurance is about $2-3B of premium. PFAS litigation and remediation exposure is in the hundreds of billions. A risk-scoring layer for lenders, insurers and PFAS defendants supports a $100M+ ARR path, with upside in taking on remediation-cost risk.
all.why_now: EPA's PFAS drinking-water MCLs (2024) and CERCLA hazardous-substance designation for PFOA/PFOS create an urgent need to predict PFAS where nobody has sampled. LLMs can now extract boring logs and tables from hundreds of thousands of consultant PDFs. Separately, the vapor-intrusion standard (ASTM E2600) and CA's 2023 supplemental VI guidance raise demand.
all.novelty_risk: Low-moderate. Incumbents (LightBox/EDR, ERIS) are database plus report shops, not ML. LLM report-writing startups are many and crowded, but they automate the consultant, not the prediction. Risks: data are biased toward known-contaminated sites (selection bias), and multi-state data assembly is heavy. California alone is a strong start.

all.name: SERFF insurance rate and rule filings (US state rate-filing public access)
all.jurisdiction: USA, all 50 states via NAIC SERFF Filing Access
all.legal_basis: State insurance rating laws, for prior-approval and file-and-use regimes. Insurers must file rates, rating rules, forms and the actuarial support (GLM factor tables, rating algorithms, territory definitions, loss-cost selections) with each state DOI. Under state public-records law these filings become public, usually once the filing is closed or approved. Some exhibits are marked trade secret and withheld, and that varies by state.
all.dataset: SERFF processed 517,571 transactions in 2023, and carriers submit 500k+ filings a year. Single homeowners filing packages reach 346,064 pages (2024), up 9x since 2009. Access is per-state through the SERFF Filing Access web UI, as PDFs and Excel workbooks. There is no bulk API, so scraping and parsing heterogeneous actuarial exhibits is the moat.
all.current_users: Crowded. S&P Global RateFilings.com (Market Intelligence), Perr&Knight and Quadrant Information Services are incumbents. Zesty.ai sells ZORRO Discover competitive intelligence and publishes on filings as an 'overlooked dataset'. Insuraviews (Milwaukee, founded 2024, VC-backed 2025) runs AI search over 50-state filings at $599/yr and up. Verisk/FilingRamp handle the filing side. FurtherAI (a16z, $25M Series A, Oct 2025) does insurance-workflow AI.
all.ml_unlock: Fully reconstruct every competitor's rating engine from its filed factor tables, so you can quote any risk as any carrier would. That enables (1) a pricing-optimisation copilot for carriers and MGAs, (2) rate-adequacy and 'who is mispriced where' signals for reinsurers and hedge funds, (3) automated filing drafting and approval prediction.
all.buyer_and_market: P&C carrier product and actuarial teams, MGAs, reinsurers. US P&C premiums are about $900B+. Competitive-intelligence and filing-software spend is maybe a few hundred $M/yr (my rough estimate), and the comparative-rater market (EZLynx, Quadrant) is similar. Getting past a niche needs a move into an MGA or pricing-as-a-service that writes premium.
all.why_now: LLMs can finally parse 300k-page heterogeneous actuarial exhibits. Homeowners and auto rate shocks from 2023-2025 make competitive pricing intelligence urgent.
all.novelty_risk: High. Several funded players and incumbents already mine SERFF (S&P, Zesty, Insuraviews, Quadrant). It is a known dataset in insurtech. Only a pricing-arbitrage MGA use case is less crowded.

all.name: UK developer-funded archaeology grey literature (OASIS / ADS Library / Historic Environment Records)
all.jurisdiction: England, Wales and Scotland. Analogues: the Netherlands under the Valletta Convention (Erfgoedwet), Ireland, and US Section 106 (NHPA) cultural resource management reports held in State Historic Preservation Office (SHPO) files.
all.legal_basis: From memory: since PPG16 (1990), and now NPPF chapter 16 (para 211 in the Dec 2023 numbering), local planning authorities require developers to pay for archaeological desk-based assessment, evaluation trenching and excavation, and to 'record and advance understanding' and make the evidence and archive publicly accessible. Reports must be deposited with the county HER and indexed through OASIS into the Archaeology Data Service. In the US, Section 106 of the NHPA forces federally permitted projects to fund cultural-resource surveys, filed with SHPOs, with restricted access.
all.dataset: OASIS has indexed fieldwork for about 20 years. My unverified estimate is that the ADS Library holds tens of thousands of grey-literature PDFs and the ~50+ HERs hold hundreds of thousands of monument and event records. Many PDFs are scanned or messy and come with trench plans, finds lists and negative results. Access is a free ADS download per report. HER data is via Heritage Gateway, sometimes licensed.
all.current_users: Academic predictive-modelling research (mostly in the US: e.g. Grand Staircase-Escalante ML models). ArchAI (Iris Kramer, Southampton spinout) won Innovate UK funding for AI site detection from lidar and satellite data for developers. Commercial units (Wessex, MOLA, Oxford Archaeology) use HERs manually. I found nobody training models on the negative and positive outcomes of developer-funded evaluations to price archaeological risk.
all.ml_unlock: An 'archaeological risk underwriting' model: for any site polygon, the probability that evaluation trenching triggers full excavation, expected cost and expected programme delay. Trained on thousands of OASIS evaluation outcomes plus lidar, geology and HER density. Could be packaged as a fixed-price archaeology guarantee or insurance for housebuilders and infrastructure (HS2 spent large sums on archaeology).
all.buyer_and_market: UK housebuilders, infrastructure owners, solar farms. UK commercial archaeology is a few hundred £M/yr (my estimate), and US cultural resource management is about $1B+. On its own this is likely below the size threshold, unless bundled into a broader pre-construction site-risk platform (combine with candidates 1 and 2: ground, contamination, heritage, ecology).
all.why_now: The UK government's planning reform (Planning and Infrastructure Act 2025, the 1.5M-homes target) is pushing to de-risk planning delays. LLMs can now extract structured outcomes from scanned grey literature.
all.novelty_risk: Low competition (ArchAI is the closest), but the market is small. Best treated as a feature of a multi-hazard site-risk company, not a standalone company.

all.name: Meta-candidate: a 'pre-construction site-risk underwriter' fusing mandated ground, contamination and heritage disclosures
all.jurisdiction: Multi-jurisdiction: NL BRO, CA GeoTracker and other state cleanup archives, state DOT boring logs, UK BGS and OASIS
all.legal_basis: Combines the regimes above: the Wet BRO subsurface registry, CCR Title 23 Ch. 30 electronic submittal, NPPF ch. 16 archaeology and NHPA Section 106. Each forces consultant work paid for by a private developer, or commissioned by government, into a public archive.
all.dataset: Hundreds of thousands of CPTs and boreholes (structured), tens of millions of environmental sample rows plus PDFs, and tens of thousands of archaeology evaluation reports (PDF). All are free, and heterogeneous enough that assembly itself is a moat.
all.current_users: Fragmented. Site-investigation consultants, EDR/LightBox and ERIS for environmental records, ArchAI for heritage, EMerald Geomodelling for bedrock. No one fuses these mandated archives into a single priced site-risk number.
all.ml_unlock: For any parcel: a predicted total below-grade cost and schedule-risk distribution (piles and foundations, contamination remediation, archaeology), with an optimal investigation plan. That is sold as a priced guarantee or insurance wrapper, so the company captures risk premium rather than SaaS fees.
all.buyer_and_market: Data-center, renewables, logistics and housing developers, construction lenders, and contractors' insurers. Below-grade surprises account for a large share of construction overruns on a multi-trillion-dollar construction market. A risk-transfer model could support a $1B+ outcome. This is the path past the $100-200M niche ceiling.
all.why_now: Record greenfield buildout (AI data centers, grid-scale solar and storage) on unfamiliar sites, PFAS liability, and LLMs that can extract legacy PDFs at scale.
all.novelty_risk: The component datasets each have academic or incumbent users, but the fused, risk-bearing product looks unbuilt. The main risk is the execution breadth of multi-source data assembly and getting carrier capacity for the insurance wrapper.

shortlist.name: Subsurface contamination and PFAS liability model (CA GeoTracker ESI plus state cleanup archives plus the PFAS disclosure stack)
merged_from: California GeoTracker ESI plus other state remediation and LUST case files: a parcel-level subsurface contamination model
California GeoTracker ESI (mandatory electronic submittal of all contaminated-site investigation data), plus other state cleanup-file archives
PFAS forced-disclosure stack (TSCA 8(a)(7) one-time PFAS report, UCMR 5 drinking-water results, state PFAS-in-products filings): PFAS liability attribution
EPA UCMR 5 and Consumer Confidence Reports: PFAS, plus mandatory Lead Service Line Inventories
CCR Rule coal-ash groundwater monitoring disclosures
shortlist.thesis: California's ESI regulations have forced every responsible party to upload consultant-paid lab results (230M+ analytical results), boring logs, well data and every report (2.6M PDFs) to GeoTracker for 20 years. It is the closest environmental analogue to SMAD. Train a parcel-level model that predicts the probability and concentration of petroleum, solvent, metals and PFAS contamination, plume extent, and remediation cost and duration. Add UCMR 5 and the 2027 TSCA 8(a)(7) PFAS census to attribute contamination to likely sources. Sell to pollution-liability insurers, CRE lenders (to triage the Phase I/II decision), remediation buyers and PFAS litigants. The end state is a 'Verisk of subsurface risk'.
shortlist.why_selected: The quirk is real and unusually rich: a state mandate for machine-readable lab data plus messy PDFs. The data is large and has never been modeled predictively. Incumbents (LightBox/EDR, ERIS) do lookups, not predictions. Buyers are large: about $4-5B in environmental insurance premium, about $1B of Phase I spend, $30B+ in remediation, and PFAS liability in the hundreds of billions. A small team could show a proof in weeks on the GeoTracker bulk downloads, for example by holding out sites and predicting exceedances. This is the Terranox playbook with contamination in place of uranium, and it is not mining. Verify the bulk-download scope, how much selection bias toward known-dirty sites there is, and whether anyone like LightBox has an ML roadmap.

shortlist.name: Virtual site investigation / pre-construction ground-risk underwriter (Dutch BRO CPTs, UK BGS boreholes, NZGD, state DOT and water-well logs)
merged_from: Statutory borehole and well-log archives as a pre-drilled ground model (BGS NGDC + US/Canada water-well logs + NZ Geotechnical Database + state DOT boring logs)
Dutch BRO subsurface registry (CPTs and geotechnical boreholes), plus the NZ Geotechnical Database and other mandated ground-investigation archives
Meta-candidate: a 'pre-construction site-risk underwriter' fusing mandated ground, contamination and heritage disclosures
UK developer-funded archaeology grey literature (OASIS / ADS Library / Historic Environment Records)
State-mandated water well driller logs (well completion reports)
shortlist.thesis: Several laws force site-investigation data into public archives: the Wet BRO, the UK Mining Industry Act s.23 and Water Resources Act, provincial and state driller-log mandates, and NZGD. Together these hold millions of CPTs and boreholes. Build a subsurface foundation model that outputs a probabilistic ground profile for any parcel: depth to bearing stratum, soft layers, groundwater, pile length and foundation cost. Add active learning that recommends where the few real boreholes should go. Sell it as screening for data center, renewables and housing developers, and eventually as a priced ground-risk guarantee or insurance wrapper. Archaeology and contamination layers can bolt on later.
shortlist.why_selected: The forced-disclosure quirk is real across several jurisdictions. The Dutch data is clean (good for a fast proof), and the UK and US data is messy scanned logs (the moat). Unforeseen ground conditions are a leading cause of construction overruns in a multi-trillion-dollar market, and the data center and renewables build-out creates urgent demand. No funded startup builds a cross-jurisdiction model: GroundedAI and Terra AI are adjacent, DrillerDB covers water wells only. A credible proof is a few weeks of work on BRO, for example predicting held-out CPT profiles. The risks to verify are transfer across geologies, liability, and whether engineers will pay before investigation. It is subsurface but not mineral exploration.

shortlist.name: AI regulatory reviewer trained on paired dossiers and regulator decisions (EMA Policy 0070, Health Canada PRCI, FDA reviews and CRLs, EU CTIS RFIs)
merged_from: Regulator dossier corpus: EMA Policy 0070 clinical reports + Health Canada PRCI + FDA approval packages/CRLs (an 'AI regulatory reviewer')
FDA Complete Response Letters (CRLs): newly forced-public rejection letters
Regulator-forced clinical study report (CSR) disclosure: EMA Policy 0070 plus Health Canada PRCI
EU Clinical Trials Regulation / CTIS: member-state assessment reports and requests for information
shortlist.thesis: Policy 0070 and Canada's 2019 regulations force publication of the full CSRs and Module 2 summaries sponsors submit. Since 2025 FDA also publishes the CRLs that explain its rejections, and CTIS exposes member-state RFIs on trial applications. This is the only corpus where both the private submission and the regulator's judgement are public at scale. Train a model that predicts the deficiencies and objections a reviewer will raise, red-teams a dossier or protocol before filing, and drafts Module 2 in the style that passed. A secondary product is PDUFA-outcome prediction for investors.
shortlist.why_selected: The forced-disclosure quirk is real and recent (Policy 0070 relaunched in 2023-25, CRLs since 2025, the CTIS back-catalogue complete in 2025). The data is huge, messy and almost untouched commercially. A CRL costs 6-18 months of delay, worth $100M+ per program. Regulatory-affairs and medical-writing spend is about $10B+, so a path to a large company exists. Medical-writing AI startups train on sponsor-internal data, not this cross-sponsor paired corpus. The main issue to verify is legal: Health Canada's non-commercial terms and EMA's terms, while the FDA material is unrestricted. A proof is feasible quickly, for example predicting CRL deficiency categories from public trial and approval data.

shortlist.name: Private-credit marking oracle from NAIC statutory filings (Schedule D/BA)
merged_from: NAIC statutory statements: insurer Schedule D/BA holdings as a private-credit price and credit oracle
shortlist.thesis: State insurance law forces about 800 life and thousands of P&C insurers to file line-by-line holdings with carrying values and NAIC designations. The same private placement, private loan or ABF tranche shows up across many insurers at different marks. Entity-resolve those instruments and treat the dispersion as noisy labels to build an independent fair-value and shadow-rating engine for private credit, a 'BVAL for private credit'. It would also flag over-marking and rating-shopping insurers.
shortlist.why_selected: This is the clearest case of 'data no single party sees whole' created by a disclosure regime. Private credit is a $1.7-2T asset class whose valuation opacity is the regulators' top worry right now (NAIC rewrite 2025-26). Independent valuation and ratings is a multi-billion-dollar pool, so a path to a large company is credible. No startup is doing cross-insurer ML reconstruction. Verify how much raw data is freely available versus NAIC, S&P or AM Best paid feeds, and how identifiable private instruments are (PPN coverage).

shortlist.name: Casualty 'litigation catastrophe model' / next-mass-tort forecaster (court dockets + FAERS/MAUDE + recalls)
merged_from: Open court records (PACER federal + 3,000+ fragmented state trial-court dockets): casualty 'litigation catastrophe model' for insurers and reinsurers
FAERS + MAUDE + recalls as a mass-tort / product-liability early-warning system
shortlist.thesis: Public-access rules make every complaint, verdict and MDL docket public, and 21 CFR 314/803 force manufacturers to report adverse events (FAERS 30M+ reports, millions of MAUDE narratives a year). Fuse the docket velocity of new filings with FDA signal trajectories and science to forecast which products and exposures become multi-billion-dollar mass torts 12-36 months ahead. Model severity by venue, judge and plaintiff firm, and output portfolio tail-loss curves. It would be the RMS/AIR of casualty, sold to reinsurers, E&S carriers, Lloyd's syndicates and litigation funders.
shortlist.why_selected: The buyers are very large: casualty reinsurers facing tens of billions of dollars of social-inflation reserve strengthening. The cat-model analogue (RMS and Verisk each earn about $0.5-1B) shows a path to a large company. Both data sources are big, messy and forced-public. Praedicat/Verisk works at the literature level and Darrow and Theo work case by case. No one runs a portfolio-level docket-plus-signal model. Risks: few labels (about 100 historical MDLs), and claims data needed for calibration. Verify how deep Praedicat goes and what state-docket access costs.

shortlist.name: Standard-essential patent essentiality and FRAND engine (ETSI declarations x 3GPP specs x patent claims)
merged_from: ETSI/ITU standard-essential patent (SEP) declarations x patent claims x technical specs: automated essentiality and FRAND royalty-stack engine
shortlist.thesis: ETSI's IPR policy forces members to publicly declare patents they claim are essential, and declaration is self-serving and unchecked (only about 20-40% are truly essential). Align each declared claim against the exact 3GPP spec clause to produce court-grade essentiality probabilities and claim charts. Roll these up into each licensor's 'true essential share', which drives FRAND rates in 5G/6G, Wi-Fi and codecs. Sell to implementers (autos, IoT), licensors, pools, funders and courts, aiming to become a neutral rate-setting clearinghouse.
shortlist.why_selected: The forced-disclosure quirk creates a systematically biased public dataset, and correcting it is worth money. Cellular SEP royalties are $20B+/yr, and individual disputes are worth hundreds of millions. The EU withdrew its SEP Regulation, so no public verifier exists. LLM claim-to-spec alignment is newly feasible, and a small team could benchmark against existing manual essentiality studies quickly. Competition is partial (IPlytics/LexisNexis, PatSnap). Verify whether their AI scoring is already accepted in court or arbitration.

shortlist.name: Establishment-level injury-risk model and workers' comp MGA (OSHA ITA case-level 300/301 data)
merged_from: OSHA Injury Tracking Application case-level data (Forms 300/301) plus OSHA and MSHA inspection records
MSHA Mine Data Retrieval System / Open Government Data (US mine inspections, violations, accidents, employment)
shortlist.thesis: OSHA's 2023 rule (29 CFR 1904.41), in force since 2024, makes large high-hazard establishments submit case-level injury narratives, which OSHA publishes with establishment identifiers. Combine these with inspection and violation history to predict each worksite's future lost-time and severe injuries and expected comp loss cost. The current alternative is experience mods that lag 2-4 years. Sell underwriting tools to comp carriers and contractor-prequalification platforms, or run an ML-native workers' comp MGA.
shortlist.why_selected: The disclosure regime is brand new (three years of case-level data), so it is under-exploited. Narratives suit LLM feature extraction. The premium pool is large (about $55-60B in US workers' comp), and contractor prequalification (ISNetworld, Avetta) is about $1B+. Verisk and NCCI have claims data but not timely narratives. A proof is feasible fast: predict next-year case rates from the 2023-24 files. The main risk is rule rescission (2019 precedent), and coverage is limited to 100+ employee establishments.

shortlist.name: Machine shadow rating agency for the unrated municipal-bond tail (EMMA continuing disclosures)
merged_from: EMMA muni continuing disclosures (audited financials and event notices for about 50k issuers)
shortlist.thesis: SEC Rule 15c2-12 forces about 50k muni issuers to file ACFRs, audited financials and event notices on EMMA. These are heterogeneous scanned PDFs that MSRB itself still reviews by hand, and late filing is itself a signal. Extract normalized financials and produce default probabilities, fair spreads and early warnings for unrated and stale-rated high-yield conduit credits (senior living, charter schools, hospitals), where nearly all defaults happen. Later steps: NRSRO-style ratings or bond insurance.
shortlist.why_selected: The quirk is real, the data is massive and messy, and the market is $4T outstanding. Public-finance rating fees (about $1B) and evaluated pricing are displaceable revenue pools. The SMA and direct-indexing boom creates demand for automated credit work. Competitors are small and unproven (Munibonds.ai, MuniPro, Spline). Risk: the FDTA will make data machine-readable and commoditize extraction, so the moat must be the default model plus distribution. Verify default-label counts and competitor traction.

shortlist.name: Cross-OEM vehicle defect, recall and warranty-liability forecaster (NHTSA manufacturer communications, TSBs, complaints, Part 573, EWR)
merged_from: NHTSA defect-signal corpus (ODI complaints + EWR + manufacturer communications/TSBs + Part 573 recall filings)
NHTSA defect-disclosure stack (manufacturer communications, TSBs, complaints, SGO crash reports, Part 573 recalls)
NHTSA Standing General Order ADS/ADAS crash reports
shortlist.thesis: The TREAD Act and 49 CFR 579.5 force OEMs to send NHTSA every dealer and owner communication about defects. These hundreds of thousands of mostly scanned PDFs are published, alongside 2M+ complaints and recall chronologies. An LLM pipeline would link complaints, silent warranty extensions and TSBs to components and shared tier-1 suppliers, then predict which components or suppliers will be recalled 6-18 months before the Part 573 filing, with expected campaign cost. Sell to recall insurers, supplier credit and equity investors, and OEM and supplier quality and procurement teams.
shortlist.why_selected: The disclosure mandate is real. The PDF corpus is large and under-exploited, since most users only use complaint counts. Stakes are big: about $50B/yr in global warranty spend, tens of billions in recalls, and record software and EV recall counts. The cross-OEM supplier linkage is something OEMs themselves cannot see. A quick backtest is possible: predict historical recalls from earlier TSBs and complaints. We Predict is the only small adjacent player. Verify buyer willingness: OEMs have richer private data, so insurers and investors may be the real wedge.

shortlist.name: Decommissioning-liability underwriter: legacy wells, CCS Class VI AoR and closure bonds (state well files, AER/Petrinex, mine closure assurance)
merged_from: US state well-file archives (Texas RRC, NDIC, OCC, etc.) used to automate legacy-well review for CO2 storage and lithium brine permits
Alberta AER well and facility records plus Petrinex production data, used to price closure liability
Mine closure / reclamation financial assurance and closure plans (bond amounts vs. true liability)
Public injection volumes and earthquake catalogs (Texas RRC H-10, Oklahoma OCC, TexNet), used to forecast disposal capacity and induced seismicity
Released offshore national data repositories (UK NSTA NDR, Norway Diskos, Australia NOPIMS, Netherlands NLOG) used for CO2 and hydrogen storage and decommissioning
shortlist.thesis: State conservation rules make about 100 years of completion and plugging records for millions of wells public, mostly scanned handwritten files. Alberta's Directive 088 and AER records do the same for closure status and costs, and mining laws publish closure plans and bond amounts. A multimodal model would read every well file to reconstruct plug and cement integrity and fix locations. It would output per-penetration leak risk (the permit-ready Class VI Area-of-Review product) and per-asset true closure cost and operator insolvency probability. The big outcome is an AI surety/MGA writing plugging, reclamation and renewables decommissioning bonds.
shortlist.why_selected: This is the strongest energy entry. The forced-disclosure archives are huge, messy and SMAD-like, with mandatory use (Class VI AoR) and a regulatory squeeze (D088 quotas, bonding rule tightening). Liabilities are enormous (C$36-260B in Alberta, tens of billions in the US), and no funded startup sells scanned-file-to-risk-score. Software alone is a $200-500M niche, so the venture case rests on risk-taking (bonding). Includes mine closure, so this counts as the single mineral-adjacent slot. Verify surety-market appetite and whether Enverus/S&P are building this.

shortlist.name: Virtual teardown / design-win graph from FCC equipment-authorization exhibits (plus ISED, Korea RRA, NCC)
merged_from: FCC Equipment Authorization exhibits (FCC ID internal photos, RF test reports, manuals), plus foreign analogs (ISED REL, Korea RRA, Taiwan NCC, Anatel)
FCC experimental licenses (Part 5), ULS, and ECFS ex parte disclosures as a corporate R&D and regulatory 'leak' feed
shortlist.thesis: 47 CFR 2.1033 and the 180-day short-term-confidentiality cap mean that internal PCB photos, RF test reports and manuals for every radio device sold in the US become public automatically. Vision models would read chip markings and module IDs across millions of grants to build a continuously updated BOM and design-win graph by OEM and ODM. Uses: semiconductor competitive intelligence, SEP-licensing enforcement (finding unlicensed cellular, Wi-Fi and UWB devices for pools and licensors), Section 889/covered-list compliance, and alt data on design-win share.
shortlist.why_selected: This is a true 'forced reveal of private engineering' quirk, the hardware analogue of SMAD. The long tail (tens of thousands of IoT grants a year) is unmined: TechInsights does physical teardowns of a few hundred flagships a year. A path to a large company exists through enforcement-linked SEP revenue on a $20B+ royalty base. It pairs naturally with the SEP-essentiality candidate. A proof is fast: OCR chips from a few thousand grants and validate against known teardowns. Verify chip-marking legibility (shields and epoxy) and buyer demand from pools.

shortlist.name: Building-level condo structural and financial distress model (Florida SIRS and milestone inspections, NJ copycat law)
merged_from: Post-Surfside Florida condo disclosure regime (SIRS reporting + milestone inspections), with copycat state laws
NYC Facade Inspection & Safety Program (Local Law 11/FISP) reports + DOB complaints/violations
shortlist.thesis: Post-Surfside laws (SB 4-D, HB 1021, HB 913) force every 3+ story Florida condo to get milestone structural inspections and a Structural Integrity Reserve Study. The data is filed with DBPR and published 'exactly as submitted', and engineer reports are obtainable under Chapter 119. Parse them, link them to permits, insurance, HOA financials and sales, and predict special assessments, unsafe orders, insurance non-renewal and price collapse per building, 12-36 months ahead. Sell to condo mortgage lenders, GSE condo-project review, master-policy insurers and brokerages. Expand nationally as other states copy the law.
shortlist.why_selected: The disclosure regime is brand new: the first full SIRS cycle was due Dec 2025, and the first statewide OPPAGA data came in July 2026. Nobody has aggregated it, and it directly explains a live market crisis (Florida's condo price slump). The buyers have money: lenders on about $300B of Florida condo mortgages, insurers and GSEs. Market size is the main question, since it must generalize beyond Florida. It was chosen over the Kansas water-rights, large-load phantom-demand and EU Data Act candidates because the forced-disclosure fit is clearer and a proof is faster. Verify DBPR bulk access and how many states are adopting similar laws.

short.dropped_notes:
Kansas WIMAS water rights / farmland water value: a good quirk, but buyers are slow ag lenders and the TAM is speculative. Strong alternate for slot 12.
Data center large-load phantom-demand model: Halcyon ($21M) and Enverus/WoodMac are adjacent. Alternate.
EU Data Act cross-OEM telemetry: the data is consent-gated, not public, OEMs can use the trade-secret handbrake, and the execution is heavy. Alternate.
UCC Article 9 liens graph: the big bureaus already ingest this data and Cobalt/Kaaj are close.
Form 5500 / benefits: the data layer is crowded (Judy Diamond, BrightScope). The AI-broker angle competes with funded insurtechs.
Hatch-Waxman / Orange Book generic entry: structured data long used by DrugPatentWatch, IPD, Evaluate. The buyer set is concentrated.
India RERA: an interesting quirk, but India-only willingness to pay caps it near $100-300M, and the multi-portal scraping is fragile.
Chile SEIA permitting copilot: a niche below the size bar unless it expands across LatAm, and there is a FONDEF academic effort.
Distribution hosting-capacity inference: a borderline niche, and Kevala/Enverus are adjacent.
NI 43-101 feasibility haircut engine and tailings cat model: mineral-related, sub-$300M unless they become a fund. The mineral slot went to the decommissioning-liability merge.
WAMEX and other open-file exploration regimes, ANP BDEP, Diskos/NDR, produced-water lithium, geothermal BHT/GDR: Terranox clones or crowded (KoBold, Zanskar, Earth Science Analytics).
Price transparency MRFs (two entries), SERFF (three entries), CBP manifests, FMCSA, EPC registers (UK/FR), permits, deeds, NFIP, Companies House/CSRD, India MCA21, MRV shipping, DSA ad libraries, 483s (two entries), FDA recalls, NEPA, GHGRP/methane, REACH, Paris MoU PSC, patent file wrappers, Chapter 11 dockets (two entries), procurement (TED/FPDS, Nordic bids), MSHA: already mined by funded incumbents or startups, or too clean to give an edge.
EU pay transparency: compliance tooling is crowded and national publication rules are uncertain.
FAA SDR/ADs: concentrated lessor buyers, and OEM data dominates.
PHMSA pipelines: public data too coarse.
CA PUR pesticides, CAP beneficiaries, RMA crop insurance, CCR coal ash (folded in as a feature), wildfire mitigation plans, PUC rate cases (two entries), FERC EQR, CEMS/REMIT, ISO queues: small markets or crowded.
Science archives (cryo-EM EMPIAR, PRIDE proteomics, NIH DMS, telescopes, ST.26 antibody sequences): journal and funder mandates, not commercial forced disclosure. Crowded AI-bio competition, and commercial capture likely goes to vendors.
Battery passport (thin data, TWAICE et al.), German MaStR (well used), BDC broadband (closing window), DSA transparency DB, ITU filings, FCC experimental (folded into the FCC teardown entry), China MEE disclosures (legal and geopolitical risk), Brazil CAR (free government tools), UK planning portals (crowded): dropped.

deep.name: Subsurface contamination and PFAS liability model (CA GeoTracker ESI as the core corpus, with other state cleanup archives and PFAS disclosures as add-ons)
deep.legal_basis_verified:
Partly verified.
- Verified: the GeoTracker ESI program exists. The Water Board's own data-fair deck states the scale: over 230 million analytical results, over 1.64 million regulated-community submittals, about 450 electronic submittals a day and about 400 regulator document uploads a day. The deck lists public access routes: "Flat Files", "Download Data" and "Download ESI Data".
- Verified: ESdat's help page describes county-level downloads of ESI data (location, well, elevation and chemistry for every site in a county) plus site data, as zip files from the Water Board site.
- Not re-verified this run: the exact regulation (23 CCR ch. 30, 3890-3895, from AB 2886; mandatory from about 2002-2005). The UST/Site Cleanup/landfill/DoD scope is consistent with the Water Board ESI FAQ and the beginner's guide.
- Unlike SMAD, there is no confidentiality period. Data is public as soon as it is filed.
- PFAS leg is weak. TSCA 8(a)(7) has been repeatedly delayed. EPA proposed broad exemptions in Nov 2025 (articles, de minimis, R&D, byproducts and impurities). Practitioners expected the revised final rule in early 2026, with submissions no earlier than 2027. Much of that dataset will likely be CBI or exempted, so do not count on it before 2028.
- UCMR 5 is real, public and complete.
deep.data_access:
GeoTracker public side: geotracker.waterboards.ca.gov, with Download Data / Download ESI Data / Flat Files, served county by county as zip files.
- Contents: EDF analytical chemistry, GEO_XY well coordinates, GEO_Z elevations, GEO_WELL depth-to-water, and site metadata (status, case type, regulator, closure).
- Coverage: 230M+ analytical rows statewide. The full corpus is probably tens of GB uncompressed.
- Cost and licence: free, public record, no licence terms that block commercial use.
- PDFs (reports and boring logs, about 2M+): per-site document pages only, no bulk endpoint. Scraping is needed, and it is rate-limit and politeness sensitive.
- Caveat: I could not fetch geotracker.waterboards.ca.gov from this cloud container. Both the curl proxy and WebFetch failed (403 on CONNECT, and a fetch error), so the host is either not allowlisted or blocks bots. A proof this week needs a laptop or another network, plus an egress allowlist change.
- Once downloaded, a 1-2 county proof (for example Los Angeles or Santa Clara) is doable in a day on a laptop.
- Other states: NJDEP (DataMiner/EDSA), Florida OCULUS and TCEQ are mostly PDF or portal data, so national coverage means heavy document ingestion.
- UCMR 5: bulk zip from EPA, available now.
deep.competitors:
No funded startup found that trains predictive models on the GeoTracker corpus, but the space around it is busy.
1. LightBox/EDR (PE-owned, the dominant data vendor for Phase I ESAs):
   - Already sells an instant "Environmental Risk Rating": an elevated/low rating per property and per record, from an algorithm built by LightBox and a panel of environmental professionals.
   - Also sells lender screens: LoanCheck, LoanCheck RSRA for SBA loans, and an Environmental Risk Screen.
   - So the "pre-Phase I triage score for lenders" slot is already filled by a cheap, rule-based product that sits on the distribution channel.
2. ERIS and GeoSearch: similar database and report shops.
3. V7 Labs: AI agents for environmental-impairment underwriters and Phase I review (document extraction). Nomic and many LLM report-writing tools also play here.
4. LiORA, formerly Environmental Material Science (Saskatoon):
   - Raised CAD $5.1M seed in 2025, led by Conexus and BDC.
   - Does AI fate-and-transport plume modeling from in-situ sensors, calibrated with PEST++, and sells to oil and gas companies.
   - Site-level, not corpus-level, but it holds the "plume prediction AI" narrative.
5. Remedy Scientific: remediation automation.
6. PFAS:
   - Verisk, with Guy Carpenter, already models PFAS casualty scenarios.
   - Moody's/Praedicat models PFAS from the scientific literature.
   - Milliman does reserving.
   - Langan and other big consultancies sell PFAS forensic source attribution as a service.
7. Lead lines: BlueConduit owns ML lead-line prediction.
8. Data management: EarthSoft EQuIS and ESdat already ingest GeoTracker EDF.
9. Academic work exists: NCSU 2024 ML for groundwater risk, older LLNL LUFT plume studies on California data, and a patent on forecasting soil and groundwater contamination migration (US 11631022).
deep.product:
Sharpest version: a pollution-legal-liability (PLL) underwriting and pricing engine for environmental insurers and MGAs.
- Input: an address or a portfolio of addresses.
- Output: the probability of a reportable release, the expected cleanup cost and duration, and the tail.
- Training data: GeoTracker cases, labelled with outcomes (time to closure, number of wells, peak concentrations), joined with historical land use (Sanborn maps, business directories) and hydrogeology.
- Second product: a cost-to-close estimate for open LUST/SLIC cases, sold to remediation buyers, guaranteed-fixed-price remediation firms and state UST funds.

First paying customer: an environmental MGA or specialty carrier writing site PLL in California (Beazley, Sompo, Ironshore/Liberty, AIG, or smaller MGAs). The alternative is a fixed-price remediation and risk-transfer firm that prices cost-cap deals.

Not the lender triage score. LightBox already sells that cheaply and owns the channel.
deep.market:
Bottom-up, with unverified items flagged.
- US environmental/pollution insurance premium: about $3-5B a year. Not verified this run; WTW's 2025 outlook gave no total, only that capacity grew with at least six new or expanded markets. A pricing and analytics vendor typically captures 1-3% of premium, so roughly $50-150M a year.
- Phase I ESA spend: about 100-300k reports a year at $2-4k, so roughly $0.3-1B. Data inputs are about 10% of that, mostly captured by LightBox and ERIS (a few hundred million dollars).
- Remediation services: about $25-30B a year in the US (commonly cited, not verified). The software and data share is small unless the company takes risk itself, for example by underwriting fixed-price cleanups or becoming an MGA.
- PFAS liability: hundreds of billions, but the analytics buyers are concentrated (a few dozen insurers and reinsurers, major law firms and big defendants).

Realistic software total addressable market: $300-800M. Pure data and SaaS likely lands in the $50-150M ARR range, which is near the threshold the founder already rejected. A large outcome needs a balance-sheet or full-stack move: become an environmental MGA, or a fixed-price remediation and risk-transfer company priced by the model (a "Lemonade/Kin for pollution liability"). That path is credible but slow and capital-intensive.
deep.revolutionary_claim:
Today nobody can price the subsurface condition of an unsampled parcel. Pricing is done by proximity lookups plus a $3-50k Phase II. A model trained on 20 years of mandated, consultant-paid sampling could estimate contamination probability, concentration and cleanup cost before anyone drills. That is a real step up, the same way SMAD moved uranium exploration from guesswork to statistical targeting.

How believable: moderate.
- Petroleum/LUST cost-to-close prediction for known sites is very believable. There are rich labels, and the old LLNL work showed plume behaviour is statistically regular.
- Predicting contamination at unsampled clean parcels is much less believable, because the training data covers only sites already flagged as dirty.
- The upside on PFAS source attribution is largely speculative until the TSCA data exists, and it may be gutted.
deep.proof_idea:
One-day proof, done on a laptop because GeoTracker blocked this container.
1. Download the ESI zips for 2-3 counties (for example Santa Clara, Alameda, Los Angeles): EDF analytical, GEO_XY and site status/closure flat files.
2. Build per-site features: case type, open date, first-year max benzene/TPHg/MTBE/PCE, number of wells, depth to water, county and soil proxies (SSURGO), and nearby-site density.
3. Task A: predict time to closure and whether the site will still be open after 10 years, using an LTCP closure-policy flag. Hold out by geography and time. Report AUC and MAE against a regulator-status baseline.
4. Task B, the honest one: for wells first sampled after year T, predict whether a benzene or PCE exceedance occurs from neighbouring sites' history and land use. Hold out sites spatially, compare against a distance-to-nearest-LUST baseline (essentially what EDR's rating does), and show the lift.
- If Task B shows real lift over distance-based screening, the company has a story.
- If only Task A works, the business is cleanup economics: a smaller, cost-to-close niche.
deep.killers:
1. Selection bias. GeoTracker contains only sites already known or suspected to be contaminated. There are no negative labels for clean parcels, so the headline product ("probability of contamination at any parcel") has no ground truth. The best available is a positive-unlabelled proxy built from Phase I/II outcomes, which are not public.
2. Distribution moat belongs to the incumbent. LightBox/EDR already sells an algorithmic Environmental Risk Rating and lender screens embedded in every Phase I workflow. A startup's better score has to displace a cheap, bundled, "good-enough" standard that ASTM and lenders accept. Regulators and lenders want ASTM-compliant documented records, not ML probabilities.
3. Market size. A pure analytics vendor to environmental insurers and lenders looks like a $50-150M ARR ceiling, the size the founder already rejected. A big outcome needs an MGA or risk-bearing pivot, which is slow, regulated and capital-heavy, and the incumbent carriers (AIG, Chubb, Beazley) already have decades of their own claims data.
4. The PFAS leg is fragile:
   - TSCA 8(a)(7) has been delayed again and narrowed by the Nov 2025 proposed exemptions, and CBI will be heavy.
   - Federal PFAS drinking-water limits (MCLs) were partly rolled back or extended.
   - Verisk, Praedicat and Langan already occupy PFAS attribution. Source attribution is a forensic, expert-witness discipline: litigants pay experts, not SaaS.
5. Not national without heavy work. California is unique. Other states are mostly PDFs, so the moat is real but slow to build, and a California-only model limits insurer adoption.
6. Low insurance loss frequency. Pollution claims are rare and long-tailed, so it will take years to prove the model beats underwriter judgement.
7. Data access friction. The host blocked cloud fetches, and the document PDFs have no bulk endpoint.

deep.name: Virtual site investigation / ground-risk screening from mandated borehole and CPT archives (Dutch BRO first, then BGS, NZGD, US DOT and well logs)
deep.legal_basis_verified: PARTLY VERIFIED, and weaker than the pitch says. (1) Netherlands, Wet basisregistratie ondergrond (2018, phased in under Besluit BRO, Stb 2019-292): this is the only genuinely forced-disclosure regime in the bundle. Government bodies (Rijkswaterstaat, provinces, municipalities, water boards) must register the CPTs and geotechnical boreholes they commission. The data is public: PDOK publishes it as an open ATOM and WMS dataset, and data.overheid.nl lists it as INSPIRE-harmonised. Important limit: private-client CPTs (most commercial building, data-centre and housing sites) are NOT required to go into BRO. The registry is biased toward public-works sites. (2) UK: Mining Industry Act 1926 s.23 only covers boreholes deeper than 30 m that search for or extract minerals. Ordinary shallow geotechnical site-investigation holes are NOT legally required to be deposited; they reach BGS voluntarily or through public clients. The SOBI index (over 1M records, back to 1790) is under the Open Government Licence. The scanned logs are 'freely available' only one at a time, and the BGS page does not say the OGL covers the scans. Copyright in the scans may stay with the depositors. (3) NZGD: a sharing scheme backed by councils and EQC/Toka Tū Ake after the Christchurch earthquakes. Access needs registration and comes with terms of use; it is not open data. (4) US state DOT boring logs are public records under freedom-of-information or public-records law, not a disclosure mandate, and their formats are scattered. State water-well completion reports (e.g. CA Water Code 13752) are genuinely mandated, but DrillerDB already works that data. Net: the 'law forces private data public' quirk really holds only for NL, and even there mostly for publicly commissioned work.
deep.data_access: NL BRO CPT: PDOK runs an ATOM download service ('BRO Geotechnisch sondeeronderzoek (CPT) ATOM'). From prior knowledge, not re-verified this session: there is a complete-set zip and the licence is public domain/CC0. There is also a public REST API (publiek.broservices.nl/sr/cpt/v1) and the Python package 'brodata' (ConePenetrationTest.from_bro_id), which fetches one CPT at a time as XML. The same ATOM/API pattern covers BHR-GT geotechnical boreholes. Record count: my estimate is a few hundred thousand CPTs including older DINO data; no source I checked stated a count. Format is structured XML/GEF holding full qc/fs/u2 depth profiles, which is excellent ML-ready data. Cost: free. Can the proof run this week? Yes, from a normal machine. NOTE: this cloud container's proxy returned 403 on service.pdok.nl and publiek.broservices.nl, so it would have to run from a laptop or a VM with open egress, or after the hosts are allowlisted. UK BGS: the SOBI index is a free bulk download (OGL). Scans of the 1M+ logs can only be viewed one at a time, there is no bulk endpoint, and pulling them at scale means scraping with an unclear licence. NZGD: free registration, terms-gated, and redistribution and commercial use restricted. US: DOT logs are mostly scanned PDFs on per-state portals, and a national corpus would take months of scraping and OCR. Cleanest proof dataset: BRO CPT plus TNO GeoTOP voxels plus AHN lidar elevation, all open Dutch data.
deep.competitors: More crowded than the candidate claims. (1) Fugro GroundIQ: an internal venture positioned as a 'next-generation platform that fuses geophysical data, geotechnical insights and AI' into 3D ground models. It has a 16-person engineering team across NL, US and France, publishes case studies on hyperscale data-centre and hydrogen-plant ground risk, launched in Australia in 2026, and states an ambition of more than EUR 100M in sales. Fugro also holds the world's largest private GI archive. This is the most direct threat. (2) Bentley/Seequent (Leapfrog, OpenGround/Keynetix HoleBASE): owns the borehole-data and ground-model workflow that engineers already use, markets directly on 'unforeseen site conditions', and could add an ML prior on public data as a feature. (3) EMerald Geomodelling (Norway, NGI spinout, 2019, Cemex Ventures-linked): ML 3D ground models from airborne EM plus sparse geotechnical data for road and rail; claims USD 25M saved and 30% less drilling for Nye Veier. (4) VIKTOR.ai (NL): BRO CPT visualisation apps, and since May 2026 AI agents that extract borehole logs and size footings. (5) GroundedAI (Vancouver, ~CAD 2M, July 2026): tunnelling ground-risk system of record. (6) Terra AI (Khosla, $20M Series A): subsurface AI, mostly resources. (7) DrillerDB: AI geology estimator built on US water-well logs, predicts depth to water by address. (8) Desk-study vendors Groundsure, Landmark, LightBox/EDR and ERIS already resell BGS and environmental data into pre-acquisition reports. (9) TNO/Deltares publish GeoTOP/REGIS 3D models free, which already sets an NL baseline. (10) Academic work at TU Delft, Deltares, Leeds and CityU HK on ML CPT interpolation and borehole planning. No funded startup sells a cross-jurisdiction 'predicted ground profile for any parcel' built from public archives, but Fugro GroundIQ plus Seequent cover the high-value customers (data centres, infrastructure) from a position of owning the data and the workflow.
deep.product: The sharpest version: a 'Ground Screen' API and report for data-centre, battery and solar site selectors that ranks candidate parcels before land is optioned. Per parcel it gives probabilistic depth to bearing layer or rock, a pile-length and foundation-cost range, groundwater, soft-layer and liquefaction flags, and a recommended placement for 2-5 CPTs that most reduce uncertainty. First paying customer: site-selection teams at hyperscalers and colo developers, or utility-scale renewables developers screening dozens of parcels per project. Their real alternative today is a $5-50k desk study plus a GI campaign per shortlisted site. A more realistic first customer in NL is an engineering consultancy or contractor bidding on design-and-construct tenders, who wants an instant ground prior for pricing. The insurance or guarantee wrapper is a phase-3 fantasy: it needs carrier capacity and a multi-year loss history.
deep.market: Bottom-up. (a) Pre-acquisition screening: a few thousand data-centre sites screened per year globally, plus ~10-30k utility-scale solar, wind and BESS parcels, plus large logistics and housing schemes. That is about 20-50k screens a year at $5-20k each, or roughly $150-700M a year if you captured the entire category, which is unrealistic. Desk-study incumbents (Groundsure-type reports) sell for hundreds to low thousands of pounds, which anchors prices low. (b) Geotechnical investigation services: market reports put geotechnical services at ~$20-34B by 2032 (einpresswire, a low-quality source), and investigation-only spend is lower, a single-digit $B. Software that reduces GI spend by 20-30% competes against the firms that are both the buyers and the gatekeepers (Fugro and others). (c) The size of the pain is real: National Academies work on highway projects ties a large share of overruns to subsurface conditions, and Seequent and Hoek document unforeseen ground as a leading cause of claims. But the money sits with contractors' risk budgets and insurers, and a software startup cannot reach it without taking on risk. Honest view: a SaaS or screening company in the $100-300M range, which is close to the size the founder already rejected. Only a risk-bearing model (guaranteed pile lengths or ground-risk insurance) reaches $1B+, and that is a capital- and track-record-heavy path that is hard to start pre-seed.
deep.revolutionary_claim: Claim: a geotechnical prior for any parcel, before anyone drills, with calibrated uncertainty, plus active-learning GI placement that cuts the number of holes needed. Believability: moderate where data is dense (NL deltaic soils with roughly a CPT every few hundred metres in urban areas, where kriging plus GeoTOP already does reasonably well, so the ML gain is incremental), and low where customers actually build (rural greenfield US data-centre and solar sites in TX, VA, OH and AZ, where public CPTs are sparse and the geology is residual soils, glacial till and bedrock that the Dutch data does not teach). Building codes (Eurocode 7, IBC ch.18) still require site-specific investigation, so the product changes the timing and amount of SI, not whether it happens. This is a useful step change in workflow, not a revolutionary one.
deep.proof_idea: One day, on a laptop with open egress (this container's proxy blocks PDOK and BRO): 1) Download the BRO CPT complete set via the PDOK ATOM feed, or loop the BRO REST API or the brodata package over a ~30x30 km box (e.g. Rotterdam-Delft or Utrecht). Also pull GeoTOP voxels (TNO/DINOloket) and AHN4 surface elevation. 2) Parse qc, fs and Rf at 0.2 m intervals and derive Robertson SBT and depth to the first sand layer with qc > 10-15 MPa over 1 m (a proxy for the Pleistocene pile-bearing layer). 3) Spatially blocked CV: hold out 1x1 km blocks with a 250 m buffer. 4) Baselines: nearest-neighbour CPT, ordinary kriging of bearing depth, and GeoTOP lithoclass lookup. Model: a gradient-boosted model or a small transformer conditioned on the k nearest CPT profiles plus GeoTOP column, elevation and distance. 5) Metrics: MAE of bearing-layer depth, the implied pile-length error in metres (and euros at ~EUR 30-60 per m of pile), and calibration of 80% intervals. 6) Active-learning test: given 3 sampled CPTs in a held-out block, choose the next 2 by maximum posterior variance vs a grid, and measure the error reduction. Kill criterion: if the model cannot beat kriging plus GeoTOP by more than 20% on bearing-depth MAE, the 'foundation model' adds little over what TNO already gives away free.
deep.killers: 1) Fugro GroundIQ is already building this exact thing (AI ground models for hyperscale data centres, a EUR 100M+ ambition). Fugro owns the largest private GI archive and the customer relationships, and Seequent/Bentley owns the engineer's workflow. A startup's edge is only public data, which incumbents can also use. 2) The forced-disclosure quirk is thin: only Dutch BRO is truly mandated, and only for public-commissioned work. The BGS s.23 duty covers mineral boreholes over 30 m, not geotechnical SI. NZGD is terms-gated, and BGS scans have no bulk access and unclear copyright. 3) Geographic mismatch: the clean data is in NL, where land is scarce and the market is small, and where kriging plus free TNO GeoTOP already exists. The demand (US data centres and solar) sits on sparse, messy, heterogeneous geology where the model is weakest. Transfer from Holocene deltaic soils to US residual and glacial soils is unproven. 4) Liability and code: engineers must still do site-specific SI and will not sign off on a prior. The product is decision support with low willingness to pay, anchored by £100-£1k desk-study reports. 5) Market ceiling: realistic screening SaaS is ~$100-300M, near the size the founder rejected. The $1B path needs balance-sheet ground-risk insurance, which needs carrier partners, loss data and years of track record. 6) Gatekeeper conflict: the GI contractors and consultancies whose spend you reduce are both the data generators and the channel. 7) Unlike SMAD (where companies spent millions on exploration whose results are now free and directly monetisable to the next explorer), BRO CPTs are cheap (~EUR 500-2k each), so re-drilling is cheap. The public archive does not replace an expensive asset, which weakens the core Terranox-like arbitrage.

deep.name: AI regulatory reviewer on forced-public regulator dossiers (EMA Policy 0070, Health Canada PRCI, FDA CRLs and reviews, EU CTIS RFIs)
deep.legal_basis_verified: Mixed, and fatal for two of the four sources. (1) Health Canada PRCI: the Food and Drugs Act s.30(1.2)(d.1/d.2) and the 2019 FDR/MDR amendments make clinical information non-CBI once a decision is made. However, the portal terms I read today (clinical-information.canada.ca/ci-rc/terms) say access is "solely for non-commercial purposes" (s.2(b)). They also say use "expressly excludes the use of the information to support a marketing authorization application anywhere in the world" (s.3.2), and that copies may not be given to anyone without an undertaking (s.3.4). That s.3.2 clause describes the product's core use, a pre-submission reviewer. (2) EMA Policy 0070: publication is real. It resumed for new-active-substance opinions from Sept 2023, and EMA's page (last modified Jan 2024) says Step 2 expansion was planned from April 2025, not confirmed done. Access is by EMA account login, as on-screen view or download "subject to terms of use". From memory, not re-fetched: the download terms limit use to academic/non-commercial research and bar use to support an MAA, the same structure as Health Canada. Treat it as restricted. (3) FDA CRLs: real and unrestricted US government works. The openFDA endpoint api.fda.gov/transparency/crl.json returned 458 records today (meta last_updated 2026-08-13), with full letter text and fields (company_name, application_number, letter_date, approval_status, letter_type, approver_center, text). Release rests on Commissioner discretion. Per prior notes it was paused in April 2026, resumed July 2026, and a rule codifying it is pending. That is not a statute, so it is reversible. Drugs@FDA review packages (FDAAA) are also unrestricted. (4) CTIS (Reg. 536/2014 Art. 81): public. I could not verify how much RFI and assessment text survives the 2024 transparency-rule revision because the search budget ran out. Prior notes flag that RFIs and assessment reports are now published only at decision or are deferred.
deep.data_access: FDA CRLs: api.fda.gov/transparency/crl.json (verified today: 458 records, full text in JSON) plus a bulk zip via open.fda.gov/data/downloads. It is free and public domain. Note that this container's egress proxy blocks api.fda.gov (curl got CONNECT 403), but WebFetch reached it, so a run from a normal cloud VM works. Drugs@FDA review PDFs: free, public domain, PDF scraping needed, approved applications only. EMA clinical data (clinicaldata.ema.europa.eu): login required, per-product redacted PDFs, no bulk API, terms restrict commercial use and MAA support. Health Canada PRCI (clinical-information.canada.ca): request-and-download per product, explicit non-commercial and no-MAA-support terms. CTIS (euclinicaltrials.eu): public portal, weak API, 24 languages, RFI coverage unverified. Volume: about 458 CRLs, a few thousand FDA review packages, and EMA plus Health Canada together at most a few hundred product dossiers. The 'paired' claim is weak. FDA does not publish the submission behind a CRL. EMA/HC publish submissions but not the Day-120 List of Questions or the actual objections; EPARs and withdrawal assessment reports only summarise major objections. Truly paired submission-and-objection data barely exists in any one jurisdiction. A proof can run this week, but only on the FDA side (CRLs plus Drugs@FDA plus ClinicalTrials.gov plus 483s).
deep.competitors: Crowded at the product layer. Regulatory writing and submission AI: Weave Bio ($20M Series A Oct 2025; $10M in 2024; Takeda deploying across 14 programs), Ritivel (YC W26; drafts CTD/CSR/IND/BLA from the sponsor's own data), Enjamb (YC; agents claimed to build FDA submission packages in 48h), Yseop, Certara CoAuthor, Formation Bio, Instem, Medidata (AI submission risk), and Veeva/IQVIA LLM features. Approval-probability prediction: GlobalData's ML 'Likelihood of Approval' model (Sept 2025, claims 85.4% accuracy, 24 years of data), plus Evaluate, Citeline/Norstella BioMedTracker, and Intelligencia AI. Regulatory intelligence over FDA/EMA documents: Redica Systems (inspection/483/warning-letter intelligence sold to big pharma; anticipates inspection and enforcement risk), Clarivate Cortellis Regulatory Intelligence, and AgencyIQ. Vivpro and Freyr's HA-query-management AI are from memory, not verified this session. A CleverX case study claims expert-trained AI cut a specialty-pharma NDA timeline by 4 months. I found nobody explicitly marketing a model trained on the cross-sponsor PRCI/Policy 0070 corpus. The likely reason is that its terms forbid it, not that nobody noticed.
deep.product: The sharpest version that survives the legal problem: an FDA-only 'CRL risk radar'. It would be trained on public-domain CRLs, Drugs@FDA reviews, 483s/warning letters (facility history) and ClinicalTrials.gov results. It flags likely deficiency categories (CMC/facility, clinical efficacy, safety, statistical, labeling) for a pending NDA/BLA. The first paying customer is a small or mid-cap biotech heading into its first NDA/BLA with no in-house institutional memory of FDA questions (big pharma already holds thousands of its own HA questions internally). A second customer is a biotech event-driven fund ahead of PDUFA dates. Both are thin. The best mid-size-company version is probably a feature inside an existing writing platform (Weave, Ritivel) rather than a standalone company.
deep.market: Bottom-up: about 50-60 novel FDA approvals per year plus about 100-150 other NDA/BLA original and efficacy filings. Call it 150-250 high-stakes US submissions per year. At $100-300k per submission for a pre-filing risk review (a consultant mock review costs that much), that is about $15-75M/yr in the US. Adding the EU and Canada roughly doubles it, about $30-150M. Biotech hedge-fund alt-data: perhaps 50-150 specialist funds at $50-250k each, about $5-30M. The direct market is about $50-200M/yr, the size Dhruv already rejected. The $7-8B regulatory-affairs-outsourcing and $4-5B medical-writing figures (unverified analyst estimates) are reachable only by becoming the general regulatory-writing platform. That is the Weave/Ritivel/Certara/Veeva race, where this dataset adds no proprietary edge.
deep.revolutionary_claim: Claim: a machine that tells a sponsor what FDA or EMA will object to before filing, avoiding 6-18 month CRL delays. Believability is low to moderate. (a) Most CRLs cite CMC/facility problems, which the clinical CSR corpus cannot predict, and facility signals (483s) are already productised by Redica. (b) The label set is about 458 CRLs with no matching submission text, so models learn base rates by division and modality, not dossier-specific deficiencies. (c) Big sponsors hold far richer private paired data (their own HA queries and responses) than the public corpus. Incremental, not revolutionary.
deep.proof_idea: Day-long proof, FDA only. Pull all 458 CRL texts from api.fda.gov/transparency/crl.json (or the bulk zip). LLM-label each letter with a deficiency taxonomy (CMC/facility, clinical efficacy, safety, statistics, bioequivalence, labeling, device/combination). Join on application_number to Drugs@FDA (application type, division, later approval and time to approval). Join to ClinicalTrials.gov (pivotal trial count, endpoint type, enrollment), and via FEI/sponsor name to FDA 483 and warning-letter data. Train a gradient-boosted model on pre-letter features only, split by time (train before 2023, test 2023-2025), to predict deficiency category and resubmission-approval time. Compare against a division-by-modality base-rate baseline. If it cannot clearly beat the base rate (likely, given n≈458), the thesis is dead cheaply. A second test: check whether the CRL text adds anything beyond what sponsors already disclosed in press releases (the FDA Law Blog found most of the 2025 batch already public).
deep.killers: 1) Legal. Health Canada's terms, verified today, explicitly forbid commercial use and any use 'to support a marketing authorization application anywhere in the world', which is exactly the product. EMA's download terms appear to match (from memory). Two of the four 'unique' sources are therefore unusable for a commercial model without a contract with the regulator. 2) The 'paired corpus' is mostly a myth. FDA publishes the rejection but not the submission, and EMA/HC publish the submission but not the question lists. Real pairs are sparse summaries (EPAR major objections, withdrawal assessment reports). 3) It is tiny: about 458 CRLs and a few hundred dossiers. That is easy to copy, and incumbents (GlobalData, Evaluate, Citeline, Redica, Cortellis) can add CRL fields in a quarter. 4) Policy fragility: CRL publication is discretionary, already paused once in April 2026, and the codifying rule is still only proposed. 5) Crowding: regulatory-writing AI is a hot funded category (Weave $30M total, Ritivel YC W26, Enjamb YC, Certara, Yseop, Veeva, IQVIA). The public corpus is not a moat against them, and they hold customers' private HA-query history, which is better training data. 6) The standalone market is about $50-200M/yr, under Dhruv's threshold. 7) Most CRLs are driven by CMC/facility issues, which clinical-dossier text cannot predict.

deep.name: Private-credit marking oracle from NAIC statutory filings (Schedule D/BA)
deep.legal_basis_verified:
Partly verified. State insurance codes, based on the NAIC model laws, require statutory annual and quarterly statements. Schedule D Part 1 (year-end long-term bond holdings) lists each holding with CUSIP or PPN identifier, description, NAIC designation, actual cost, fair value, the method used to get fair value, par value, book/adjusted carrying value, and acquisition date. The NAIC's own product page confirms that CUSIP, description, NAIC designation, fair, statement, book and par value are in its Schedule D/DA/DB data product. The filings are public records at the state level. The NAIC's compiled bulk data, however, is sold under a license agreement: the financial products page says delivery follows "the execution of a license agreement" and payment of an invoice. So the law makes the data public, but the law does not make it free or redistributable in bulk.

A new disclosure helps the thesis. NAIC item 2025-19 takes effect 31 Dec 2026 and requires insurers to report private placements backed only by a private letter rating, with fair value and book value (FactSet). The first such filings arrive around March 2027.

Important caveats:
- The full line-by-line holdings appear only at year-end. Quarterly statements mostly show acquisitions and disposals (Schedule D Parts 3 and 4), so each instrument gets roughly one mark per insurer per year.
- Schedule BA shows fund and LP interests, not the loans inside them.
- Many private placements are carried at amortized cost, and their "fair value" usually comes from the same few pricing vendors or the asset manager's own matrix model, so the cross-insurer labels are not independent.
deep.data_access:
Free bulk access does not exist, which I checked on the NAIC's own pages:
- **InsData:** individual PDF statements of more than 4,800 insurers, bought one at a time, up to 10 years back.
- **Bulk CSV:** quote-based, through idp@naic.org with a data request form, under a license agreement, delivered within about two weeks of payment.
- **Schedule D/DA/DB detail product:** sold separately. Prices are not posted; from my background knowledge, a full multi-year detail feed typically runs tens of thousands of dollars a year, but I could not confirm that.
- **Redistributors:** the NAIC has a licensed-redistributor program, but the page gives no terms.
- **Commercial alternatives:** S&P Capital IQ Pro (formerly SNL) and AM Best already sell parsed holdings searchable by CUSIP across insurers. Seats cost about $25-60k or more a year, from background knowledge.
- **Free scraps:** some insurers post their statutory statements on their own websites as PDFs, and some state departments supply PDFs on request.

**Volume:** roughly 800 life and 2,500+ P&C companies, with millions of holding lines a year.

**Can a proof run this week from a cloud container on the actual NAIC data?** No, because it needs a paid license and the two-week delivery. A weak proxy is possible: scrape 20-50 insurers' self-posted statement PDFs and parse Schedule D Part 1. A stronger free proxy is the same idea on SEC data. Business development companies (BDCs, the listed private-credit funds) must publish schedules of investments in inline XBRL every quarter on EDGAR, with fair value per loan, and the same loans recur across many BDCs. That data is free, quarterly and available today, but it is also already mined by competitors (see below).
deep.competitors:
This space is crowded.

**Already use the cross-insurer CUSIP view as a product:**
- **S&P Global Market Intelligence:** Capital IQ Pro shows every insurer holding a given CUSIP/PPN, with book and fair value. It also publishes regular private-credit analyses of the NAIC data.
- **AM Best:** statutory data products.
- **NAIC Capital Markets Bureau and SVO:** see all filings and can build exactly this oracle for regulatory use. The NAIC president's agenda for summer 2026 names private credit and AI.
- **FactSet:** aggregates insurer private-security data.
- **Clearwater Analytics:** a public company of roughly $450M+ in revenue that does accounting and NAIC reporting for most US insurers. It sees client holdings and the prices used before filing, which is a better, real-time version of the same cross-holder view.

**Private-credit pricing and valuation incumbents:**
- Bloomberg BVAL.
- ICE Data Services.
- JPMorgan PricingDirect.
- Solve.
- Houlihan Lokey (portfolio valuation).
- Lincoln International (private market valuations, which already publishes a private-credit marking index).
- Kroll and KBRA (KBRA does private letter ratings and the DLD direct-lending database).
- Egan-Jones.
- Fitch Solutions and PitchBook LCD.
- Octus and 9fin, which track BDC marks loan by loan.

**Venture-backed startups:**
- **73 Strings:** AI valuation and monitoring for private markets. It raised about $55M, including from Blackstone, Fidelity and Golub, from background knowledge.
- **CredCore:** private debt analytics, raised $16M in 2025 (Axios).
- **Cardo AI:** private credit data infrastructure.
- **Empirasign:** already licenses NAIC insurer transaction data (price, par, date, counterparty) and matches it with N-PORT fund holdings in a searchable private-credit report, linking borrowers by LEI.

**What nobody appears to sell:** an explicit ML model that treats cross-insurer mark dispersion as noisy labels. That is a feature gap, not a white space.
deep.product:
The sharpest version is not a "BVAL for private credit". Incumbents own that, and an ML black box will not pass ASC 820 audits. The sharper wedge is a regulatory and surveillance analytics tool for private-credit exposure on insurer balance sheets:
1. For each private placement or PPN, show the cross-holder distribution of fair value and NAIC designation.
2. Flag outlier marks and suspected rating-shopping on private letter ratings (PLRs). From YE2026, item 2025-19 makes PLR-only placements visible, and the tool would match them against KBRA, Egan-Jones and SVO designations.
3. Score each insurer's "mark aggressiveness".

First paying customer type, in order of willingness:
- Reinsurers and sidecar investors doing due diligence on Bermuda/offshore reinsurance deals with private-equity-backed life insurers.
- Short sellers and hedge funds covering PE-owned insurers such as Athene/Apollo, Global Atlantic/KKR and F&G.
- State regulators and the NAIC, who buy slowly and in small amounts.

Asset managers selling to insurers would be hostile, because the tool exposes their marks.
deep.market:
Bottom-up, the market is small. These figures are my own estimates, from background knowledge rather than sources fetched in this run:

| Buyer | Count | Price per year | Total per year |
|---|---|---|---|
| Life and P&C insurers that would pay for peer-mark analytics | about 150 | $50-150k | $10-20M |
| Reinsurers, sidecar capital, rating agencies and banks doing NAV lending | about 100 | $100k | about $10M |
| Hedge funds and short sellers | about 50 | $100-200k | about $5-10M |
| Regulators | 50 states plus the NAIC | small | small |

Total addressable market for this data product: roughly $30-60M a year, which is below the $100-200M floor the founder already rejected.

The large pools are evaluated pricing (ICE and Bloomberg pricing and reference data, about $2-3B) and independent private valuation (Houlihan, Lincoln and Kroll portfolio valuation, roughly $1B or more). Winning those requires becoming the audited mark of record from transaction and lender data, which NAIC filings alone cannot supply: they give one stale mark per insurer per year. Private credit AUM is about $1.7-2T, and private investments are 38.7% of insurer corporate bond holdings (FactSet).

A path to a large company exists only if this becomes a full private-credit pricing and ratings vendor competing with Solve, Bloomberg, KBRA and 73 Strings. The NAIC data would be one input, not the moat.
deep.revolutionary_claim:
The claim is a third-party fair value and shadow rating for otherwise unpriced private placements, built from many holders' disclosed marks. It is only moderately believable, for three reasons:
1. The labels are stale. There is one year-end mark per holder, filed about two months later.
2. The labels are correlated. Most holders source marks from the same vendor or the originating manager's matrix model, and club deals are often allocated by a single manager (for example Apollo/Athene) across affiliated insurers that use identical marks.
3. Coverage is partial. Fund-wrapped (BA) and SPV/rated-note structures hide the underlying loans.

The genuinely new part is surveillance of private-letter-rating inflation once the 2025-19 disclosures land in 2027. That is a useful regulatory analytics feature, not a revolution.
deep.proof_idea:
A one-day proof on free data uses SEC BDC filings as the proxy, because NAIC bulk data needs a paid license.
1. Pull inline-XBRL schedules of investments for about 50 BDCs for 8 quarters from EDGAR.
2. Entity-resolve identical loans across BDCs by borrower name, facility, spread and maturity.
3. Measure the cross-holder dispersion of fair value as a percentage of par.
4. Test whether a model on dispersion plus borrower features predicts the next quarter's non-accruals or markdowns better than the median mark.

In parallel, parse Schedule D Part 1 from 10-20 insurer statutory PDFs that insurers post on their own sites. Count how many PPNs appear at two or more insurers, and how often the fair values are identical, which would show whether the labels are non-independent.

The kill test: if more than about 70% of multi-holder privates show identical marks, or the marks come from a single manager's affiliates, the noisy-label premise fails.
deep.killers:
1. **Not free bulk data.** NAIC compiled data is licensed and paid. Redistribution and derived-product rights must be negotiated, and the NAIC can refuse or price out a would-be competitor to its own analytics.
2. **Incumbents already show the cross-insurer CUSIP view.** S&P Capital IQ Pro and AM Best do, and Clearwater sees pre-filing prices across most US insurers in real time. Any of them can add a dispersion and outlier model as a feature.
3. **The labels are stale and correlated.** Full holdings come once a year. Fair values are often vendor or manager matrix prices, the same deals sit with affiliates under the same manager, and amortized-cost carrying values make the "noisy label" signal mostly noise.
4. **Hard identification.** PPN coverage is incomplete, BA fund wrappers and rated-feeder structures hide the underlying assets, and entity resolution only gets you to the instrument, not to borrower fundamentals.
